meta.title: JEREBU.EXE haze history: transboundary haze episodes affecting Malaysia and Singapore, 1997–2026
meta.description: Major transboundary haze episodes affecting Malaysia, Singapore or both, with legal, policy and other milestones, compiled from public sources. Every claim links to the source passage it rests on.

selectionCriteria.note: Written by the AI agent before any research result was read, while the first research workflow was still running. An episode is included when criterion A and at least one of B1, B2 or B3 are met by evidence opened during the research. An AI proposal awaiting human review.

definitions.text: Smoke haze from vegetation and/or peatland fires affected Malaysia and/or Singapore in the period, and an official body, intergovernmental body, scientific agency or peer-reviewed study describes the haze as transboundary (originating at least partly outside the affected country) — or, failing those, at least two independent reputable news reports citing officials say so.

Officially reported air quality in the "unhealthy" band or worse (Singapore PSI above 100; Malaysia API above 100), on more than one day or at more than one monitoring location, reported by the responsible agency or by reputable reporting citing it.
Extraordinary public measures attributed to the haze: an emergency declaration, school closures, or official advice to reduce outdoor activity beyond routine forecasts.
The episode is described as major, severe or among the worst in peer-reviewed literature or an official retrospective.

confidenceMethod.question: How well does the evidence opened in this session support the core account of this episode — that it happened, roughly when, and that it affected Malaysia and/or Singapore as described?
confidenceMethod.note: Written by the AI agent before any research result was read, at the same time as the selection criteria, and quoted here as written. Confidence describes the evidence for the record as compiled, not the severity of the episode. It is an AI-assigned rating awaiting human review, and it never replaces sources. After the final review, the ratings were re-applied literally: where any condition of the medium definition holds, an episode is rated medium, not high.

definitions.text: The core account is supported by at least one government, legal, intergovernmental, scientific-agency or peer-reviewed source AND corroborated by at least one independent source; key figures are quoted from primary or peer-reviewed sources; no unresolved material conflict about the core account.

Credible evidence supports the core account, but important elements (impact in one country, peak readings, the period) rest on a single source, on news reporting only, or are incomplete; or minor conflicts remain.
The core account rests on a single source or on reporting only, or sources materially disagree, or key elements could not be verified.

meta.compiledBy: Claude Code, an AI coding agent made by Anthropic (model: Claude Opus 5.5), with AI research and verification sub-agents, during Experiment 002
notes: AI GENERATED + SOURCE ATTACHED. No human has checked or verified this dataset yet. Do not treat it as established fact until a named person has verified it.

Every claim has at least one source reference with the exact passage relied on. A check of "verbatim" means the passage was matched by script against the text downloaded from the source on the accessed date; "not-machine-checked" means it was read through a page-reading tool and could not be matched by script.
Quoted passages remain the copyright of their publishers. They are short excerpts included so that each claim can be checked.

Air-quality readings are recorded as each source published them. Some figures, labelled analysis, were worked out by the AI agent from an agency's published data, such as the highest 24-hour PSI in a year; their notes say how. Malaysia's API and Singapore's PSI are different indices, and both changed during the study period. Do not compare readings across indices or years without accounting for this.
No company or individual is named as responsible for any fire or haze. Legal outcomes are recorded without party names pending human review (docs/METHODOLOGY.md, section 8).
An absent year or field means no evidence meeting the criteria was found in the sources searched. It is not evidence that nothing happened.

events.title: July–November 1997: Sarawak, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and the wider region

period.label: July–November 1997

refs.quote: From July to October 1997, ASEAN countries in particular Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore, were badly affected by smoke haze caused by land and forest fires.

From late July to the beginning of October 1997, countries of Southeast Asia experienced severe smoke haze pollution from uncontrolled forest fires mainly in the Indonesian states of Kalimantan and Sumatra. In Singapore, the impact of the 1997 haze was felt in the period from the end of August to the first week of November 1997 as a result of prevailing winds.
Occurred during September to November 1997.
The air quality returned to normal in November coinciding with the monsoon season.
the haze only made it to the front page of ... on 23 August 1997. The Pollutants Standard Index (PSI) levels stayed at 91 for three hours that day.
refs.pinpoint: Chapter 4 (Singapore), opening section (a newspaper's name is elided)

refs.quote: By early November, the air-quality had improved significantly. On 22 November the Ministry of the Environment declared the haze over

period.note: Sources date the episode differently by place: ASEAN environment ministers give July–October 1997 for the region; a study by a Singapore Ministry of Health author gives late July to early October for the region and end-August to the first week of November for Singapore; Malaysia's Department of Environment gives September–November 1997; a WHO summary of Malaysia's country report gives August–October. According to the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Singapore chapter), Singapore's Ministry of the Environment declared the haze over on 22 November 1997. The start (July) and end (November) months are the AI agent's reading of these sources. The separate February–April 1998 haze in northern Borneo is not included in this entry.

summary.text: The Regional Haze Action Plan adopted by ASEAN environment ministers in December 1997 states that from July to October 1997 Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore were badly affected by smoke haze from land and forest fires, and that the Philippines and Thailand were affected to a lesser degree.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: From July to October 1997, ASEAN countries in particular Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore, were badly affected by smoke haze caused by land and forest fires. The Philippines and Thailand were affected to a lesser degree.
Adopted in Singapore on 23 December 1997
In light of the latest haze experience, the ASEAN Environment Ministers have agreed on this Regional Haze Action Plan

summary.note: An intergovernmental assessment of which countries were affected, and how badly, by smoke haze from land and forest fires, so it is labelled analysis; the plan's adoption is recorded under Response between governments. Read from an unofficial text published by the NUS Centre for International Law.

summary.text: Malaysia's Department of Environment dates the 1997 episode in Malaysia to September–November 1997 and states that it was caused not only by external sources that exacerbated the contribution from internal sources but also coincided with El Niño, which prolonged the dry season that year.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Occurred during September to November 1997. It was caused not only by external sources that exacerbated the contribution from internal sources but also coincided with the El Nino, which prolonged the dry season in that year.

summary.note: The agency's own assessment of origin; the chronology does not name the external sources.

summary.text: Singapore's environment ministry stated in 2014 that Singapore had been affected by recurrent haze from land and forest fires in Indonesia since 1991, and listed 1997 among the years in which the haze was 'particularly severe'.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Singapore has been affected by recurrent haze resulting from land/forest fires in Indonesia since 1991. In 1994, 1997, 2006, 2010, and 2013, the haze was particularly severe.

summary.note: Official retrospective statement by the ministry; a statement of where the haze came from, attributed to the ministry.

summary.text: A peer-reviewed study by a Singapore Ministry of Health author states that from late July to the beginning of October 1997 countries of Southeast Asia experienced severe smoke haze pollution from uncontrolled forest fires mainly in Kalimantan and Sumatra, and that in Singapore the impact was felt from the end of August to the first week of November 1997 because of the prevailing winds.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: From late July to the beginning of October 1997, countries of Southeast Asia experienced severe smoke haze pollution from uncontrolled forest fires mainly in the Indonesian states of Kalimantan and Sumatra. In Singapore, the impact of the 1997 haze was felt in the period from the end of August to the first week of November 1997 as a result of prevailing winds.

impact.text: During the ten-day state of emergency in Sarawak (19–28 September 1997), only essential activities such as food retailing, electricity and water provision and law enforcement were allowed to operate, according to the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Malaysia chapter).
impact.label: fact

refs.quote: When the Air Pollution Index (API) reached 500, a ten-day state of emergency was declared in Sarawak (19–28 September). During this period, only essential activities, such as food retailing, electricity and water provision, and law enforcement were allowed to operate.
Cost of Wage Loss during the State of Emergency in Sarawak Arising from the August–October Haze in 1997 Compared with the Same Period in 1996

impact.text: Schools, businesses and Kuching airport in Sarawak were closed during the 1997 haze, according to a 2021 newspaper retrospective.
impact.label: fact

refs.quote: SARAWAK was hit by one of the worst haze episodes in the country in 1997. Schools, businesses and the Kuching airport were forced to close as smoke from forest and peat fires in the region blanketed the state.
refs.pinpoint: Paragraphs 1–2 (only the opening paragraphs are visible without a subscription)

impact.note: The retrospective does not give closure dates or numbers of schools. The contemporaneous 29 September 1997 report cited under Malaysia: Government response says schools and businesses are closed under a haze emergency.

impact.text: The 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Malaysia chapter) estimated the value of haze damage to Malaysia from August to October 1997 at RM802 million (US$321 million).
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: The estimated value of the haze damage to Malaysia from August to October 1997 is RM802 million or US$321 million
refs.pinpoint: Chapter 3 (Malaysia), section 'The aggregate value of the haze' and Table 3.17

impact.note: Economic valuation, not a measured loss. Per the study's Table 3.17, the largest components are productivity losses during the Sarawak state of emergency and the decline in tourist arrivals; it also counts cost of illness, flight cancellations, fish landings, fire-fighting, cloud seeding and masks. Other versions of the estimate differ (see Where sources disagree).

airQuality.text: Malaysia's Department of Environment records that air quality worsened at several places in Sarawak and that the Air Pollutant Index (API; averaging period not stated) reached above the 500 level, the point at which a haze emergency was declared.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: The air quality worsened at several places in Sarawak to such an extent that between 19 September to 28 September (10 days), a Haze Emergency had to be declared in Sarawak when the Air Pollutant Index (API) reached above the 500 level.

airQuality.note: Malaysia's API in 1997 (averaging period not stated in the source); not comparable with Singapore's PSI. The chronology names no station and gives no peak value. Not counted as criterion B1 evidence: the passage reports that the API reached above 500 and that air quality worsened at several places, but does not say at how many stations or on how many days the API was above 100. The emergency it describes is counted under B2 (see Malaysia: Government response).

airQuality.text: A summary of Malaysia's country report to a WHO workshop held in Kuala Lumpur in June 1998 states that the 1997 haze occurred between August and October, with the highest Air Pollutant Index (API) of 850 observed in Kuching, Sarawak (date and averaging period not stated).
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: The 1997 haze occurred between August and October with the highest Air Pollution Index (API) of 850 observed in Kuching, Sarawak.
refs.pinpoint: Annex, Summary of Country Reports: Malaysia (PDF p. 195)

refs.quote: WHO BI-REGIONAL WORKSHOP ON HEALTH IMPACTS OF HAZE-RELATED AIR POLLUTION Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. June 1-4, 1998 SUMMARY OF COUNTRY REPORTS

airQuality.note: The summary writes 'Air Pollution Index'; Malaysia's Department of Environment calls the index the Air Pollutant Index. Date and averaging period of the 850 reading not stated. Other sources give 838 (a single-day reading on 23 September 1997 by the AI agent's date calculation, attributed to the Environment Department) and 839 ('reportedly' the highest, on 23 September 1997) for Kuching (see Where sources disagree).

airQuality.text: Malaysia's Environment Department, as reported in The Korea Times on 29 September 1997, said Kuching's Air Pollutant Index (averaging period not stated) had risen to 838 on the previous Tuesday and had since fallen to 31.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: The Environment Department said the Air Pollutant Index in Kuching had fallen to 31, which was in the ``good'' range, after rising to 838, past the ``hazardous'' to health range, last Tuesday.

airQuality.note: 'Last Tuesday' in a report dated Monday 29 September 1997 would be 23 September 1997 (AI agent's date calculation). Averaging period not stated. Read from a third-party reprint of the report.

airQuality.text: WHO health guidelines published in 1999 state that in 1997 smoke raised particle pollution in many areas for several months from late July, and give as an example a 24-hour average PM10 concentration of 930 µg/m3 recorded in Kuching, Sarawak.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: In 1997, smoke from the fires resulted in elevated levels of particle air pollution for a period of several months in many areas (beginning in late July 1997), with a severe episode occurring during most of the month of September. ... a 24-hour average PM10 (mass of particles with aerodynamic diameters smaller than 10 micrometre) concentration of 930 µg/m3 was recorded in the city of Kuching (Sarawak Province, Malaysia)
refs.pinpoint: Section 2.1.1, under 'Impact of fire-generated smoke on human health' (printed p. 29; PDF p. 30)

airQuality.note: A concentration (24-hour average PM10), not an index value. Date of the reading not stated. The guidelines attribute the passage to a 1998 study, which was not opened. A different value appears in another study (see Where sources disagree). The guidelines also describe 'a severe episode occurring during most of the month of September'; that is their characterisation, not a measurement.

airQuality.text: A 2022 scoping review, summarising a 2005 study of hospital admissions in Kuching, gives a daily maximum PM10 concentration of 852 µg/m3 on 22 September 1997.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: Daily maximum PM10 (on Sep 22, 1997): 852 μg/m
refs.pinpoint: Table 2, row for the 2005 Kuching study (cardiorespiratory hospitalisations, 1995–1998)

airQuality.note: A concentration, given in the review's table as a 'daily maximum PM10'; the table does not define the averaging. The table also gives its own air quality index class for the value ('AQI >500', 'Hazardous'); that is the review's classification, not a Malaysian API reading, and is not compared here with any API value. The 2005 paper's full text was not opened.

airQuality.text: The Korea Times report of 29 September 1997 gave Kuala Lumpur's API (averaging period not stated) as 153 on the Sunday evening and 116 on the Monday, and said Penang had recorded a 'hazardous' level on the Saturday.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: In Kuala Lumpur a heavy thunderstorm Sunday night, which briefly flooded some streets and areas, cleared the air and the API had fallen to 116 Monday from 153 Sunday evening.
On Saturday the northwestern Penang city had a hazardous level but that too went down Sunday.

airQuality.note: By the AI agent's date calculation the Saturday, Sunday and Monday are 27, 28 and 29 September 1997. The report cites the Environment Department for the Kuching figures; the Kuala Lumpur and Penang figures are not separately attributed, so this claim is not tagged as criterion evidence.

airQuality.text: A 2023 peer-reviewed analysis of Department of Environment PM10 data (hourly data, plotted as a daily time series) from four Peninsular Malaysian stations found that in 1997 PM10 rose from early September and peaked at the end of September and in October, with Nilai recording the highest concentration of the four stations during the peak, of almost 500 µg/m3, and Larkin the lowest, 200 µg/m3.
airQuality.label: analysis

refs.quote: Figure 2 depicts the comparison of daily PM10 level in 1997, 2005, 2013 and 2015 for all study areas.

In 1997, PM10 level started to rise in early September and reached the peak at the end of September and October. Bukit Rambai and Shah Alam were monitored to have almost the same intensity of PM10 level during the peak, however Nilai recorded the highest concentration of almost 500 µg/m3.
The least concentration of PM10 during the peak was recorded in Larkin with the concentration of 200 µg/m3
at urban-industrial areas namely Shah Alam (Selangor), Nilai (Negeri Sembilan), Bukit Rambai (Melaka) and Larkin (Johor), during the haze episode in 1997, 2005, 2013 and 2015

Continuous hourly data of air pollutants and meteorological parameters in the year that Malaysia experienced historic HPE (1997, 2005, 2013 and 2015) were chosen in this study. Table 3 shows the air pollutants and weather parameters that were obtained from DOE, Malaysia.

airQuality.note: Nilai is in Negeri Sembilan and Larkin in Johor. The values are described from the study's daily PM10 time-series figure (Figure 2); the passage does not give dates or say whether they are 24-hour means. A concentration, not an API value.

airQuality.text: According to The Korea Times report of 29 September 1997, the Environment Department said winds from the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea were helping to clear the air; the newspaper also wrote, without attributing it to the department, that previously the wind had blown from Indonesia, pushing the pollution into Malaysia.
airQuality.label: analysis

refs.quote: Besides the welcome rain, the Environment Department said winds blowing from the South China Sea into Peninsular Malaysia and the from the Sulu Sea near the Philippines into Sarawak were helping clear the air.
Previously the wind blew from Indonesia, which resulted in the pollution being pushed into Malaysia.

airQuality.note: Wind direction as reported. The sentence about where the pollution came from is the newspaper's own statement, not the Environment Department's. Read from a third-party reprint of the report.

responses.text: A Haze Emergency was declared in Sarawak for 10 days, from 19 to 28 September 1997, when the Air Pollutant Index reached above 500, according to Malaysia's Department of Environment.
responses.label: fact

refs.quote: between 19 September to 28 September (10 days), a Haze Emergency had to be declared in Sarawak when the Air Pollutant Index (API) reached above the 500 level.
When the Air Pollution Index (API) reached 500, a ten-day state of emergency was declared in Sarawak (19–28 September).
