Further concerned on the ecological, economic, health and political impacts brought about by transboundary pollution caused by land and forest fires;
WE, THE ASEAN MINISTERS FOR THE ENVIRONMENT, HEREBY AGREE:

To cooperate and render assistance wherever available, to prevent and control all domestic sources of pollution and activities that could contribute towards transboundary pollution, including haze formation;

diplomaticResponse.note: 1997 Jakarta Declaration on Environment and Development, read from an unofficial text published by the NUS Centre for International Law.

diplomaticResponse.text: Malaysia's government sent firefighters to help put out fires in Indonesia during the 1997 haze.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: At the end of September 1997, 107 firemen from Sarawak and seventy-eight from Sabah travelled to West Kalimantan to join the 1,200 firemen from peninsular Malaysia already fighting fires.

Conditions in Peninsular Malaysia and Sarawak became so critical that the Malaysian Government decided to assist Indonesia in putting out the fires. A total of 1 262 firefighters (the largest ever recorded) from Malaysia were deployed to Sumatra and Kalimantan to combat the forest fires.

diplomaticResponse.note: The numbers differ: the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Malaysia chapter) gives 1,200 firemen from Peninsular Malaysia already fighting fires plus 107 from Sarawak and seventy-eight from Sabah sent to West Kalimantan at the end of September 1997; the FAO chapter gives a total of 1,262 deployed to Sumatra and Kalimantan without a date (see Where sources disagree).

diplomaticResponse.text: Indonesia's country report, as summarised by WHO, states that measures to reduce and mitigate the impact of the fires were taken with the cooperation of neighbouring and other countries, which provided technical and material support in fire fighting, air quality monitoring and personal protection.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Under the coordinating Minister of Social Welfare measures were undertaken to reduce and mitigate the impact of the fires with the cooperation of neighboring and other countries which provided technical and material support in fire fighting, air quality monitoring and personal protection measures.
refs.pinpoint: Annex, Summary of Country Reports: Indonesia (PDF p. 194)

diplomaticResponse.note: The summary does not name the countries or give dates.

diplomaticResponse.text: ASEAN environment ministers adopted a Regional Haze Action Plan in Singapore on 23 December 1997, with the objectives of preventing land and forest fires through better management policies and enforcement, establishing mechanisms to monitor fires, and strengthening regional fire-fighting capability.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Adopted in Singapore on 23 December 1997
In light of the latest haze experience, the ASEAN Environment Ministers have agreed on this Regional Haze Action Plan

to prevent land and forest fires through better management policies and enforcement; ... to establish operational mechanisms to monitor land and forest fires; and ... to strengthen regional land and forest fire-fighting capability and other mitigating measures.

diplomaticResponse.note: Also recorded as the related milestone 'Regional Haze Action Plan adopted by ASEAN environment ministers in Singapore' under What changed; mentioned here briefly because it responded to this episode.

aftermath.text: Meteorological Service Singapore described the 1997/1998 haze as the last major haze event to affect the region before 2015, noting that both events occurred during a strong El Niño.
aftermath.label: analysis

refs.quote: During the traditional dry Southwest Monsoon season in 2015, Singapore and many parts of the region were affected by transboundary smoke haze from uncontrolled land and forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan. The prolonged transboundary haze event, which occurred over a period of three months, was the worst in recent history. The last major haze event to affect the region was in 1997/1998. Both events occurred during a strong El Niño, which exacerbated the dry weather conditions in the region.

aftermath.note: Other sources characterise the years between 1997/1998 and 2015 differently (see Where sources disagree).

aftermath.text: A 2016 peer-reviewed study of Indonesian fire activity states that it is widely accepted that the worst event on record was in 1997, and makes the case, from visibility data, that 2015 ranked after 1997 and alongside 1991 and 1994 as among the worst Indonesian fire events on record.
aftermath.label: analysis

refs.quote: It is widely accepted that the worst event on record was in 1997

We make the case that the 2015 Indonesian fire season was the most severe season since the NASA's Earth Observing satellite system began observations in the early 2000s, and, by examining visibility data before the EOS period, that 2015 ranked after 1997 and alongside 1991 and 1994 as among the worst Indonesian fire events on record
The last major event occurred in 2006 over southern Sumatra and south-central Kalimantan, under a combination of moderate El Niño and positive Indian Ocean Dipole conditions

aftermath.note: Refers to Indonesian fire events (based in part on airport visibility records), not to air quality in Malaysia or Singapore specifically, so it is not tagged as criterion B3 evidence. The same introduction says 'The last major event occurred in 2006' (see Where sources disagree).

aftermath.text: The 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book estimated the damage from the 1997 fires and haze to Indonesia and its neighbours at some US$4.5 billion, a figure its authors describe as conservative, with by far the largest share borne by Indonesia.
aftermath.label: analysis

refs.quote: In spite of this, the damage estimates are significant, amounting to some US$4.5 billion.
The total economic value of these damages are conservatively estimated to be US$4.47 billion, by far the largest share of which was borne by Indonesia herself.
Nevertheless, the total estimated value of damages to Indonesia and her neighbours from the 1997 fires and haze is substantial.

Haze-related damages not estimated here include long-term health damages, reduced crop productivity, aesthetic value of reduced visibility, avertive expenditures, accidents, loss of life, evacuations, and loss of confidence by foreign investors.
It assessed only the damages for the 1997 episode—not those that occurred in 1998. The total damages for the entire El Niño-related event were considerably higher than those reported here.

aftermath.note: Economic valuation of fire damage (timber, agriculture, forest benefits, fire-fighting, carbon) and short-term haze damage (health, tourism, some production losses) in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. The book states that it 'assessed only the damages for the 1997 episode—not those that occurred in 1998' and that 'the total damages for the entire El Niño-related event were considerably higher than those reported here'.

selection.note: Criterion A is met by Malaysia's Department of Environment (external sources that exacerbated the contribution from internal sources), Singapore's environment ministry (haze from land and forest fires in Indonesia, 2014) and a peer-reviewed study by a Singapore Ministry of Health author (fires mainly in Kalimantan and Sumatra; particle sizes consistent with combustion sources over 500 km from Singapore); an FAO working paper is not counted, as FAO states that such papers do not reflect its official position. B1 is met by Singapore's 24-hour PSI above 101 on twelve days between 13 September and 25 October 1997 according to a 2014 peer-reviewed analysis of NEA data (WHO's summary of Singapore's country report gives 12 days with the PSI over 100, averaging period not stated), or fourteen days in the unhealthy range on 24-hour readings according to the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Singapore chapter); Sarawak's API above 500 is not counted, as no day or station count is given. B2 is met by a ten-day haze emergency in Sarawak, 19–28 September 1997, during which schools and businesses were closed; Singapore Ministry of Health advice of 24 September 1997 for persons with chronic heart and lung problems is not counted, as it is tied to a PSI threshold (above 100) and the ministry said there was otherwise no need to take extraordinary precautions (treated as routine, as in 2016, pending a human ruling on 'beyond routine forecasts'). B3 is met by 'particularly severe' (Singapore's environment ministry, 2014), 'severe smoke haze pollution' (the peer-reviewed study) and the last 'major' haze event to affect the region before 2015 (Meteorological Service Singapore).

attribution.note: Malaysia's Department of Environment, Singapore's environment ministry and the ASEAN environment ministers quoted in this entry describe transboundary smoke from land and forest fires, and Indonesia's country report, as summarised by WHO, records help from neighbouring countries in fighting the fires. No public dispute about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. Malaysia's Department of Environment also describes a contribution from sources within Malaysia, and an FAO working paper notes fires reported in Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak.

confidence.rationale: Medium. The core account (a smoke-haze episode from about July/August to November 1997 that affected Malaysia, with a ten-day haze emergency in Sarawak from 19 to 28 September, and Singapore, where the PSI was in the unhealthy range on 12 or 14 days) is supported by government sources (Malaysia's Department of Environment chronology for the dates, the emergency and the API above 500; Singapore's environment ministry, 2014, for the 1997 peak 24-hour PSI of 138; Meteorological Service Singapore's 2015 assessment; Singapore's Ministry of Health), intergovernmental sources (WHO's 1999 summaries of the Malaysian and Singaporean country reports, read from a pre-publication version; the ASEAN Regional Haze Action Plan, read from an unofficial text) and peer-reviewed studies (a study of the 1997 haze in Singapore by a Ministry of Health author; a 2014 analysis of NEA's PSI data). It is corroborated by a contemporaneous news report of 29 September 1997 (read from a reprint) and by the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book, whose Malaysia and Singapore chapters are cited throughout this entry (for the economic estimates, the Sarawak emergency, the Singapore PSI table and the fourteen-day count) and count as one source. The FAO working paper is not relied on for the core account, as FAO states that such papers do not reflect its official position. The rating is medium because minor conflicts about figures remain unresolved and Malaysia's peak readings are incomplete: Singapore's 1997 peak PSI (24-hour: 138, or 144 for 24 October in the ministry table as reproduced in the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book; 134, metric not stated, in a review); Kuching's highest API (a reading of 838; 839, 'reportedly' the highest; 850, 'the highest'), which rests on a WHO summary and news reports because no Department of Environment station data were found; Kuching PM10 values reported with different averaging (a 24-hour average of 930 µg/m3; a 'daily maximum' of 852 µg/m3); and the number of unhealthy-PSI days in Singapore (12 or 14). Sources give different months for different places, and the start and end months shown are the AI agent's reading of them (see How these dates were chosen). Contemporaneous official records were not opened: NEA's archived daily PSI for 1997, the Department of Environment's station-level API data or its 1997 Environmental Quality Report, the 1997 Ministry of the Environment and Ministry of Health press releases, Hansard, and the notice declaring the Sarawak emergency. This is an AI-assigned rating awaiting human review.

contradictions.text: Singapore's 1997 peak PSI. The 2014 Scientific Reports study (NEA 24-hour maximum PSI at 4 pm), Singapore's environment ministry (2014) and the WHO summary of Singapore's country report give 138 (19 September 1997 in the 2014 study). The 2022 PLoS ONE scoping review, summarising the 2000 MOH-authored study, says 'The highest PSI recorded was 134' without stating the metric. In addition, the Ministry of the Environment's 24-hour PSI table for August–November 1997 reproduced in the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Appendix 4.1) shows 138 for 19 September but 144 for 24 October (AI agent's reading of the table; the same table has two September cells that look truncated, '5' and '4', so a transcription error in the ebook is possible). Not resolved; NEA's archived daily data would settle it.

Number of days in Singapore with PSI in the unhealthy range in 1997: 12 (WHO summary of Singapore's country report, 'over 100'; the 2014 Scientific Reports study, 'twelve days >101 between 13 Sept. - 25 Oct.', from NEA's once-daily 4 pm readings) versus fourteen (the Singapore chapter of the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book, August–October, 24-hour PSI daily readings; NLB Infopedia, 14 days, citing the same 1999 chapter). The AI agent counted 12 days above 100 (13, 14, 19, 24, 25 and 28 September; 2, 3, 13, 23, 24 and 25 October) in the ministry table reproduced in the same ISEAS/IDRC book, which agrees with 12. The difference is unexplained; different counting conventions may be involved.

'226' versus '138' for Singapore in 1997. Channel NewsAsia (2006) calls 226 the highest 3-hour average PSI, in September 1997. NLB Infopedia ('the highest PSI reading of 226 recorded in September') and NASA Earth Observatory (2013, 'The previous record occurred in 1997, when the index hit 226') give 226 without the averaging period, while Singapore's environment ministry gives 138 as the 1997 24-hour PSI record. The figures are probably different metrics (3-hour versus 24-hour PSI), but the sources that omit the averaging period conflict with the 24-hour record.

Kuching's API in September 1997: 850 as the highest (WHO summary of Malaysia's country report; date and averaging period not stated) versus a reading of 838 on the Tuesday before 29 September 1997, i.e. 23 September by the AI agent's date calculation (Environment Department figure in The Korea Times report of 29 September 1997) versus 839 on 23 September 1997, 'reportedly' the highest ever (Malaysiakini, 2013). At the declaration of the emergency on 19 September: 650 (Malaysia's National Disaster Management Agency, 2019). Malaysia's Department of Environment says only that the API 'reached above the 500 level'. No official primary record of the peak was opened.

Kuching PM10 in 1997: a 24-hour average of 930 µg/m3 (WHO 1999 guidelines, citing a 1998 study; date not stated) versus a daily maximum of 852 µg/m3 on 22 September 1997 (2022 PLoS ONE scoping review, summarising a 2005 hospital-admissions study). Different studies, possibly different stations, and different averaging (the review does not define 'daily maximum'), so the two values may not be comparable; not reconciled.

Singapore health surveillance in 1997: the MOH-authored study (abstract) reports a 30% increase in outpatient attendance and a 12% increase in upper respiratory tract illness per PM10 rise from 50 to 150 µg/m3; the WHO summary of Singapore's country report gives a 30 per cent increase in hospital attendance and a 2 per cent increase in upper respiratory tract illness for the same rise. The peer-reviewed abstract is followed here; the WHO text may contain a transcription error (AI agent's judgement, unverified).

Malaysia's 1997 haze-damage estimate: RM802 million (RM801.90 million in Table 3.17 of the Malaysia chapter of the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book, adjusted cost of illness RM21.02 million) versus RM816 million (FAO chapter citing the same research programme's study, Table 3-5, adjusted cost of illness RM36.16 million); the same book's Table 6.2 gives RM794.3 million for Malaysian haze damages, without fire-fighting costs. Versions of one research programme's estimate with different components.

Malaysian firefighters sent to Indonesia: the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book says 107 from Sarawak and seventy-eight from Sabah went to West Kalimantan at the end of September 1997 to join 1,200 from Peninsular Malaysia already fighting fires (about 1,385 in all, by the AI agent's sum); the FAO chapter gives a total of 1,262 deployed to Sumatra and Kalimantan, without a date.

Area burned in Indonesia in 1997: an estimated 165,000 hectares (Indonesia's country report, WHO summary) versus about 1.5 million hectares in Sumatra and 3.06 million in Kalimantan (preliminary remote-sensing assessment cited in the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book, which adopted 5 million hectares and also reports an Indonesian government estimate of some quarter of a million hectares of forest damaged). The figures probably use different definitions (forest only versus all land) and methods.

Economic damage of the 1997 haze to Singapore: S$97.5–110.5 million (1999 ISEAS/IDRC book; NLB Infopedia, citing that book) versus $163.5–$286.2 million (a 2002 study as cited in a 2021 RAND report; currency not stated in the passage). Different studies with different scopes and methods.

Whether 1997/1998 was the last major haze event before 2015. Meteorological Service Singapore's assessment of 2015 says 'The last major haze event to affect the region was in 1997/1998'; the 2016 peer-reviewed study of Indonesian fire activity says 'The last major event occurred in 2006 over southern Sumatra and south-central Kalimantan'; and Singapore's environment ministry (2014) lists 2006, 2010 and 2013, as well as 1997, among the years in which the haze was 'particularly severe'. The statements measure different things (haze across the region, fire events in Indonesia, haze affecting Singapore), and all three treat 1997 as major or severe; not resolved.

evidenceGaps: No contemporaneous 1997 Singapore government record was opened directly (Ministry of the Environment or Ministry of Health press releases, Parliament Hansard): National Archives and Hansard pages did not return text to scripts and no 1997 record URLs were found. The 24 September 1997 MOH press release was read only as reproduced in the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book.

No contemporaneous Malaysian official record was found online: the Department of Environment's Malaysia Environmental Quality Report 1997, Dewan Rakyat Hansard for September–October 1997, and any Sarawak or federal notice of the 1997 haze emergency (which authority declared it, under what law) were not found.

NEA's archived daily 24-hour PSI and hourly 3-hour PSI values for 1997 were not found online; Singapore figures rest on the WHO summary, a 2014 peer-reviewed analysis of NEA data, the environment ministry's 2014 statement and a table reproduced in the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book.
Station-level Malaysian API values for 1997 (DOE) were not found; the Kuching peak rests on a WHO summary of Malaysia's country report and a news report citing the Environment Department.

Only abstracts were read for the MOH-authored Singapore study (2000), the Kuching hospital-admissions study (2005), the Malaysian mortality study (2002) and the Indonesian field study (2002); the 1998 study cited by WHO for the 930 µg/m3 Kuching reading was not opened.
A peer-reviewed study of health effects in Indonesia using household survey data (Demography, 2005) could not be opened (eScholarship returned HTTP 202; RePEc has no abstract; not in PubMed).

Old ASEAN Secretariat pages on the 1997 haze (asean.or.id) no longer resolve; the Internet Archive returned HTTP 429 (too many requests) to the download scripts used, and the page-reading tool used could not reach web.archive.org. The official ASEAN copies of the Jakarta Declaration and the Regional Haze Action Plan were not opened (unofficial NUS texts used).
Numbers of schools closed in Sarawak, and whether schools elsewhere in Malaysia or in Singapore closed in 1997, were not found in official sources.

Impacts on people in Indonesia rest on WHO's summary of Indonesia's country report (whose text layer garbles the case counts), the abstract of one field study and a RAND brief. No Indonesian government record of the 1997 health, school or transport impacts was opened, and no statement by Indonesia's government during the episode was found in a reputable source (searches during this research for reports of statements by Indonesia's President to ASEAN ministers in September 1997 found none in a source that meets the project's source hierarchy; the only pages found were a politician's own statements, which were not used); Indonesia's account appears here only through the WHO summary.
unresolvedQuestions: What was Kuching's highest API in September 1997, on what date and with what averaging period: 838, 839 or 850?
Was Singapore's highest 24-hour PSI in 1997 138 on 19 September, or does the 144 for 24 October in the table reproduced in the ISEAS/IDRC book reflect a different series or a transcription error?
Which counting convention produced fourteen unhealthy PSI days for Singapore in August–October 1997 rather than 12?
On what date and at what time was the 3-hour PSI of 226 recorded, and does any official source confirm it?
Which authority declared the September 1997 haze emergency in Sarawak, under what legal basis, and how many schools were closed?
How do the 1997 Malaysian API and the post-1997 revised API relate, given that the 1999 ISEAS/IDRC book (Malaysia chapter) notes that the API calculations were being revised in February 1998?

What did Indonesia's national and provincial authorities record about the 1997 haze's effects on people there (health-facility visits, school closures, transport disruption), and what did Indonesia's government say publicly during the episode?

Is the 'National Haze Task Force' that the WHO summary of Singapore's country report says was established the Haze Task Force formed in September 1994, or a separate body set up during the 1997 episode?

events.title: August–October 2002: Sarawak, Kuala Lumpur and Singapore

period.label: August–October 2002

refs.quote: was forced to cancel several flights by small aircraft since Thursday as air quality had deteriorated, said a spokesman for Sarawak's Miri Airport.

Below average rainfall was recorded in most parts of the region in August 2002 with southern Sumatra, Kalimantan and Java receiving more than 75% below average rainfall (Fig 1). The dry weather conditions resulted in increased occurrences of forest and land fires over Kalimantan and parts of central and southern Sumatra (Figs 2 & 3). Most parts of Kalimantan and parts of southern Sarawak was affected by the resultant moderate to thick smoke haze, while the rest of the region mainly experienced slight haze.

Weather conditions continued to be dry in southern Sumatra and Kalimantan in the first 2 weeks of October. Consequently, the fires continued to persist over these areas. The prevailing south to south-easterly winds brought light to moderate smoke haze over Singapore, southern Peninsular Malaysia and Sarawak.
refs.pinpoint: 'Update of Regional Weather and Smoke Haze', section 1.2

refs.quote: In Malaysia, a spokesman for the meterorological department said visibility in parts of the country dropped to between three and six kilometres today due to winds blowing smoke into Malaysia.

period.note: Start: flights in Sarawak were cancelled from Thursday 15 August 2002 (AFP), and NEA describes smoke haze over parts of southern Sarawak during August. 'Unhealthy' API descriptors were reported in Sarawak around 20–22 August and 22–24 September 2002, and Malaysiakini reported air quality around Kuala Lumpur as affected from early in the week beginning 23 September. NEA says showers brought much improved conditions in the last week of August, so the August and September phases may have been separate (AI reading). End: NEA describes light to moderate smoke haze over Singapore, southern Peninsular Malaysia and Sarawak in the first two weeks of October, and on 17 October 2002 a Malaysian Meteorological Department spokesman told AFP that smoke had cut visibility in parts of Malaysia to 3–6 km. No source gives an end date, and the end month is uncertain (see 'Evidence not found': NEA's releases of 15 October and 15 November 2002 were not archived with their text). Day-level dates are computed by the AI agent from the reports' dates.

summary.text: Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) stated that below-average rainfall in August 2002 increased forest and land fires over Kalimantan and parts of Sumatra, and that most of Kalimantan and parts of southern Sarawak were affected by the resulting moderate to thick smoke haze; its review of September 2002 again described Kalimantan and parts of southern Sarawak as affected by moderate to thick smoke haze.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Below average rainfall was recorded in most parts of the region in August 2002 with southern Sumatra, Kalimantan and Java receiving more than 75% below average rainfall (Fig 1). The dry weather conditions resulted in increased occurrences of forest and land fires over Kalimantan and parts of central and southern Sumatra (Figs 2 & 3). Most parts of Kalimantan and parts of southern Sarawak was affected by the resultant moderate to thick smoke haze, while the rest of the region mainly experienced slight haze.

Below average rainfall continued to be recorded in most parts of Kalimantan and southern Sumatra in September 2002. The rainfall was as much as 75% below normal in these areas (Fig 1). The dry weather conditions caused increased occurrences of forest and land fires over these areas (Figs 2 & 3). Kalimantan and parts of southern Sarawak was affected by moderate to thick smoke haze.
refs.pinpoint: 'Update of Regional Weather and Smoke Haze', section 1.1 (review of September 2002)

summary.note: An agency's assessment of where the smoke haze was, based on satellite pictures and weather data; it gives no air-quality measurements for Sarawak. In the September review, 'these areas' are most parts of Kalimantan and southern Sumatra. Both pages are undated; see the sources' notes for capture dates.

summary.text: Malaysiakini reported on 22 August 2002 that, according to Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE), seven areas in Sarawak (Kuching, Sibu, Sarikei, Samarahan, Sri Aman, Kapit and Petra Jaya) had been declared to be in the 'unhealthy' category, meaning an Air Pollutant Index between 101 and 200, the previous day.
summary.label: observation

refs.quote: According to the Department of Environment (DOE), seven areas in Sarawak were yesterday declared to be in the 'unhealthy" category, meaning the Air Pollutant Index was between 101 and 200. These areas are Kuching, Sibu, Sarikei, Samarahan, Sri Aman, Kapit and Petra Jaya (Kuching).

summary.note: Malaysia's API, reported as a descriptor only (index values were reported not to be published; see 'Malaysia: Air quality'). Time and averaging period not stated. 'Yesterday' is probably 20 or 21 August 2002: the publication time the site stores for 2002 articles (here 05:42 on 22 August) dates from a 2008 migration and cannot fix the day. No DOE record of these descriptors was found.

summary.text: In September 2002 a DOE control director told AFP that six Sarawak monitoring stations (Kuching, Sarikei, Samarahan, Sri Aman, Kapit and Petra Jaya) had recorded unhealthy air readings, and in a later report that Kapit and Samarahan still did while the other four had returned to moderate; Malaysiakini separately reported on 27 September 2002 that the Sarawak DOE had said on the Tuesday of that week that air quality at the Kapit and Samarahan stations remained 'unhealthy'.
summary.label: observation

refs.quote: control director of the department of environment, said six monitoring stations in Sarawak state Kuching, Sarikei, Samarahan, Sri Aman, Kapit and Petra Jaya recorded unhealthy air readings.
Two stations in Sarawak Kapit and Samarahan posted unhealthy readings," ... control director of the department of environment told AFP
He said the air quality in four other monitoring stations Kuching, Sarikei, Sri Aman and Petra Jaya now showed moderate readings. These stations posted unhealthy readings yesterday.

On Tuesday, the Sarawak Department of Environment said that air quality at the Kapit and Samarahan stations remained "unhealthy" due to persistent haze resulting from forest and ground fires from Kalimantan.

summary.note: API descriptors only; values, times and averaging periods were not given. The two AFP reports were published by Malaysiakini on 23 and 24 September 2002, so the six-station readings are probably those of 22 or 23 September, and the Tuesday in Malaysiakini's report is 24 September 2002 (dates computed by the AI agent). The source's dashes around the station names were lost in text extraction.

summary.text: NEA reported that dry weather persisted over southern Sumatra and Kalimantan in the first two weeks of October 2002, that the fires continued there, and that south to south-easterly winds brought light to moderate smoke haze over Singapore, southern Peninsular Malaysia and Sarawak.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Weather conditions continued to be dry in southern Sumatra and Kalimantan in the first 2 weeks of October. Consequently, the fires continued to persist over these areas. The prevailing south to south-easterly winds brought light to moderate smoke haze over Singapore, southern Peninsular Malaysia and Sarawak.
refs.pinpoint: 'Update of Regional Weather and Smoke Haze', section 1.2

summary.note: NEA's description of the extent of smoke haze; it gives no Malaysian air-quality values. NEA's 24-hour PSI readings for Singapore in this period are under 'Singapore: Air quality'.

impact.text: Haze disrupted air services in Sarawak in mid-August 2002: a Miri Airport spokesman told AFP (report of 17 August) that several flights by small aircraft had been cancelled since Thursday as air quality deteriorated, and that flights serving the state's rural areas had been delayed or cancelled because smaller aircraft could not land or take off in the hazy conditions; Malaysiakini reported that an airline cancelled at least six rural flights in northern Sarawak on Friday for the safety of passengers. NASA Earth Observatory noted on 20 August 2002 that smoke had recently disrupted air traffic in Malaysia on the north-western part of Borneo.
impact.label: fact

refs.quote: He said that a number of flights servicing the state's rural areas had to be delayed or cancelled as smaller aircraft which fly at lower altitudes could not land or take off in the hazy conditions.
was forced to cancel several flights by small aircraft since Thursday as air quality had deteriorated, said a spokesman for Sarawak's Miri Airport.

Meanwhile, as the haze continued to worsen, reducing visibility and hampering low-level aircraft flights, national carrier ... announced the cancellation of at least six rural flights in the northern region of Sarawak for the safety of passengers on Friday.
In addition to being a health hazard, the smoke can disrupt air traffic, as it did recently in Malaysia, on the northwest portion of Borneo.

impact.note: Thursday and Friday are 15 and 16 August 2002 (computed by the AI agent from the reports' dates). The airline's name is replaced by an ellipsis in the quote (project rule). AFP's opening sentence, which also says where the haze came from, is not used here: statements about the haze's origin are attributed in the claim on Malaysian officials' views below. No airline or airport record was found.

impact.text: A Malaysian Meteorological Department spokesman told AFP that visibility in Sarawak and neighbouring Sabah on Friday was 'one of the worst in years' (report of 17 August 2002).
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: A spokesman from the Meteorological Department here told AFP that visibility levels in Sarawak and its neighbouring Sabah state on Friday were "one of the worst in years".

impact.note: Friday is 16 August 2002 (computed). A comparative characterisation by the department's spokesman as reported, not a measurement: no visibility values were given in this report, so it is labelled analysis.

impact.text: Malaysian officials said the September 2002 haze came from fires in Indonesia: AFP quoted officials as saying forest and ground fires in Indonesian Borneo had brought haze to Sarawak (23 September) and an official in Kuching as saying 'The haze is from forest fires burning out of control in Kalimantan' (24 September); Malaysiakini reported (27 September) that the DOE said the haze affecting Kuala Lumpur and much of Sarawak was a result of open burning in Indonesia, quoting its director-general: 'We believe it is coming from Indonesia', and that she said there had been no open burning around Kuala Lumpur in the past few days that could contribute to it.
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: Haze caused by forest and ground fires from Indonesia's Borneo island has hit Sarawak, officials said today.
The haze is from forest fires burning out of control in Kalimantan. If the fire is not put out, the haze will return.
The Department of Environment (DOE) said today that the haze (library photo) affecting Kuala Lumpur and much of Sarawak is a result of open burning in neighbouring Indonesia.
"We believe it is coming from Indonesia," she said when contacted today.
said the there has been no open burning around Kuala Lumpur which could contribute to the haze during the past few days.

impact.note: Officials' views of where the haze came from, as reported; attributed. The AFP reports were read as published by Malaysiakini, so the two news organisations' reports are independent in authorship but were found on one website. The quoted 'the there' is the source's typo. No statement by Indonesian officials disputing these views was found (see 'Evidence not found'). A Sarawak newspaper's report of local bushfires in August is recorded in the next claim.

impact.text: Malaysiakini's review of Sarawak newspapers on 20 August 2002 said The Borneo Post had run a front-page report about bushfires aggravating the situation, and quoted the report as saying that, although the DOE had not detected any hotspots in the state recently, these fires, 'which might not be at a scale detectable by satellite', had left the state's Natural Resources and Environment Board 'with its hands full'.
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: Another English daily, ... also ran a report on its front page about bushfires aggravating the situation.

Although the Department of Environment did not detect any hotspots in the state recently, these fires, which might not be at a scale detectable by satellite, have left the Natural Resources and Environment Board [a state body] with its hands full," the report said.

impact.note: A newspaper's account, relayed second-hand by Malaysiakini; the Borneo Post report itself was not found. 'The state' is read as Sarawak from the context: the article reviews Sarawak newspapers, and the Natural Resources and Environment Board is a Sarawak body, which Malaysiakini glosses as 'a state body' (AI reading). The report gives no place, number or size for the fires and says nothing about who lit them. It is recorded because it reports local fires adding to the haze in Sarawak in August; it does not contest the officials' September statements (previous claim) and does not show how much local fires contributed. In the first quote the newspaper's name is replaced by an ellipsis only because text extraction separated it from the comma; the name is given in the claim text.

impact.text: Malaysiakini reported on 27 September 2002, in an article quoting the DOE director-general, that air quality around Kuala Lumpur had been affected since early that week and had improved with rain the previous day.
impact.label: observation

refs.quote: The air quality around the capital, affected since early this week, had improved with yesterday's downpour.

impact.note: The sentence is the outlet's narration, placed between quotations of the director-general; it is not explicitly attributed to her. The week began on Monday 23 September 2002 (computed). No API value or descriptor for Kuala Lumpur stations was given; the Kuala Lumpur element rests on this single report.

impact.text: Malaysia's environment minister said on 1 October 2002 that the haze was more serious that year in Sarawak and parts of neighbouring Sabah but 'not so bad' on Peninsular Malaysia, and that it was expected to persist until early the following year but was unlikely to worsen.
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: Environment Minister ... said the haze was more serious this year in Sarawak state on Borneo island and parts of neighbouring Sabah but "not so bad" on peninsula Malaysia.
Haze enveloping parts of Malaysia due to forest fires in Indonesia is expected to persist until early next year but is unlikely to worsen, a minister said today.

impact.note: The minister's assessment as reported by AFP. Sabah's air quality was not documented in any source found.

airQuality.text: Malaysiakini reported on 20 August 2002 that the haze had brought Kuching's air quality to unhealthy levels and reduced visibility by almost 90 percent, and that visibility in the city was down to 1.2 km; on 22 August it reported that visibility in Sarawak had dropped to 800 metres the previous day from 1.2 km the day before, and that officials at emergency operations centres said air quality in Kuching remained unhealthy after overnight rain had improved visibility.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: The 400,000 residents in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak, are increasingly concerned at the worsening haze which has already caused the air quality to reach unhealthy levels and reduced visibility by almost 90 percent.
Today, visibility in the city is down to 1.2km.
Yesterday, Sarawak was hit by smog ... with visibility dropping to only 800 metres from the previous day's 1.2km.
Visibility has improved in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak, after overnight downpour but the air quality level remains unhealthy, according to officials manning emergency operations centres today.

airQuality.note: Descriptor only: no API value, station or averaging period is given, and the 20 August report does not say who classified the air as unhealthy. The 22 August report gives the 800-metre reading for 'Sarawak' without naming a place. 'Yesterday' in that report is probably 20 or 21 August 2002 (see the note on the DOE descriptors under 'What happened'). The third quote omits the outlet's own, unattributed statement of where the smog originated; officials' statements on origin are attributed under 'Malaysia: Impact'.

airQuality.text: AFP reported on 23 September 2002 that a deputy minister of science, technology and environment, quoted by the Bernama news agency, said that the pollution index in Sarawak had exceeded 170 ('unhealthy').
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: deputy science, technology and environment minister ... "The haze level in Sarawak is quite serious. The pollution index in the state has exceeded 170 (unhealthy)," he was quoted as saying by Bernama news agency.

airQuality.note: Presumably Malaysia's API: the source says only 'pollution index'. Station, time and averaging period not stated, and the figure reached this record third-hand (Bernama, then AFP, then Malaysiakini). It is the only numeric API value found for this episode, at a time when index values were reported not to be published (next claim). The words omitted from the quote are the deputy minister's remarks on the causes of the fires, which are not repeated (project rule).

airQuality.text: Reports during the episode said Malaysia was not publishing Air Pollutant Index values: Malaysiakini reported that only descriptors had been released since 1997; Sarawak's deputy chief minister said the state disaster relief committee would not release API readings because they changed constantly and could mislead people; and the DOE director-general declined to give the current API assessment.
airQuality.label: fact

refs.quote: However, index figures have not been released since the height of the haze in 1997, only the descriptors
refs.pinpoint: paragraph 7 (the quote ends before the reason the report gives)

refs.quote: the deputy chief minister said. ... told reporters that the state disaster relief committee would not release the API readings because they change constantly and this could easily mislead the people.
refs.pinpoint: paragraphs 14–15 (section 'No plans to release API readings', paragraphs 2–3)

refs.quote: declined to reveal the current Air Pollution Index (API) assessment, saying only that health advice, if necessary, would be provided by the Health Ministry.

airQuality.note: Severity therefore cannot be quantified from published API values. The deputy chief minister's statement is recorded as made; that does not establish the reasons for not releasing readings. Numeric API values were published again from 10 August 2005 (see the August 2005 episode and the milestones under 'How haze is measured'). The reason that Malaysiakini and AFP gave for the withholding, without citing an official, is in the next claim.

airQuality.text: Malaysiakini wrote on 20 August 2002 that index figures had not been released 'as the government was concerned over undue alarm, especially among foreign tourists, at the figures', and gave the same reason on 22 August; an AFP report it carried on 24 September 2002 said the government had been reluctant to release the index, 'fearing it may scare away tourists'.
airQuality.label: allegation

refs.quote: However, index figures have not been released since the height of the haze in 1997, only the descriptors, as the government was concerned over undue alarm, especially among foreign tourists, at the figures.
The government has since decided not to release the index figures for fear that it would cause undue alarm, especially among tourists.
The government has been reluctant to release the air pollution index, fearing it may scare away tourists.
refs.pinpoint: paragraph 9 (section 'Release API readings', paragraph 3; AFP report, 24 September 2002)

airQuality.note: Labelled an allegation: none of these reports cites an official or a document for this reason, and no government document giving it was found during this research. Sarawak's deputy chief minister gave a different reason for not releasing readings (previous claim). See also the milestones on Malaysia's API reporting under 'How haze is measured'.

responses.text: After chairing an emergency high-level meeting of officials, Sarawak's Deputy Chief Minister said the state government would distribute masks in Kapit, Sibu and Samarahan; the same Malaysiakini report (22 August 2002) said one million masks would be distributed by the relevant government agencies, with priority for schoolchildren, institutions and people with health problems.
responses.label: fact

refs.quote: after chairing an emergency high-level meeting of officials ... Deputy Chief Minister ... said the state government would be distributing masks in Kapit, Sibu and Samarahan.
One million masks would be distributed by the relevant government agencies, with priority to be given to school children, institutions and people with health problems.

responses.note: As reported; no Sarawak government record was found. The one-million figure follows the Deputy Chief Minister's statement but is not explicitly attributed to him. No emergency declaration was found in the sources for this episode.

impact.text: NEA attributed hazy conditions in Singapore in September and October 2002 to smoke haze carried by the prevailing winds: 'slightly hazy conditions' in the days before its release of 20 September, when it reported a significant increase in hot spots in Kalimantan and Sumatra and said south to south-easterly winds were carrying some of the smoke haze towards Singapore; smoke haze carried from Kalimantan by easterly winds on 25 September; and 'generally hazy conditions' over the weekend before its release of 14 October, from smoke haze carried from southern Sumatra and Kalimantan.
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: Over the past few days, satellite pictures have shown that the number of hot spots in Kalimantan and Sumatra has increased significantly.

The prevailing south to south-easterly winds in the region are carrying some of the smoke haze towards Singapore. This has resulted in slightly hazy conditions in Singapore over the past few days. Our 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index or PSI in the last few days hovered in the moderate levels of 52 to 55.

Singapore's 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index or PSI at 4.00pm today was 57, which is in the moderate range. This morning, the low level winds in the region turned easterly and carried smoke haze from Kalimantan to Singapore.

Prevailing south to south-easterly winds have carried some of the smoke haze from southern Sumatra and Kalimantan over to Singapore. This has resulted in generally hazy conditions in Singapore over the weekend. Our 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index or PSI yesterday reached 70, which is still within the moderate level.

impact.note: The responsible agency's view of where the haze came from. The weekend before 14 October 2002 was 12–13 October (computed).

airQuality.text: NEA reported 24-hour PSI readings for Singapore in the moderate range: 52 to 55 in the days before its release of 20 September 2002, 57 at 4 pm on 25 September 2002, and 70 on the day before its release of 14 October 2002.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: The prevailing south to south-easterly winds in the region are carrying some of the smoke haze towards Singapore. This has resulted in slightly hazy conditions in Singapore over the past few days. Our 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index or PSI in the last few days hovered in the moderate levels of 52 to 55.

Singapore's 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index or PSI at 4.00pm today was 57, which is in the moderate range. This morning, the low level winds in the region turned easterly and carried smoke haze from Kalimantan to Singapore.

Prevailing south to south-easterly winds have carried some of the smoke haze from southern Sumatra and Kalimantan over to Singapore. This has resulted in generally hazy conditions in Singapore over the weekend. Our 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index or PSI yesterday reached 70, which is still within the moderate level.

airQuality.note: Singapore's 24-hour PSI as defined in 2002 (PM2.5 was added only in 2014). The reading of 70 was for 13 October 2002 (computed from 'yesterday'). None of these readings is in the unhealthy range (above 100).

airQuality.text: AFP reported on 17 October 2002 that NEA had said on the Tuesday of that week that smoke haze had pushed Singapore's pollution index to its highest reading of the year so far; AFP gave no value, averaging period or time for the reading.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: On Tuesday, Singapore reported that the smoke haze from Indonesia had pushed the pollution index to its highest reading this year, the National Environment Agency said.

airQuality.note: Tuesday is 15 October 2002 (computed). 'Highest reading this year' means the highest up to that date, and whether the reading was in the unhealthy range is not known. AFP's sentence also reports NEA as saying the smoke haze was from Indonesia; NEA's own releases attribute Singapore's haze in this period to smoke haze from Kalimantan and southern Sumatra ('Singapore: Impact'). NEA's own release of 15 October 2002 was not archived (see 'Evidence not found').

health.text: A Sarawak tabloid, quoting a Health Department officer, reported that the department had sent letters to government departments and schools asking them to cut down on outdoor activities for the time being, as a precaution, and had drawn up a contingency plan for a further deterioration (relayed by Malaysiakini on 20 August 2002).
health.label: fact

refs.quote: As a precautionary measure the department had sent out letters to government departments and schools to cut down on outdoor activities for the time being.
the newspaper reported that the department at a meeting last week had drawn up a contingency plan to be put into effect if the situation deteriorated further.

health.note: Government health advice, reported second-hand: Malaysiakini's review of a Sarawak English-language tabloid that quoted a department officer. The article does not name the state; from its context (Sarawak newspapers, Kuching), the department is presumably Sarawak's state health department (AI reading). The letters themselves were not found.

health.text: A DOE control director told AFP in a report published on 23 September 2002 that people were being advised not to engage in strenuous outdoor activities and to drink lots of water, and said that, currently, schools in the state would remain open.
health.label: fact

refs.quote: control director of the department of environment, said six monitoring stations ... For now we are advising people not to engage in strenuous outdoor activities. Drink lots of water," he told AFP.
said currently schools in the state would remain open.

health.note: Official advice to reduce outdoor activity, as reported by a news agency; no written advisory was found. No school closures in Malaysia were reported in the sources found for this episode.

regionalContext.text: NEA reported that daily hotspot counts reached August maxima of 1298 over Kalimantan (17 August) and 449 over Sumatra (20 August), and highs of 746 over Borneo (17 September 2002) and 277 over Sumatra (19 September 2002).
regionalContext.label: observation

refs.quote: At one stage, hotspot counts over Kalimantan and Sumatra reached an August maximum of 1298 (on 17 Aug) and 449 (on 20 Aug) respectively
Hotspots counts reached a high of 746 in Borneo on 17 September 2002, while in Sumatra the number of hotspots reached a high of 277 on 19 September 2002.
refs.pinpoint: 'Update of Regional Weather and Smoke Haze', section 1.1

regionalContext.note: Satellite hotspot counts as reported by NEA. A hotspot marks a heat source; it says nothing about who started a fire or who holds the land. NEA's text gives the August maximum for 'Kalimantan' and the September high for 'Borneo'; both pages cite a figure captioned 'Daily hotspot counts over Sumatra and Borneo', so whether the two areas differ is not clear (AI reading).

regionalContext.text: NEA linked the fires to dry weather: rainfall in August 2002 was more than 75% below average over southern Sumatra, Kalimantan and Java and remained below average over most of Kalimantan and southern Sumatra in September 2002, under what NEA described as weak to moderate El Niño conditions.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: Below average rainfall was recorded in most parts of the region in August 2002 with southern Sumatra, Kalimantan and Java receiving more than 75% below average rainfall
indicating the presence of weak to moderate El Niño conditions.
Below average rainfall continued to be recorded in most parts of Kalimantan and southern Sumatra in September 2002.
refs.pinpoint: 'Update of Regional Weather and Smoke Haze', section 1.1

regionalContext.text: ESA published a Terra MODIS image of 19 August 2002 that, according to its caption, shows haze across Central Kalimantan spreading across the entire island of Borneo, and NASA Earth Observatory reported that a satellite image of 17 October 2002 detected numerous fires through the smoke over Borneo.
regionalContext.label: observation

refs.quote: This TERRA-MODIS image acquired 19 August 2002 shows thick haze across Central Kalimantan and spreading across the entire island of Borneo.
satellite passed over the island of Borneo on October 17, 2002, ... captured this true-color image and detected numerous fires (red dots) through the thick smoke.

regionalContext.note: Neither caption names Malaysia; they are cited for the extent of smoke over Borneo. Both captions call the haze or smoke 'thick'; that is the agencies' description of the images, not a measurement, so it is left out of the claim. The ESA page credits the image to NASA. The NASA caption's general remarks on fire use are not repeated.

regionalContext.text: AFP reported on 1 October 2002 that hundreds of schools in Indonesia had been closed, flights disrupted and many residents of Borneo and Sumatra were wearing masks outdoors, as pollution 'hit dangerous levels' in some provinces.
regionalContext.label: observation

refs.quote: Hundreds of Indonesian schools have been closed, flights disrupted and many residents of Borneo and Sumatra islands have donned masks before venturing out, as pollution hit dangerous levels in some provinces.

regionalContext.note: Impacts on people in Indonesia, from a news-agency summary. AFP gives no index, value, province or date for 'dangerous levels'. No Indonesian government figures were found.

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study of air-quality data recorded by the Environmental Impact Agency of Palangka Raya at three sites in that city, in Central Kalimantan, reported daily PM10 concentrations above 250 µg/m³ on 84 days in 2002 and said the levels suggest that people living in Palangka Raya were subject to unhealthy conditions for a long time during the 2002 dry season; it describes Central Kalimantan, especially the area around Palangka Raya, as covered by thick smoke almost every day during the fires of 2002, which it says lasted four months.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: Several components of air quality, namely carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, nitrogen dioxide, ozone and particulate matter less than 10 μm in diameter, were monitored since 2001 by the Environmental Impact Agency of Palangka Raya at three sites in Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan.
This study focused on daily concentrations of carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate matter less than 10 μm in diameter (PM10) from 2001 to 2004.

The PM10 values were higher than 250 μg m -3 for 84 days in 2002. The high levels in air pollutant materials suggest that people living in Palangka Raya were subject to unhealthy conditions for a long time during the dry season in 2002.
During the forest fires in 2002 that lasted for 4 months, Central Kalimantan, especially the area surrounding Palangka Raya, was covered by thick smoke almost every day
refs.pinpoint: section 'Socio-economics and health' (PDF p. 7; journal p. 281)

regionalContext.note: Impacts on people in Indonesia: the study's interpretation of monitoring data supplied by the Environmental Impact Agency of Palangka Raya. It describes exposure, not health outcomes. Concentrations are given in µg/m³ as published; the study also classifies them on a United States index, whose categories are not used here and are not to be compared with Singapore's PSI or Malaysia's API. The paper also lists deaths, illnesses, airline losses and lost work 'in 2002', but cites them to reports of Indonesia's State Ministry of Environment dated 1998, one of them titled as an analysis of the 1997 fires (AI reading of the paper's reference list), so they are not used; its statements on school and airport closures give no source and are not used either (see 'Evidence not found').

regionalContext.text: A 2009 peer-reviewed study described 2002 as one of two minor fire episodes in Indonesia during 1997–2006 (with 2004) detected in the Global Fire Emissions Database, against major episodes in 1997/98 and 2006, and said the drought and haze in 2002 were weaker than in 1994 and 2006.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: During 1997–2006, there were two major fire episodes in Indonesia (1997/98, 2006) and two minor episodes (2002, 2004) detected in the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED; ref. 4), which occurred during droughts of different strengths

Although the 1994 and 2006 events, for example, did occur during moderate El Niño conditions, it was the positive IOD conditions that distinguished them from 2002, when the drought and haze were weaker (Fig. 4).

regionalContext.note: The study concerns fire activity, drought and haze in Indonesia; it does not assess air quality in Malaysia or Singapore. Relevant to criterion B3, which is not met.

diplomaticResponse.text: AFP reported on 24 September 2002 that Malaysia's environment minister had written to his Indonesian counterpart the previous month 'to complain about the annual haze hazard', and had voiced Malaysia's concern to him over fresh fires in Indonesian Borneo and Sumatra on the sidelines of the UN Earth Summit in Johannesburg earlier in September.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Environment Minister ... will lead a team of Malaysian experts to West Kalimantan later this week to determine the cause of the forest fires, and meet his Indonesian counterpart ... Earlier this month on the sidelines of the Earth Summit, ... voiced Malaysia's concern to ... over fresh fires on Indonesia's Borneo and Sumatra islands ... last month wrote a letter to ... to complain about the annual haze hazard
refs.pinpoint: paragraphs 11–13 (section 'Release API readings', paragraphs 5–7; AFP report, 24 September 2002)

refs.quote: The two ministers last met on the sidelines of the UN Earth Summit in Johannesburg last month

diplomaticResponse.note: As reported by AFP; the letter was not found. AFP says the concern was voiced 'earlier this month' (report of 24 September) and that the ministers met 'last month' (report of 1 October). The rest of the second quoted sentence, which repeats a generalisation about who sets fires, is omitted (project rule). No Indonesian reply to the letter was found; Indonesia's documented responses in this period are NEA's account of what Indonesian officials told it and OCHA's report of Indonesia's appeal of 7 October (both below).

diplomaticResponse.text: NEA said it had been sending satellite pictures of hotspots and fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan to Indonesia's environment and forestry ministries and had written to its Indonesian counterparts about the fires and the resulting smoke haze, later asking for more urgency in fire-control efforts; it reported that Indonesian officials said they were taking action and that Indonesia's State Ministry of Environment had assured it local authorities were stepping up fire-fighting.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Over the past weeks, NEA has been sending satellite pictures of hotspots and fires detected in Sumatra and Kalimantan to the Environment and Forestry Ministries of Indonesia. NEA has also written to its counterpart in the Environment Ministry to alert them of the fires, the impact of resulting smoke haze on our air quality, as well as our concern over the worsening situation.
The Indonesian officials have informed NEA that they are taking action to deal with the situation.

NEA has written to its Indonesian counterparts to ask for more urgency in intensifying their efforts to control forest and plantation fires. The Indonesian State Ministry of Environment is taking the situation seriously and has assured NEA that the local authorities in Sumatra and Kalimantan are stepping up fire-fighting efforts on the ground.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account of the exchange; no Indonesian record of it was found.

diplomaticResponse.text: Indonesia's environment minister held talks with Malaysia's environment minister on 7 October 2002; a UN OCHA situation report, citing Deutsche Presse-Agentur for the talks, said Indonesia appealed to Malaysia and other neighbouring countries that day for their understanding and assistance in tackling forest fires and warned that haze was likely to continue into the next year.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Minister of Environment, ... held bilateral talks with the Malaysian environmental minister, ... at Putrajaya, as reported by the Deutsche Presse-Agentur. Indonesia appealed to Malaysia and other neighbouring countries on Monday (7 Oct.) for their understanding and assistance in tackling forest fires, and warned of further haze likely to continue into the next year.
the matter was raised at a meeting in Kuala Lumpur between ... and his Indonesian counterpart on Oct 7.

diplomaticResponse.note: OCHA places the talks at Putrajaya; AFP says the meeting was in Kuala Lumpur (see 'Where sources disagree'). OCHA names DPA as its source for the talks; the sentence on Indonesia's appeal is not separately attributed. OCHA relays press reports; no government record of the talks was found.

diplomaticResponse.text: AFP reported on 1 October 2002 that, according to Malaysia's environment minister, a visit by Malaysian experts to West Kalimantan planned for the previous week had been postponed at Indonesia's request because of insufficient helicopters; on 17 October the DOE director-general told AFP that a delegation led by Malaysia's environment minister would visit Pontianak, West Kalimantan, on 4 November to study the causes of the fires and advise on open-burning control.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: said a plan to bring a team of Malaysian experts to west Kalimantan last week to develop a framework to tackle forest fires was postponed at Indonesia's request due to insufficient helicopters.
The delegation, led by Environment Minister ... will visit Pontianak in West Kalimantan province on Nov 4, Department of Environment director-general ... told AFP
His team of environmental officials and fire-fighting experts will study the causes of forest fires there and advise on an open-burning control system imposed in Malaysia 10 years ago, she said.

diplomaticResponse.note: Plans as announced, and the Malaysian minister's account of the postponement; no Indonesian statement about it was found. Whether the November visit took place was not checked.

selection.note: Criterion A is met: Singapore's NEA, an official body, states that fires over Kalimantan and parts of Sumatra produced the moderate to thick smoke haze that affected parts of southern Sarawak in August 2002, and that winds carried smoke haze from Kalimantan and southern Sumatra to Singapore in September and October; Malaysian officials quoted by two news organisations (Malaysiakini and AFP) also said the haze came from fires in Indonesia, while a Sarawak newspaper, relayed by Malaysiakini, reported local bushfires aggravating the situation in August. B1 is met only through reporting that cites DOE ('unhealthy' API descriptors at seven Sarawak areas in August and at six stations, then two, in September), and B2 only through news reports of official advice to cut outdoor activity (Health Department letters to schools and departments, reported by a Sarawak tabloid and relayed by Malaysiakini; a DOE official's advice against strenuous outdoor activity, reported by AFP). B3 is not met: a peer-reviewed study describes 2002 as a minor fire episode, and no official retrospective describing it as major was found.

attribution.note: Singapore's National Environment Agency, and Malaysian officials quoted in news reports, describe smoke from fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra. No public dispute about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. A Sarawak newspaper, relayed by Malaysiakini, reported that local bushfires made the haze worse in August.

confidence.rationale: Medium. The core account is that smoke haze affected Sarawak from mid-August into October 2002, Kuala Lumpur in late September, and Singapore at moderate 24-hour PSI levels in late September and mid-October. It is supported by a government source, Singapore's NEA (its 2002 haze reviews and news releases, read from Internet Archive copies), and corroborated independently by NASA Earth Observatory and ESA image captions and by contemporaneous news reports (Malaysiakini's own reports and AFP reports carried by Malaysiakini). Singapore's 24-hour PSI readings are quoted from NEA's releases. That NEA attributed the haze to fires in Kalimantan and southern Sumatra, and Malaysian officials to fires in Indonesia, is recorded as their assessment, not as this project's finding. MEDIUM conditions recorded in this entry hold: the Malaysian elements (the 'unhealthy' descriptors at Sarawak stations, the advice to cut outdoor activity and the mask distribution) rest on news reporting only, all read on Malaysiakini, and the Kuala Lumpur element on a single report; no DOE or Sarawak government record was found, and the one numeric index figure found ('exceeded 170') reached this record third-hand; Singapore's peak reading (the value behind the 'highest reading this year' that AFP attributed to NEA on 15 October 2002) and the end of the episode are not documented; and minor conflicts remain under 'Where sources disagree' (the place of the 7 October ministerial talks; and severity, where an Indonesian remote-sensing journal article says the 2002 haze distribution was 'not too significant' and a 2009 peer-reviewed study in Nature Geoscience describes 2002 as a minor fire episode in Indonesia). The core account does not rest on a single source or on reporting alone, so the LOW conditions do not hold. AI-assigned rating awaiting human review.

contradictions.text: Place of the 7 October 2002 ministerial talks: a UN OCHA report citing Deutsche Presse-Agentur says the Indonesian and Malaysian environment ministers met at Putrajaya, while AFP (via Malaysiakini) says the meeting was in Kuala Lumpur; an earlier AFP report (1 October) quoted Malaysia's minister as saying his Indonesian counterpart would visit Kuala Lumpur on 7–8 October. Not resolved. AI note: Putrajaya, Malaysia's federal administrative centre, is near Kuala Lumpur, so the difference may be one of wording rather than of fact.

Severity: NEA described 'moderate to thick smoke haze' over Kalimantan and parts of southern Sarawak in August and September 2002, a Meteorological Department spokesman described visibility in Sarawak and Sabah on the Friday before AFP's report of 17 August as 'one of the worst in years', and DOE officials (as reported) gave 'unhealthy' descriptors for seven Sarawak areas in August and six monitoring stations in September; but a 2004 Indonesian remote-sensing study says that 'haze distribution that occurred in the year 2002 was not too significant' (from NOAA and Feng Yun data), and a 2009 peer-reviewed study describes 2002 as one of two minor fire episodes in Indonesia detected in the Global Fire Emissions Database, with weaker drought and haze than 1994 and 2006. The measures differ (smoke extent seen by satellite, visibility, fire emissions, Malaysian station descriptors), and both studies concern Indonesia rather than Malaysia. Not resolved.

evidenceGaps: No DOE primary record for August–October 2002 was found: the Internet Archive's 2002 captures of DOE's website (then www.jas.sains.my) contain no haze or API pages (its api.html returned 404 in captures of 2 August, 2 November and 13 December 2002), and DOE's Environmental Quality Report for 2002 sits in a login-only digital library and was not read.

No published API values were found for this episode; the only number found is a deputy minister's 'exceeded 170', reported third-hand without station, time or averaging period. Peak values in Sarawak, Sabah and Kuala Lumpur are unknown.

No primary statement by the Sarawak state government was found: archived pages of the state Natural Resources and Environment Board (www.nreb.gov.my, captures of September–December 2002) and of the Malaysian Meteorological Department (www.kjc.gov.my, August–November 2002) contain no haze reports.

All Malaysian reporting used here was read on Malaysiakini (its own reports and AFP reports it carried). Searches for 2002 coverage by The Star, New Straits Times, Bernama, Borneo Post, BBC, Reuters and AP returned only later years; the search engine is weak on 2002.

Health: a Health Department officer, quoted by a Sarawak tabloid that Malaysiakini relayed on 20 August 2002, said the department was still waiting for hospital and clinic data on respiratory cases; no Ministry of Health Malaysia data for this episode were found.

Singapore: NEA's 'Year 2002 Press & Speech Releases' list (Internet Archive capture of 5 January 2003) includes 'Update On Smoke Haze And Health Precaution' (15 October 2002) and 'Clearer Skies In Two Weeks: Northeast Monsoon will end haze' (15 November 2002), but neither release was archived with its text, so the PSI value behind AFP's 'highest reading this year' (reported by NEA on 15 October 2002) and the end of the haze in Singapore are not documented. The November title suggests (AI reading of a title only) that haze was still present or expected in mid-November 2002. NEA's PSI table page was archived only in July and December 2002.
Brunei: no 2002 air-quality source was found, although Sarawak and Sabah, which border Brunei, were affected.

Indonesia: impacts on people rest on one AFP summary and one peer-reviewed study of air quality in Palangka Raya. That study (Tropics, 2007) also lists deaths, illnesses, airline losses and lost work in Central Kalimantan 'in 2002', but cites them to reports of Indonesia's State Ministry of Environment dated 1998, one of them titled as an analysis of the 1997 fires, so they were not used. UN OCHA's Indonesia situation reports Nos. 89–96, which preceded No. 97 (4–11 October 2002), have no archived copies, and no Indonesian government source on hotspots, air quality, health or school closures in 2002 was opened.

Indonesia's position: no statement by Indonesia's government on where the haze affecting Malaysia and Singapore came from, and no Indonesian reply to the Malaysian minister's letter of August 2002, was found. Indonesia's side appears only in NEA's account of what Indonesian officials told it and in OCHA's relay of a news agency report of 7 October. A news clipping dated 7 October 2002 in search results ('Indonesia vows to combat haze from forest fires', India Environment Portal) could not be downloaded (HTTP/2 error; no Internet Archive copy) and was not read.

Local fires in Sarawak: the only source found is The Borneo Post's report as relayed by Malaysiakini on 20 August 2002; no record by Sarawak's Natural Resources and Environment Board or by DOE of fires in Sarawak in August–October 2002 was found.
unresolvedQuestions: What API values and averaging periods did DOE record at Kuching, Sibu, Sarikei, Samarahan, Sri Aman, Kapit and Petra Jaya in August and September 2002, and what was the peak? Does DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2002 describe the episode?
Did any Kuala Lumpur or Klang Valley station reach 'unhealthy' in late September 2002? The DOE director-general declined to give the API.

Why does DOE's 'Chronology of Haze Episodes in Malaysia' (undated; the PDF was created in September 2015; cited in other episodes, such as August 2005) have no entry for 2002? How did the haze affect Sabah and Brunei in August–October 2002?
Did the Malaysian delegation's planned visit to Pontianak on 4 November 2002 take place, and with what outcome?

When did the haze end in Malaysia and Singapore? Did NEA's release of 15 November 2002 ('Clearer Skies In Two Weeks: Northeast Monsoon will end haze') describe haze still affecting Singapore in November?
How much did local fires in Sarawak contribute to the haze there in August 2002, as The Borneo Post's report (relayed by Malaysiakini) suggested?
Did Indonesia's government respond publicly to Malaysia's and Singapore's letters in 2002, and did it state a view on where the haze affecting its neighbours came from?
What did Indonesian health and education authorities record for Central and West Kalimantan in 2002? The figures a 2007 study gives for 2002 are cited to reports dated 1998.

period.label: August 2005

impact.text: A peer-reviewed study using daily visibility data for 2005–2015 from Changi Airport (Singapore) and Melaka ('Malacca' in the study) found an additional extreme haze event at Melaka in August 2005 that was not among Singapore's peaks, and refers to the absence of haze in Singapore during August 2005.
impact.label: analysis

refs.quote: To identify episodes of extreme haze in the Malay Peninsula, we use 2005–2015 hourly visibility data, averaged to daily means, from Changi Airport in Singapore and from the Malacca site
The Malacca time series reveals the same four peaks, with the October 2010 and June 2013 events somewhat less extreme than those in Singapore and with an additional event in August 2005.
The absence of haze in Singapore during August 2005 could be explained by two different phenomena.

impact.note: Visibility-based assessment. This research found no NEA PSI readings for August 2005.

impact.text: The same study suggested two possible explanations for the absence of haze in Singapore: a northward shift in boreal summer of MJO-related wind changes (the boreal summer intraseasonal oscillation), and two tropical storms in the western Pacific, during 1–5 and 8–12 August, whose wind fields may have influenced smoke transport between Riau and the Malay Peninsula.
impact.label: hypothesis

refs.quote: First, during boreal summer (May–October), the east-west trajectory of the MJO (and therefore MJO-related changes in wind direction) slowly shifts toward the north, with August–September marking the time period of peak shift. This northerly summertime MJO is sometimes called the boreal summer intraseasonal oscillation
Second, two separate tropical storms, one during 1–5 August and one during 8–12 August, are visible in the western Pacific around the time of the August 2005 haze event
The northward propagation of low-level wind fields related to these storms may have influenced smoke transport between Riau and the Malay Peninsula during this time.
