regionalContext.note: The statement's own date is not given. AP glossed the hotspots as 'fires'; a satellite hotspot is a heat anomaly and does not establish land ownership, who lit a fire or legal responsibility.

regionalContext.text: Environment News Service reported on 16 August 2005 that a helicopter survey by the Global Fire Monitoring Center (GFMC) around the Simpang Kubu River near Dumai, on Sumatra's east coast, found hundreds of small fires in that area of Riau province, and that the GFMC reported no forest burning, with fires in grasslands from previous land-clearing, scrubland, woody slash from secondary regrowth and some young oil palm plantations.
regionalContext.label: observation

refs.quote: JAKARTA, Indonesia , August 16, 2005 (ENS)

A helicopter survey today by the Global Fire Monitoring Center (GFMC) around the Simpang Kubu River, near the port city of Dumai, Sumatra's major east coast port, revealed hundreds of small fires burning in this area of Riau province.

The GFMC report indicates that no forest is burning, but the fires occur in grasslands resulting from previous land-clearings, scrub land, woody slash from secondary forest re-growth, and some young palm oil plantations.

regionalContext.note: A description of where fires were seen and on what land types, not of who lit them. The report dates the survey 'today', taken here to be 16 August 2005, the report's date.

regionalContext.text: Indonesia reported to the ASEAN senior environment officials that the smoke haze was mainly caused by land fires, particularly on peatland; the officials recognised the difficulty of mitigating peatland fires and fires in remote locations.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: Indonesia reported that the smoke haze is mainly caused by land fires, particularly on peatland. The Senior Officials recognised the difficulty of mitigating such peatland fires, and fires which occur in remote locations.

regionalContext.text: Indonesia told the ASEAN senior environment officials that it had mobilised 1,000 personnel, including forest rangers, Manggala Agni fire brigades, the army and police, and that the fires were under control; BBC News had earlier reported that more than 1,000 separate fires were still burning in Sumatra and that Indonesian officials warned it could be several days before they were brought under control.
regionalContext.label: fact

refs.quote: Indonesia has mobilised 1,000 personnel comprising forest rangers, Manggala Agni fire-brigades, army, police, NGOs and forest concessionaires. Indonesia informed that the fires are now under control.
But more than 1,000 separate fires are still burning in Sumatra, and Indonesian officials have warned that it could be several days before they are brought under control.

regionalContext.note: BBC report of 12 August 2005; ASEAN statement of 17 August 2005. 'More than 1,000 fires' is BBC's figure, not a satellite hotspot count.

regionalContext.text: Smoke haze in Indonesia was also reported: the ASEAN senior environment officials' statement of 17 August 2005 refers to smoke haze pollution in Sumatra; AP reported on 11 August 2005 that parts of Indonesia were also affected; and a Singapore Civil Defence Force web page titled 'Rokan Hilir Bush Fires, Sumatra, Indonesia (2005)' states that the haze affected Indonesia as well as Malaysia and Thailand, quoting The Straits Times of 22 August 2005 as reporting that thousands of hectares of land in Rokan Hilir, Bangko and Kubu had been covered in smoke for weeks.
regionalContext.label: observation

refs.quote: Penang, Malaysia, 17 August 2005: The ASEAN Senior Officials on the Environment (ASOEN) met on 16 – 17 August 2005 and as a matter of priority addressed the current fires and haze situation in the region.
The Senior Officials viewed with concern the fires in North Sumatra and Riau Provinces which caused serious smoke haze pollution in Sumatra, parts of Peninsular Malaysia and Southern Thailand.
Winds blow most of the fumes across the narrow Strait of Malacca to Malaysia, although parts of Indonesia are also affected.
Rokan Hilir Bush Fires, Sumatra, Indonesia (2005)
resulting in haze affecting not only Indonesia but Malaysia and Thailand as well
According to Straits Times (dated 22 August 2005), 'thousands of hectares of land in Rokan Hilir, Bangko and Kubu, about 400 km from Pekanbaru, have been blanketed in smoke for weeks'.

regionalContext.note: These reports describe smoke over places in Indonesia; none gives readings, health data or numbers of people affected, and no Indonesian government record of impacts on people in Sumatra in August 2005 was found (see 'Evidence not found'). The Singapore Civil Defence Force page is undated and relays a newspaper report. The ASEAN statement calls the pollution 'serious' (its assessment) and also says where the smoke came from (see 'What happened').

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study identified August 2005 as one of two severe haze events in the Malay Peninsula in 2005–2015, besides June 2013, that occurred without El Niño conditions; common to all three were anomalously strong westerly winds over Riau province during late phases of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and negative phases of the Indian Ocean Dipole, and the study locates the fires associated with the August 2005 haze in Riau province.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: the June 2013 haze occurred in the absence of an El Niño, during negative Indian Ocean Dipole conditions, with smoke carried eastward to the Peninsula from fires in the Riau province of central Sumatra. We show that June 2013 was not an exceptional event; inspection of visibility data during 2005–2015 reveals two other severe haze events in the Malay Peninsula (August 2005 and October 2010) occurring under similar conditions.

Common to all three events was a combination of anomalously strong westerly winds over Riau province concurrent with late phases of the Real-Time Multivariate Madden-Julian Oscillation Index, during negative phases of the Indian Ocean Dipole.
Riau province, where fires associated with haze in the Malay Peninsula occurred during August 2005, October 2010, and June 2013, is shown in blue.

regionalContext.note: Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres (2018). The other event besides June 2013 was October 2010. A meteorological analysis; it does not address who started fires.

regionalContext.text: In the analysis of the 2018 study (Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres), strong westerlies over Riau began to strengthen on 27 July as the MJO index (RMM) entered phase 5, haze arrived in Melaka ('Malacca' in the study) on 2 August and peaked on 10–11 August, and the westerlies dropped off abruptly after the index left phase 8 on 12 August.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: Published online 13 JUN 2018

The haze event in the Malacca-Kuala Lumpur region during August 2005 was again characterized by strong westerlies over Riau, which began to strengthen on 27 July just as the RMM index entered phase 5.
As in the June 2013 event, westerly wind speeds during August 2005 remained elevated as haze arrived in Malacca on 2 August and peaked on 10–11 August.
The strong westerlies dropped off abruptly after the RMM index exited phase 8 on 12 August.
In this case, the first sign of haze in Malacca appears to have preceded fire activity in Riau, which began on 5 August and quickly ramped up.

regionalContext.note: RMM = Real-time Multivariate MJO index. The authors note that haze at Melaka appears to precede fire activity in Riau (from 5 August) in their fire-count data, which they say may be due in part to uncertainty in the fire counts (see 'Where sources disagree').

regionalContext.text: A 2023 peer-reviewed study's (EnvironmentAsia) back-trajectory analysis found that during the August 2005 haze the air masses reaching its study stations in Peninsular Malaysia originated from Sumatra and arrived from the south-west.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: EnvironmentAsia 16(1) (2023) 111-125
From Figure 3 (a), the trajectory during haze in August 2005 showed that the air masses clearly originated from Sumatra, arriving the study area from southwest direction.

Figure 4 shows the backward trajectories that were used to calculate the 120-hours (four days) at the height of 500m above ground level (AGL). Larkin was excluded from this analysis since it has no to minimal effects of HPE as discussed earlier.

regionalContext.note: EnvironmentAsia (2023). Modelled back trajectories (HYSPLIT, 120 hours, 500 m above ground level) for three of the study's four stations (Shah Alam, Nilai and Bukit Rambai; Larkin was excluded); the text refers to 'Figure 3 (a)', although the trajectory maps appear to be in Figure 4 (an observation by the AI agent). The passage describes where air masses came from, not where any particular fire was or who started fires.

diplomaticResponse.text: Indonesia's forestry minister and Malaysia's environment minister met in Sumatra on Thursday 11 August (BBC News); according to Environment News Service, at an 11 August meeting in Medan, North Sumatra, Indonesia agreed to accept Malaysia's offer of cloud seeding over Sumatra and technical assistance on non-burning land-clearing techniques. AP reported that the two countries agreed that day to use cloud seeding, and BBC News that ministers from both countries agreed a three-point plan 'to tackle the source of the fires burning across Sumatra'.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: on Thursday, Indonesian Forestry Minister ... met Malaysian Environment Minister ... in Sumatra, where more than 900 fires are reported to be burning.
refs.pinpoint: Section '900 fires burning'; article of 11 August 2005

refs.quote: At an August 11 meeting in Medan, North Sumatra, Indonesia agreed to accept Malaysia's offer of cloud seeding over Sumatra and technical assistance on the use of non-burning techniques for land clearing.
The two countries did agree Thursday to use cloud seeding to try to induce rain over Sumatra to stop the burning of the forests.
On Thursday ministers from both countries agreed a three-point plan to tackle the source of the fires burning across Sumatra.

diplomaticResponse.note: Ministers' names withheld (ellipses in the BBC quote). The contents of the three-point plan were not found.

diplomaticResponse.text: According to the ASEAN senior environment officials' statement, Malaysia mobilised 100 firefighters with equipment and 25 personnel of its Special Malaysian Assistance Rescue Team (SMART) to assist Indonesia and was arranging cloud seeding in the affected areas, Thailand said it was ready to provide assistance on request, and Viet Nam offered 15 firefighters with equipment; Environment News Service reported that the Malaysian firefighters were sent to Pekanbaru, Riau.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Malaysia offered assistance to Indonesia and subsequently mobilised 100 fire-fighters and equipment, 25 SMART (Special Malaysian Assistance Rescue Team) personnel, and is currently making arrangements for cloud seeding in the affected areas.
Thailand is ready to provide any assistance as may be requested. Viet Nam has offered to send 15 fire-fighters and equipment.
Malaysia has dispatched 100 firemen to Pekan Baru, Riau equipped with transport, fire fighting equipment and personal protective gear.

diplomaticResponse.note: ENS spells the town 'Pekan Baru'.

policyDevelopments.text: Malaysia's deputy prime minister said on 9 August that there were no plans to make the Air Pollutant Index public; according to Oxford Business Group, after a cabinet meeting the next day it was announced that the API would be made public with immediate effect, and DOE had figures posted on its website by the end of the day; DOE's archived API pages list daily tables from 10 August 2005.
policyDevelopments.label: fact

refs.quote: This appeared to be the current government’s view too, when Deputy Prime Minister ... said on August 9, “We will just monitor the situation and give advice,” advising that there were no plans to make the API public.
He was responding to Deputy Prime Minister ... statement yesterday that Malaysians must be content with the information on the haze as the government has no plans to make the index public.
The next day however, the government position changed rapidly and following a cabinet meeting, the announcement came that the ban on disclosure of the API was to be dropped with immediate effect.
The department of environment had figures posted on its website by the end of the day
Air Pollutant Index (API) 10th August 2005 11th August 2005 12 th August 2005 13th August 2005 14th August 2005

policyDevelopments.note: The OBG page is dated 22 July 2010, apparently a later re-posting, and reports these events as current; Malaysiakini's report of 10 August 2005 corroborates the deputy prime minister's statement of the previous day. OBG's own words are that 'the ban on disclosure of the API was to be dropped'; descriptions of the API as a secret are recorded separately, as an allegation. The name of the deputy prime minister is withheld (ellipses). OBG's API values for 10 August differ from DOE's archived table (see 'Where sources disagree'). See also the milestones on Malaysia's API reporting (1997 and August 2005) under 'How haze is measured'.

policyDevelopments.text: Malaysiakini reported in August 2002 that API index figures had not been released since the height of the 1997 haze, only the descriptors.
policyDevelopments.label: fact

refs.quote: Published: Aug 20, 2002 7:38 AM
However, index figures have not been released since the height of the haze in 1997, only the descriptors

policyDevelopments.note: Context for DOE's descriptor-only reports in early August 2005 (see 'Malaysia: Air quality'); see also the milestones on Malaysia's API reporting under 'How haze is measured'.

policyDevelopments.text: ARTICLE 19 and the Centre for Independent Journalism (CIJ) wrote in a report dated January 2007 that the API 'remained a State secret from the haze crisis of 1997/8 until the haze crisis of August 2005'; Oxford Business Group described the API as having 'been an official secret since 1997'.
policyDevelopments.label: allegation

refs.quote: January 2007 © ARTICLE 19 and CIJ
the Air Pollutant Index (API) remained a State secret from the haze crisis of 1997/8 until the haze crisis of August 2005.
refs.pinpoint: Introduction (per the table of contents), PDF p.12 (printed p.2)

refs.quote: This worsening air quality and the anticipated longevity of the problem had put the government under increasing pressure to publish the API, which has been an official secret since 1997.

policyDevelopments.note: Labelled an allegation: neither source cites a government document on the API's classification, and none was found during this research. No government statement on whether the API was classified was found either; the officials' statements recorded here concern whether readings would be published, not their classification. 'Haze crisis' is the report's wording.

policyDevelopments.text: At their meeting of 16–17 August 2005 (statement datelined Penang, 17 August), ASEAN senior environment officials set up a Panel of ASEAN Experts on Fire and Haze Assessment and Coordination, which ASEAN environment ministers had agreed to establish, to undertake rapid assessments on the ground during critical periods of fires and haze and to recommend immediate responses.
policyDevelopments.label: fact

refs.quote: Penang, Malaysia, 17 August 2005: The ASEAN Senior Officials on the Environment (ASOEN) met on 16 – 17 August 2005 and as a matter of priority addressed the current fires and haze situation in the region.

To further enhance the existing regional mechanism, the ASEAN Environment Ministers agreed to establish a Panel of ASEAN Experts on Fire and Haze Assessment and Coordination. The Panel will undertake rapid assessment of the situation on the ground during critical periods of fires and haze, and provide recommendations to facilitate immediate response and effective mobilisation of resources in the region. Pursuant to the decision, the Senior Officials have at this Meeting set up the Panel.

policyDevelopments.note: The statement does not say when the ministers agreed to establish the panel.

legalDevelopments.text: Environment News Service reported on 16 August 2005 that Indonesia had deployed a team of investigators to verify hotspots and collect evidence for law enforcement purposes, and that Indonesia's forestry minister said the managements of 10 companies were being questioned by the Environment Ministry.
legalDevelopments.label: fact

refs.quote: JAKARTA, Indonesia , August 16, 2005 (ENS)
Indonesia has deployed a team of investigators to verify the hotspots and collect evidence for law enforcement purposes.
The managements of the 10 companies are currently being questioned by the Environment Ministry

legalDevelopments.note: Questioning and investigation are not findings of wrongdoing, and no outcome was found during this research. A satellite hotspot does not establish land ownership, who lit a fire or legal responsibility. Parties withheld under METHODOLOGY section 8; the sources do not name the companies. ENS reports the minister's remarks as made on Monday (15 August 2005) and attributes the remark immediately before this passage to Indonesia's official Antara news agency. The report's sentence giving the context of the questioning is not reproduced because it concerns responsibility for the fires (see 'Unresolved questions').

legalDevelopments.text: In their statement of 17 August 2005, the ASEAN senior environment officials noted enforcement actions taken by Indonesia.
legalDevelopments.label: fact

refs.quote: Penang, Malaysia, 17 August 2005: The ASEAN Senior Officials on the Environment (ASOEN) met on 16 – 17 August 2005 and as a matter of priority addressed the current fires and haze situation in the region.
In this respect, the Senior Officials noted the enforcement actions taken against errant parties by Indonesia.

legalDevelopments.note: The statement's wording is 'enforcement actions taken against errant parties by Indonesia'. 'Errant parties' names no party and is not a finding; the statement does not describe the actions, and it does not link them to the companies reported by Environment News Service.

aftermath.text: DOE's chronology records that on 16 August 2005, 13 stations recorded good air quality and 38 moderate; Environment News Service reported on 16 August 2005 that the air quality emergencies declared in Malaysia the previous week had been lifted and that the haze was moving northwards to northern Peninsular Malaysia, Penang, Butterworth and Kota Bharu.
aftermath.label: observation

refs.quote: The air quality returned to normal on 16 August 2005 with 13 stations recorded good air quality level and 38 stations at moderate level.
JAKARTA, Indonesia , August 16, 2005 (ENS)

The air quality emergencies declared in various locations of Malaysia last week have now been lifted due to the changed wind direction and increased rainfall. The smoky haze is now moving northwards to the northern parts of Peninsular Malaysia, Penang, Butterworth and Kota Bahru.

aftermath.note: DOE's chronology describes air quality as having 'returned to normal' on 16 August 2005 (DOE's assessment), the end date used for this episode. DOE's counts refer to its API bands (averaging period not stated). ENS attributed the lifting of the emergencies to the changed wind direction and increased rainfall, and spells the town 'Kota Bahru'.

selection.note: Criterion A is met: NASA Earth Observatory, the ASEAN senior environment officials' statement of 17 August 2005 and a 2018 peer-reviewed study describe the haze in Malaysia as smoke from fires in Sumatra (NASA: on its eastern shore; ASEAN: in North Sumatra and Riau provinces; the 2018 study: in Riau province), and a 2023 study's back trajectories show air masses arriving from Sumatra. B1 is met by DOE's API tables (values above 100 at several stations on each of 10–13 August 2005 and above 500 at two on 11 August; averaging period not stated), B2 by the Haze Emergency of 11–13 August, school closures reported by AP and BBC News, and official advice to limit outdoor activities, and B3 by DOE's undated chronology (more severe than 1997 for Peninsular Malaysia) and the 2018 study (a severe haze event).

attribution.note: NASA and ASEAN senior environment officials describe fires in Sumatra causing smoke haze in Peninsular Malaysia; a peer-reviewed study associates the haze with strong westerly winds over Riau province, where it locates the associated fires, and a second study's back-trajectory analysis shows air masses arriving from Sumatra. No public dispute between governments about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened: Indonesia agreed to accept Malaysia's offer of cloud seeding, and Malaysia sent firefighters to Riau. A business publisher wrote that peat fires in Selangor were 'also blamed', without saying by whom, while Malaysia's Fire and Rescue Department was reported as saying the haze was not the result of fires in the country (see Where sources disagree). Officials of both countries also made public statements about companies' possible role in the fires; these concern responsibility, not where the smoke came from, and are not recorded as claims (see Unresolved questions).

confidence.rationale: Medium (AI-assigned, awaiting human review). The core account (haze over the Klang Valley and the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia from early August 2005; a Haze Emergency at Port Klang and Kuala Selangor from 11 to 13 August after API values above 500; air quality described by DOE as back to normal on 16 August) rests on primary records of Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE): its chronology of haze episodes and its API tables for 10–13 August 2005 (Internet Archive copies). It is corroborated by sources independent of DOE: the ASEAN senior environment officials' statement of 17 August 2005, NASA Earth Observatory, a 2018 peer-reviewed study (haze at Melaka from 2 August, peaking on 10–11 August), a Tourism Malaysia media release of 11 August 2005, and AP and BBC reports. The API values and emergency dates are quoted from DOE's records, which settle the differing dates and values given in later or secondary sources (NADMA's '1 August, API 231', a book preface's 'September 2005', a study's µg/m3 wording and Oxford Business Group's 10 August values). The rating is medium, not high, because conditions in the MEDIUM definition hold: the end date rests on DOE's chronology alone (NASA Earth Observatory says the haze lifted starting on 13 August); the school closures and transport disruption in Malaysia are known only from AP and BBC reports and NASA Earth Observatory captions, with no official record found; and minor conflicts remain unresolved, about airport disruption, the extent of the haze on 11 August, severity compared with 1997, when fire activity began in Riau, and whether fires in Malaysia contributed. The entry also records that Singapore's apparent non-involvement rests on a visibility-based study and a ministry's list of severe years, with no NEA readings found, and that effects in Indonesia and southern Thailand rest on the ASEAN statement, news reports and a Singapore Civil Defence Force page quoting a newspaper. What would firm up the record: DOE's emergency declaration and press statements of August 2005, its API tables for 14 and 16 August, NEA's PSI records for August 2005, Ministry of Education records of school closures, and Indonesian government records of the fires and their effects in Riau and North Sumatra.

contradictions.text: Metric of the 11 August 2005 readings. DOE's chronology says the Air Pollution Index (API) exceeded 500 at Port Klang ('Pelabuhan Klang' in the chronology) and Kuala Selangor, and DOE's 11 August table shows API values of 529 and 531 there at 11.00 am. A 2023 peer-reviewed study (EnvironmentAsia), citing 'DoE, 2013', instead says the 'PM10 concentration exceeded 500 µg/m3' in these two areas. The API is a unitless index, not a concentration; the primary DOE records use the index, so DOE's API wording is used and the µg/m3 figure is not adopted (assessment by the AI agent).

Month of the episode. The preface to the 2006 reprint of an ISEAS/IDRC book on the 1997–98 fires says parts of Peninsular Malaysia were severely affected by smoke 'in September 2005'. DOE (chronology and contemporaneous API tables), NASA Earth Observatory and BBC News date the episode and the emergency to August 2005 (emergency 11–13 August). The primary DOE records settle the month; the preface's 'September' is not adopted (assessment by the AI agent: probably an error).

Date and reading of the 2005 emergency. Free Malaysia Today (Bernama, 17 September 2019), reporting a statement by Malaysia's National Disaster Management Agency (NADMA), says a haze emergency was declared 'on Aug 1, 2005 in Kuala Selangor and Port Klang, Selangor, when the API was 231'. DOE's chronology gives 11 August 2005 with the API above 500; a tourism media release dated 11 August 2005 (published by Tourism Malaysia) reports the declaration; and DOE's contemporaneous table shows 529 and 531 at 11.00 am on 11 August. These primary records support 11 August and values above 500, so the NADMA figures are not adopted.

'First time above 500'. AP (11 August 2005) said it was the first time the 500 level had been passed in Malaysia. DOE's chronology records that the API reached above 500 in Sarawak in September 1997, when a Haze Emergency was declared there. AP's statement may refer only to Peninsular Malaysia (a possibility suggested by the AI agent); it is not adopted.

Severity compared with 1997. DOE's undated chronology calls the August 2005 episode more severe than 1997 'as far as Peninsular Malaysia is concerned'. BBC News said on 12 August 2005 that air pollution in Malaysia had 'yet to match the 1997 levels', and on 11 August called the haze 'the worst since 1998'; AP (11 August 2005) called it 'the country's worst environmental crisis since 1997', and NASA Earth Observatory (20 August 2005), citing AP, 'the worst haze crisis since 1997-1998'; the Global Fire Monitoring Center, as reported by Environment News Service on 16 August 2005, said the event was no worse than on previous occasions and that the wind direction had brought most of the smoke to Kuala Lumpur. These characterisations differ in scope (Peninsular Malaysia or the whole country; haze or fires) and are recorded, not reconciled.

Airports. BBC News (11 August 2005) said the haze was disrupting airports; a tourism media release published by Tourism Malaysia, dated 8.00 pm the same day, said all flights at KLIA were arriving and departing as scheduled. The two may refer to different airports or times of day (a possibility suggested by the AI agent); no airport-operator record was found.

API values for 10 August 2005. Oxford Business Group says the figures posted on 10 August showed Kuala Lumpur at 181 and Shah Alam and Kuala Selangor at 316 and 326. DOE's archived table for 10 August shows Kuala Lumpur at 176 (11:00 am) and 276 (5:00 pm), Shah Alam at 290 and 349, and Kuala Selangor at 291 and 418. OBG may have used readings from another hour (a possibility suggested by the AI agent); the DOE table is used here.

Timing of fires and haze. AP (4 August 2005) reported DOE as saying satellite images showed 587 hotspots in Riau and northern Sumatra. The peer-reviewed MJO study's fire-count data show fire activity in Riau beginning on 5 August, after haze first appeared at Melaka on 2 August, which its authors say may be due in part to uncertainty in the fire counts. The two may use different satellite products, areas and definitions (a possibility suggested by the AI agent); not reconciled.

Extent of the haze on 11 August 2005. The tourism media release dated 11 August 2005 (8.00 pm) said the haze was 'localized to specific areas along the Klang Valley' and that 'the rest of the country is haze-free', naming Penang, Langkawi, the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia, Sarawak and Sabah as having good air quality. DOE's API table for the same day (averaging period not stated) shows readings in DOE's unhealthy band (101–200) at stations outside Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya at 11.00 am and 5.00 pm: Tanjung Malim, Perak (132 and 127); Nilai (170 and 175) and Seremban (131 and 140), Negeri Sembilan; Bukit Rambai, Melaka (118 and 113); and Jerantut, Pahang (121 and 116). By the AI agent's count, most stations in the places the release names were in DOE's moderate band (51–100). The release gives no readings and may describe visible haze rather than API bands (a possibility suggested by the AI agent); DOE's table is the agency's measurement record.

Whether fires in Malaysia contributed. Oxford Business Group wrote that 'peat fires in the capital state of Selangor, south of the government city, Putrajaya, are also blamed' for the smoke, without saying by whom or giving evidence. Malaysiakini reported on 10 August 2005 that Malaysia's Fire and Rescue Department said the haze was not a result of fires in the country, and that its director-general said the hotspots seen in satellite images of Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak had all been put out. AP's report dated 4 August 2005 cites DOE as saying that satellite images showed 17 hotspots in Sarawak. No source opened estimates whether, or how much, smoke from fires in Malaysia contributed to the haze in the Klang Valley; not reconciled.

evidenceGaps: Singapore: no National Environment Agency PSI readings, health advisories or press releases for August 2005 were found; NEA and environment ministry releases of 2005 (for example in the National Archives of Singapore) were not searched in this research.

DOE documents linked from its API page in August 2005 (a 'Declaration of Haze Emergency Status Area' PDF and two press statements on the open-burning prohibition) were not archived: no capture of the declaration PDF was found, and the Internet Archive holds only 404 captures of the two press statements, made on 23 September 2005 under different paths. The prohibition order's date, legal basis and terms, and the text of the emergency declaration, are therefore unknown.
DOE's daily API tables for 14 and 16 August 2005 were not archived; hourly API values and the averaging period DOE used in 2005 were not found.
No official count of closed schools (Ministry of Education Malaysia) and no airport-operator or port record of flight or shipping disruption were found; these rest on BBC and AP reports.

Health: no Ministry of Health Malaysia attendance or admission figures for August 2005 were found. A 2018 review in the Malaysian Journal of Public Health Medicine gives a hospital admission cost of MYR 1.8 million for the 2005 haze, citing a 2014 study whose abstract reports a different measure (an average annual economic loss valued at MYR273,000, based on the inpatient cases the study associated with haze in its study years 2005, 2006, 2008 and 2009); the full 2014 paper was not opened, so the cost figure is not used.

Indonesia: no Indonesian government source (for example the Ministry of Forestry or the meteorological agency) on hotspot counts, air quality or impacts on people in Riau and North Sumatra in August 2005 was found, and web searches in English and Indonesian found no contemporaneous report of school closures, flight disruption or respiratory illness there that month. Effects in Indonesia rest on the ASEAN statement, AP and Environment News Service reports and a Singapore Civil Defence Force page quoting The Straits Times. ASMC hotspot counts for August 2005 were not found.
The special ASEAN senior officials' meeting in Kuala Lumpur on 13 August 2005 is documented only by Environment News Service; no ASEAN record of it was found.

Southern Thailand: the impact rests on the ASEAN statement and an ENS report of warnings and mask distribution by Thailand's Disaster Prevention and Mitigation Department; no Thai government source was opened.

No DOE statement or study opened in this research assesses whether fires in Malaysia contributed to the August 2005 haze; the only statements found are those recorded under 'Where sources disagree' (Oxford Business Group; the Fire and Rescue Department as reported by Malaysiakini).
unresolvedQuestions: What averaging period did DOE use for the API values it published at 11.00 am and 5.00 pm in August 2005, and what were the hourly peaks on 10–12 August?
Why does NADMA's 2019 list give 1 August 2005 and an API of 231 for this emergency, when DOE's records give 11 August and values above 500?
What were the date, legal basis and scope of the DOE Director General's open-burning prohibition order listed on DOE's API page?
Was the 10 August 2005 decision to publish API readings recorded formally (for example in a cabinet or ministry statement), and did DOE publish any numeric API values between 1998 and 9 August 2005?
Did any Kuala Lumpur station record an 'unhealthy' API descriptor between 1998 and July 2005? AP (4 August 2005) said Kuala Lumpur last reported unhealthy air quality in 1997.
What was the outcome of the investigations and questioning reported in Indonesia in August 2005?
Did Singapore's PSI leave the good or moderate range at any time in August 2005?

How did the governments of Indonesia and Malaysia follow up the public statements that officials of both countries made on 11–15 August 2005 about companies' possible role in the fires (reported by AP, BBC News, Environment News Service and Oxford Business Group)? These statements are allegations about responsibility for the fires; they are not recorded as claims here because no finding about responsibility was found, and a company operating in an area where fires were reported is not thereby shown to be responsible for them.
Did fires in Malaysia, such as the peat fires in Selangor that Oxford Business Group said were 'also blamed', contribute to the August 2005 haze in the Klang Valley, and if so how much?

events.title: July–November 2006: Singapore, Sarawak and Peninsular Malaysia

period.label: July–November 2006, more intense from late September to October

refs.quote: Malaysia experienced slight to moderate haze episodes in mid-July, ... and late September to October 2006.
refs.pinpoint: p.2, row 4 (2006); the elided word is 'mid-August', hyphenated across a line break in the PDF

refs.quote: Increased rainfall brought by the Inter-Monsoon helped to gradually ease the haze situation in the region and conditions return to normal by mid November 2006.

period.note: Start from the earliest 2006 episode in DOE's chronology (mid-July); end from NEA's statement that conditions returned to normal by mid-November 2006, the only source opened that gives an end date. NEA's Annual Report 2006/07 reports unhealthy air quality in Singapore on three days in October 2006.

summary.text: Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) stated in its Annual Report 2006/07 that dry weather from early June 2006 increased land and forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and that in October 2006 the winds blew dense smoke haze to Singapore first from southern Sumatra and later, after turning southeasterly, from Kalimantan.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: The onset of the Southwest Monsoon season in the region in early June 2006 brought the traditional dry season to the southern ASEAN countries. The drier weather conditions resulted in increased land and forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan.

In October 2006 prevailing southerly to southwesterly winds blew the dense smoke haze directly from southern Sumatra to Singapore. When the prevailing wind direction later changed to southeasterly, Singapore was also affected by dense smoke haze blown from Kalimantan.
National Environment Agency | Annual Report 2006/07

summary.note: NEA's statement of where the smoke came from is the agency's assessment (in this passage, based on the direction of the prevailing winds) and is attributed as such.

The quote elides 'mid-August', which is hyphenated across a line break in the PDF.

regionalContext.text: Bernama reported from Kuching on 5 October 2006 that a forecaster from the State Meteorological Services Department said the southwesterly winds were bringing the haze from hotspots in Kalimantan into the state, and that the haze was expected to clear by mid-October.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: October 05, 2006 19:54 PM
KUCHING, Oct 5 (Bernama)
Meanwhile a forecaster from the State Meteorological Services Department said the haze was expected to be cleared by mid-October
will reduce the strength of the southwesterly bringing the haze from hotspots in Kalimantan into the state

regionalContext.note: The forecaster's view of where the haze came from, as reported; attributed. 'The state' is Sarawak, the subject of the report. The clearing by mid-October was a forecast made on 5 October, not a record of when the haze cleared. A single news report: not counted for criterion A, which is met by official sources elsewhere in this record.

diplomaticResponse.text: Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on 11 October 2006 that the Prime Minister had written to Indonesia's President to express disappointment over the recurring haze problem, 'which has been particularly serious this year', and that MFA had conveyed its concerns in a Third Person Note handed to the chargé d'affaires of the Indonesian Embassy in Singapore on 9 October 2006.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: 11 October 2006
to express his disappointment over the recurring haze problem, which has been particularly serious this year
MFA had also conveyed these concerns on the haze issue in a Third Person Note which was handed to the Charge d'Affaires of the Indonesian Embassy in Singapore on 9 October 2006.
After the PSI peaked at 128 on 7 October 2006, our Prime Minister wrote to
on 10 October 2006 to express our concern over the recurring haze problem

diplomaticResponse.note: NEA's Annual Report dates the letter to 10 October 2006.

diplomaticResponse.text: AFP reported that on 11 October 2006 Indonesia's President apologised, on behalf of the Indonesian government, to neighbouring countries for the haze ('this incident'), saying it was not intentional and that Indonesia was continuously trying to tackle it and prevent it in future; AFP also reported that Indonesia agreed to convene a meeting of regional environment ministers.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Posted: 11 October 2006 2058 hrs
On behalf of the Indonesian government, I have to apologise to the neighbouring countries for this incident even though clearly this is not an intentional (act) by Indonesia
agreed to convene a meeting of regional environment ministers to tackle the problem
Clearly, this is not a problem we intend to inflict to our neighbours and we are continuously trying to tackle it and prevent it in future

diplomaticResponse.note: A diplomatic apology as reported by AFP; it is not a finding about who caused the fires or about legal responsibility.

diplomaticResponse.text: Singapore had announced a meeting in Singapore on 13 October 2006 of environment ministers from the ASEAN countries affected by the haze; on 11 October its foreign ministry said Singapore was happy to shift the meeting to Indonesia because the forest fires were on Indonesian territory.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: a meeting of Environment Ministers from the ASEAN countries affected by the haze will be held in Singapore on 13 October 2006. Its objective is to muster ASEAN's resources to help Indonesia cope with the present haze problem.
11 October 2006
Singapore was happy to agree to shift the meeting to Indonesia. As the forest fires are on Indonesian territories, this is a more appropriate venue.

diplomaticResponse.text: Channel NewsAsia reported on 12 October 2006 that Indonesia's President had called Singapore's Prime Minister that afternoon and assured him that Indonesia would take effective measures to prevent forest fires in future; citing Singapore's Foreign Affairs Ministry, it said the two leaders also agreed that Indonesia and regional countries would take concrete steps and develop a long-term plan to prevent the haze, and it added that Indonesia would also ratify the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution signed in 2002.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Posted: 12 October 2006 1943 hrs
assured him that Indonesia will take effective measures to prevent forest fires in future
The Foreign Affairs Ministry said the two leaders also agreed that Indonesia and regional countries would take concrete steps and develop a long term plan to prevent the haze.
Indonesia will also ratify the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution signed in 2002.

diplomaticResponse.note: The report does not make clear whether the ratification sentence reports the call or is the broadcaster's own statement.

diplomaticResponse.text: The Sub-regional Ministerial Meeting on Transboundary Haze Pollution, attended by ministers and senior officials responsible for the environment from Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, was held in Pekanbaru on 13 October 2006; it noted that the haze problem had not been adequately addressed by the region, while acknowledging the efforts taken by countries in the region, and agreed to set up a Ministerial Steering Committee of the five countries' environment ministers.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: The Sub-regional Ministerial Meeting on Transboundary Haze Pollution was held in Pekanbaru on 13 October 2006. The Meeting was attended by the Ministers and other high ranking officials responsible for the environment from Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.
noted the haze problem has not been adequately addressed by the region, while acknowledging the efforts taken by countries in the region

The Meeting also agreed to set up a Ministerial Steering Committee to oversee the implementation of short and long-term plans to effectively tackle the haze problem. The Committee will comprise the Environment Ministers from Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.

diplomaticResponse.text: The Pekanbaru meeting's joint statement recorded that the meeting appreciated Indonesia's efforts to tackle land and forest fires and was committed to support Indonesia, and that it 'respectfully urged' Indonesia to finalise urgently its ratification of the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in accordance with its national law.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: the Meeting appreciated the Indonesian efforts to tackle land and forest fires that resulted in transboundary haze pollution and was committed to support Indonesia in its endeavor
The Meeting respectfully urged Indonesia to urgently finalize the ratification of ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in accordance with its national law.

diplomaticResponse.text: Bernama reported on 12 October 2006 that Malaysia would ask haze-affected countries in the region to set up a special fund to fight the forest fires in Indonesia, and that the proposal would be submitted at the Pekanbaru meeting the next day; the meeting's joint statement recorded its appreciation of Malaysia's initiative on operationalising an ASEAN transboundary haze pollution control fund.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: October 12, 2006 16:28 PM
Malaysia will ask the nations affected by the haze in the region to set up a special fund to fight the source of the problem and the raging forest fires in Indonesia.
the proposal on the special fund would be submitted at the Asean Environment Ministers meeting in Pekan Baru, Indonesia, tomorrow
operationalization of the ASEAN transboundary haze pollution control fund to which the Meeting appreciated highly Malaysia’s initiative in this regard

diplomaticResponse.note: Bernama's summary of Malaysia's proposal; the agency's wording, not a minister's, is reported here.

diplomaticResponse.text: At the Pekanbaru meeting on 13 October 2006, Indonesia's environment minister said Indonesia was open to suggestions that would increase its effectiveness in suppressing current and future fires and welcomed assistance from within and outside the region, AFP reported.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Posted: 13 October 2006 2013 hrs
We are open to suggestions that will increase our effectiveness in suppressing current and future fires, and we welcome assistance from within and outside the region

diplomaticResponse.text: Channel NewsAsia reported on 7 October 2006 that Singapore had offered Indonesia assistance 'to fight the problem', including cloud-seeding operations, and quoted Singapore's environment minister as saying the offer still stood.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Posted: 07 October 2006 1945 hrs
Singapore has offered assistance to Indonesia to fight the problem.
This includes cloud 'seeding' operations to induce rain
the offer that we have made still stand

diplomaticResponse.text: A chronology of Singapore's haze assistance, annexed to an NEA news release of 20 June 2013, lists for 2006 an assistance package of high-resolution satellite pictures and hotspot coordinates, a C-130 aircraft for cloud seeding and a contingent of firefighters as 'Offered Assistance Package but not taken up'; Singapore Infopedia (National Library Board) gives the same account.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Jakarta, Indonesia, 20 June 2013
Chronology of Singapore’s Haze Assistance

2006 Offered Assistance Package but not taken up High resolution satellite pictures and hotspot coordinates to facilitate Indonesia in the identification of fire locations; One C-130 aircraft for cloud seeding operations; A Contingent of SCDF Fire-fighters

In 2006, Singapore offered the Indonesia government an assistance package that included an aircraft for cloud-seeding operations, visuals to help identify fire locations and a contingent of firefighters, but the offer was not taken up.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account, published in 2013; Infopedia cites this NEA release for its sentence. No Indonesian account of the 2006 offer was found, and no contemporaneous source opened says when or why it was not taken up (see “Where sources disagree” and “Unresolved questions”).

diplomaticResponse.text: At its first meeting, on 9 November 2006 in Cebu, the Sub-Regional Ministerial Steering Committee on Transboundary Haze Pollution endorsed its terms of reference and Indonesia's Plan of Action in Dealing with Transboundary Haze Pollution and agreed that member countries could, through Indonesia's central government, adopt fire-prone districts or regencies; the statement adds that Indonesia will chair the committee (MSC) and the TWG for the first two years.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: The First Meeting of the Sub-Regional Ministerial Steering Committee (MSC) on Transboundary Haze Pollution was held on 9 November 2006 in Cebu City, Philippines.

The MSC agreed with Indonesia’s proposal that Member Countries of the MSC may, through the Central Government of Indonesia, wish to adopt one or more fire-prone districts/regencies for enhancing capacity to deal with land and forest fires.
The MSC endorsed the Terms of Reference (TOR) for the MSC on Transboundary Haze Pollution; and Indonesia’s Plan of Action in Dealing with Transboundary Haze Pollution.
Indonesia will chair the MSC and TWG for the first two (2) years.

diplomaticResponse.text: Singapore's Second Minister for Foreign Affairs told Parliament on 14 November 2006 that Indonesia and Singapore both agree the haze is a serious transboundary problem with very harmful effects on Singapore and other countries neighbouring Indonesia, and even more so on Indonesia itself.
diplomaticResponse.label: analysis

refs.quote: 14 November 2006
Both of us agree that the haze is a serious transboundary problem with very harmful effects - on Singapore and other countries neighbouring Indonesia, and even more so on Indonesia itself.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's statement of a shared position; no Indonesian statement on this point was opened.

diplomaticResponse.text: In the same reply, Singapore's minister said Singapore had urged its ASEAN partners to make a joint statement on the haze at the United Nations, that Indonesia's representatives at the UN did not want the issue mentioned, and that Singapore therefore made its own statement, which he described as 'a factual statement which acknowledged the commitments and efforts made by Indonesia and other countries'.
diplomaticResponse.label: allegation

refs.quote: 14 November 2006

Singapore had strongly urged our ASEAN partners to make a joint statement on the haze. Unfortunately, the Indonesian representatives in the UN did not want the haze issue mentioned at all. Hence we had no choice but to make our own statement.
We made a factual statement which acknowledged the commitments and efforts made by Indonesia and other countries.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account of a disagreement. Indonesia's position, as recorded by the UN, is in the next claim. The full text of Singapore's UN statement was not found (see “Evidence not found”).

diplomaticResponse.text: The UN summary record of the General Assembly Second Committee's meeting of 26 October 2006 records that Indonesia's delegate, replying to Singapore's statement of the previous day, registered 'serious concern and displeasure' at its 'unnecessary and misleading references to Indonesia', reiterated her government's strong commitment to addressing the haze, said Indonesia remained open to any initiative to maximise cooperation but that existing ASEAN and bilateral arrangements should be used 'instead of misusing the forum of the United Nations', and said the Indonesian Embassy in Singapore had told her the previous day that the air there was clear and healthy.
diplomaticResponse.label: allegation

refs.quote: Summary record of the 22nd meeting Held at Headquarters, New York, on Thursday, 26 October 2006, at 3 p.m.

speaking in exercise of the right of reply, said that her delegation wished to register serious concern and displeasure at the statement made the previous day by the delegation of Singapore, particularly the unnecessary and misleading references to Indonesia.
refs.pinpoint: p.4, para 20 (the delegate's name, which precedes this passage, is withheld)

refs.quote: She reiterated her Government’s strong commitment to addressing the problem of the haze episodes caused by fires.
In addition, it had set aside some US$ 10 million for cloud-seeding and fire-fighting operations and had leased two Russian fire-fighting aircraft.

There were already bilateral and regional arrangements within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) for addressing the problem of haze pollution, and her Government remained open to any initiative that would maximize cooperation on the problem.
Full use should be made of those arrangements, instead of misusing the forum of the United Nations.
she had contacted the Indonesian Embassy in ... Singapore the previous day and had been informed that the air in Singapore was clear and healthy
refs.pinpoint: pp.4–5, para 24 (the ellipsis marks the page break)

diplomaticResponse.note: Indonesia's position as summarised in the UN's official summary record, which is a paraphrase rather than a verbatim transcript and is 'subject to correction'. The record adds that the government had set aside some US$10 million for cloud-seeding and fire-fighting operations. The reply also raised other bilateral issues, which are not repeated here. The delegate's name is withheld. Singapore's reply follows.

diplomaticResponse.text: At the same meeting, Singapore's delegate, replying in turn, said that Singapore was heartened by the commitment Indonesia was showing in dealing with the haze and that his government was appreciative of the measures taken so far; on air quality in Singapore, he said he understood that heavy rainfall and a change in the prevailing wind patterns accounted for the recent improvement, but that earlier in October readings had reached 'the very unhealthy level of 150 on the Pollutant Standard Index', according to the UN summary record.
diplomaticResponse.label: allegation

refs.quote: Summary record of the 22nd meeting Held at Headquarters, New York, on Thursday, 26 October 2006, at 3 p.m.
said that Singapore was heartened by the commitment that Indonesia was showing in dealing with the haze problem. His Government was appreciative of the measures taken thus far
refs.pinpoint: p.5, para 25 (the delegate's name, which precedes this passage, is withheld)

refs.quote: he understood that heavy rainfall, coupled with a change in the prevailing wind patterns, accounted for the recent improvement
earlier in October, air quality readings had reached the very unhealthy level of 150 on the Pollutant Standard Index

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's position in the same exchange, as summarised in the UN's summary record (a paraphrase, not a verbatim transcript). The record gives no date or averaging period for the reading of 150, and NEA's own scale places 150 in the 'Unhealthy' band, not 'Very unhealthy' (see “Where sources disagree”). The delegate's name is withheld.

diplomaticResponse.text: The minister also said that Indonesia's Industry Minister had absented himself from a Joint Steering Committee meeting on 3 November 2006 on Special Economic Zones in Batam, Bintan and Karimun, in protest against Singapore's statement on the haze at the United Nations.
diplomaticResponse.label: allegation

refs.quote: 14 November 2006

the recent exchange of correspondence between our Ambassador in Jakarta and the Indonesian Industry Minister, following his decision to absent himself from the Joint Steering Committee meeting on 3 November to discuss the implementation of our Special Economic Zones (SEZ) initiative in Batam, Bintan and Karimun. He was protesting against Singapore's statement on the haze problem at the United Nations.

diplomaticResponse.note: Reported by Singapore's minister; the Indonesian minister's own statement and his correspondence with Singapore's ambassador were not found, so his position is given only as Singapore described it. Indonesia's objection to Singapore's UN statement is recorded in the UN summary record (see the two claims above).

aftermath.text: NEA's Annual Report 2006/07 states that the prolonged dry season delayed the Inter-monsoon season by a few weeks to the end of October 2006, and that increased rainfall then gradually eased the haze, with conditions returning to normal by mid-November 2006.
aftermath.label: analysis

refs.quote: The prolonged dry season delayed the onset of the Inter-monsoon season in the southern ASEAN region by a few weeks to end October 2006. Increased rainfall brought by the Inter-Monsoon helped to gradually ease the haze situation in the region and conditions return to normal by mid November 2006.
National Environment Agency | Annual Report 2006/07

aftermath.note: NEA's account of the meteorology that ended the episode.

aftermath.text: NEA reports that Singapore collaborated with Jambi province in November 2006 to develop a master plan to deal with land and forest fires in Muaro Jambi Regency, covering land clearing without the use of fire and the prevention and mitigation of peatland fires.
aftermath.label: fact

refs.quote: We then collaborated with Jambi to develop a Master Plan to deal with land and forest fires in Muaro Jambi Regency in November 2006.
refs.pinpoint: section 'Prevention is Better than Cure', para 1

refs.quote: The Master Plan set out the strategy and approach for land clearing without the use of fire as well as the prevention and mitigation of peatland fires in Muaro Jambi Regency.
refs.pinpoint: section 'Prevention is Better than Cure', para 2

aftermath.text: The 2016 PNAS study states that, apart from brief episodes that produced locally high pollution levels (for example in Riau in 2013), fire activity and pollution levels in Indonesia in general did not approach those of 2006 in the following years, and that the 2015 fire season was more severe than the major 2006 episode.
aftermath.label: analysis

refs.quote: There have been brief episodes under isolated dry conditions that produced locally high pollution levels, for example, in the central Sumatran province of Riau in 2013 ( 10 ), but in general, fire activity and pollution levels have not approached those of 2006 in the intervening years.
The 2015 fire season and related smoke pollution in Indonesia was more severe than the major 2006 episode

refs.pinpoint: citation line of the PubMed Central copy

aftermath.note: The statement concerns fire activity and pollution in Indonesia. It is not a statement about Singapore or Malaysia, where Singapore's 24-hour PSI reached 246 on 20 June 2013 according to MEWR (see “Singapore: Air quality”).

selection.note: A is met: NEA (release of 7 October 2006; Annual Report 2006/07) said smoke haze from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan was carried to Singapore and towards Peninsular Malaysia, MEWR (2014) described recurrent haze in Singapore from land and forest fires in Indonesia, and Singapore's Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (14 November 2006) called the haze a serious transboundary problem. B1 is met by DOE's records of unhealthy API status at several stations (17–19 July, mid-August and 7 October 2006), AFP's report, citing DOE data, of unhealthy readings in Kuala Lumpur and four other regions (18 October), and NEA's 24-hour PSI above 100 on 7 and 8 October with three unhealthy days counted in October. B2 is met by Sarawak's advice to keep small children indoors; NEA's band-linked health advisory of 7 October is not tagged (treated as routine, as in 2016). B3 is met by MEWR ('particularly severe') and a 2018 peer-reviewed study (one of the four most significant haze events in Singapore in 2005–2015); the 'major' episode described by the 2009 and 2016 studies concerns fire activity in Indonesia and is not counted, and Meteorological Service Singapore's assessment of 2015 names 1997/1998 as the last major haze event to affect the region (see “Where sources disagree”).

attribution.note: Singapore's National Environment Agency describes smoke from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and NASA smoke from fires on Sumatra and Borneo; Malaysian officials, as reported by Malaysiakini on 18 July 2006, said the haze was caused by forest fires in Indonesia. No public dispute about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. The exchanges between Singapore and Indonesia recorded under Response between governments concern how the haze was raised at the United Nations.

confidence.rationale: Medium. The core account, that smoke haze affected Malaysia in episodes from mid-July 2006 and affected Singapore and Malaysia more intensely from late September to October 2006, is supported by government records (NEA's October 2006 releases, its daily 24-hour PSI table and its Annual Report 2006/07; DOE's chronology; MEWR's 2014 consultation paper; MFA statements) and corroborated by independent sources: ASEAN statements of 13 October and 9 November 2006, the UN summary record of 26 October 2006, NASA, peer-reviewed studies (Nature Geoscience 2009; PNAS 2016; Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres 2018) and contemporaneous news (Channel NewsAsia, AFP, Bernama, The Star, Malaysiakini, AsiaOne). Singapore's 24-hour PSI readings are quoted from NEA. The rating is medium because important elements rest on a single source or are incomplete: the end of the period (mid-November 2006) rests on NEA's Annual Report alone; Malaysia's readings, including the highest API that DOE reports (221 at Sri Aman), rest on DOE's later, undated chronology and on news reports, because DOE's 2006 daily API record was not opened, and DOE gives no dates or values for the mid-August episode in Sarawak; and which three October days NEA counted as unhealthy is not established. Minor conflicts also remain, none of them about the core account: how significant the 2006 haze was, whether Singapore's September haze was serious, the strength of the 2006 El Niño, the band given to a reading of 150 in the UN summary record, the day of a Sarawak cabinet decision, the description of Singapore's assistance offer and modelled death estimates. Not opened: DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2006 or daily API data, NEA's daily 24-hour PSI for 17–31 October 2006, official 2006 health records and Indonesian official records. AI-assigned rating awaiting human review.

contradictions.text: Day of Sarawak's cabinet decision and start of cloud seeding: Bernama (5 October 2006) says the school-closure threshold was approved at the state cabinet's weekly meeting on Thursday morning and that cloud seeding began on Tuesday; The Star (7 October 2006) says the cabinet decided on Wednesday and that cloud seeding had been carried out since Wednesday. Not resolved; both agree on the API 300 threshold.

Singapore's readings on 7 October 2006: AsiaOne's standfirst (the line under its headline) says 'PSI at 9 pm hit 150, the worst for a 24-hour period since 1997', but its own table labels 150 a 3-hour PSI reading, Channel NewsAsia reports 150 as the 3-hour PSI, and NEA's 24-hour table gives 128 for that day. Primary evidence (NEA's table) settles that the 24-hour value was 128 and 150 was a 3-hour value.

September 2006 in Singapore: NLB Infopedia says 'In September 2006, Singapore again experienced serious haze pollution', while NEA's Annual Report 2006/07 says air quality reached the moderate range on 14 days in September and unhealthy levels only in October, and NEA's daily table shows no September 24-hour PSI above 66. 'Serious' is not an index band; the primary record shows no unhealthy day in September.

Sources describe the significance of the 2006 haze differently. DOE describes Malaysia's 2006 episodes as 'slight to moderate'; MEWR (2014) lists 2006 among the years in which the haze in Singapore was 'particularly severe'; the 2018 study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres counts October 2006 among 'the four most significant haze events in Singapore' in 2005–2015; the PNAS (2016) study, on fire activity in Indonesia, says 'The last major event occurred in 2006'; and Meteorological Service Singapore's Annual Climate Assessment 2015 says 'The last major haze event to affect the region was in 1997/1998'. The sources describe different places or things (haze in Malaysia, in Singapore and across the region; fires in Indonesia) and use no common definition; this record does not resolve the difference.

Singapore's 2006 assistance offer: Channel NewsAsia (7 October 2006) describes it as including cloud-seeding operations and table-top exercises, with the minister saying the offer still stood; NEA's 2013 chronology and NLB Infopedia list high-resolution satellite pictures and hotspot coordinates, a cloud-seeding aircraft and a contingent of firefighters, and say the package was not taken up. The descriptions differ, and no contemporaneous source opened says when or whether the offer was declined.

Modelled 2006 deaths differ by study: the 2016 Environmental Research Letters study estimates 34,600 (Indonesia), 2,300 (Malaysia) and 700 (Singapore) excess adult deaths, 37,600 in total; the 2020 Environmental Research Letters study estimates 22,088 excess premature deaths across Equatorial Asia and cites the 2012 Nature Climate Change study's estimate of 6,000 cardiovascular deaths. Applying the 2016 study's relative risk, the 2020 study estimates 42,520 for 2006, and it suggests that the largest uncertainty lies in the exposure-response function. All are modelled estimates; none is a count.

Strength of the 2006 El Niño is described differently: NEA's Annual Report 2006/07 refers to 'the development of a weak El Nino'; a scientist quoted in NASA's Goddard release said 'the current El Nino is rather weak compared to that of 1997-98'; the Nature Geoscience (2009) and PNAS (2016) studies describe 'moderate El Niño' conditions together with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole; the 2018 study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres writes that the October 2006 event is 'well understood to be the consequence of strong El Niño-pIOD conditions'. The sources do not use a common definition, and this record does not resolve the difference.

Band of the 150 reading: the UN summary record of 26 October 2006 records Singapore's delegation as saying that earlier in October readings 'had reached the very unhealthy level of 150 on the Pollutant Standard Index' (averaging period not stated). NEA's Annual Report 2006/07 gives 101–200 as 'Unhealthy' and 201–300 as 'Very unhealthy'; Channel NewsAsia reports 150 as the 3-hour PSI at 9 p.m. on 7 October; and NEA's 24-hour table gives 128 for that day. On NEA's own scale 150 is in the unhealthy band, and this record follows NEA. The summary record is the UN's paraphrase, not a verbatim transcript.

evidenceGaps: DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2006 is listed in DOE's Enviro Digital Library (edl.doe.gov.my/overview/51344) but downloading requires a login, which was not attempted; the archived DOE page with daily API averages for October–November 2006 (cited by Wikipedia) returned HTTP 500 from the Wayback Machine. Malaysia's 2006 readings therefore rest on DOE's later chronology and on news reports.

No official 2006 record of healthcare use was opened for Singapore or Malaysia. The Channel NewsAsia item 'Doctors see an increase in patients with haze-related symptoms' (article 234371) has only an empty archive copy, and no 2006 Ministry of Health (Singapore) or Ministry of Health Malaysia release or figures were found.

Singapore's statement at the UN on 25 October 2006 was found only in the UN's summary record (A/C.2/61/SR.20), which paraphrases it; no full text was found. No Indonesian government account of the Industry Minister's absence from the 3 November 2006 meeting, or of his correspondence with Singapore's ambassador, was found; Indonesian-language sources were not searched.

NEA's archived daily 24-hour PSI table covers only 1 September to 16 October 2006; values for 17–31 October come only from NEA releases (for example 102 at 4 p.m. on 20 October). NEA's Annual Report gives 'three days' of unhealthy air in October without naming them.
No source opened reports actual school closures in Malaysia or Singapore in 2006; Sarawak's API 300 threshold is documented, but not whether it was ever triggered.
No official estimate of the economic cost of the 2006 haze to Malaysia or Singapore was found; a Channel NewsAsia item on an estimated loss (article 235112) has only empty archive copies.

Singapore Hansard (sprs.parl.gov.sg), Malaysian Hansard, NLB NewspaperSG (Straits Times, 2006) and ASMC's 2006 haze reviews were not accessed. A National Archives of Singapore copy of NEA's 20 June 2013 release on Singapore's past assistance packages returned an empty page (HTTP 202); an archived copy of NEA's original release was read instead.

Indonesian official sources (hotspot data from Indonesian ministries, provincial air-quality readings, school or airport closure orders) were not opened; impacts on people in Indonesia rest on NASA, an ASEAN statement and a Channel NewsAsia report.

No Malaysian government document opened gives the origin of the 2006 haze: DOE's chronology reports readings for 2006 but, unlike its entries for 2010–2012, does not describe the haze as transboundary. Malaysian officials' views of where the haze came from are known here only from news reports: Malaysiakini (18 July 2006) reported officials as saying it was caused by forest fires in Indonesia, and Bernama (5 October 2006) quoted a forecaster of the State Meteorological Services Department on haze brought into Sarawak from hotspots in Kalimantan.
unresolvedQuestions: Did Indonesia formally decline Singapore's 2006 assistance package, and when? NEA's 2013 chronology and Infopedia say it was not taken up, while on 7 October 2006 Singapore's minister said the offer still stood; no Indonesian account was found.

Which three days in October 2006 did NEA count as 'unhealthy', and on which averaging basis? NEA's table gives 24-hour PSI above 100 on 7 and 8 October and 98 on 16 October, NEA's release gives 102 at 4 p.m. on 20 October, and an AFP report of 18 October 2006 said Singapore registered in the unhealthy range 'for the second day Tuesday' (averaging period not stated).
On what basis did DOE classify 2006 as 'slight to moderate' despite a 'very unhealthy' reading at Sri Aman and unhealthy status at twenty Peninsular stations on one day?
What were the dates and API values of Sarawak's mid-August 2006 episode, which DOE reports without figures?
Was Sarawak's API 300 school-closure threshold a standing state policy after 2006, and did it influence later federal guidance?

How severe was the July 2006 haze in Peninsular Malaysia? DOE records 'unhealthy' status at three west-coast stations on 17–19 July 2006 and describes the year's episodes as 'slight to moderate'; the 2018 study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, which measures extreme haze days by visibility at Singapore and Melaka, writes that the fires in July 2006 (one of the high-fire months in Riau that it discusses) 'did not lead to severe haze in the Malay Peninsula'.

events.title: Mid- to late October 2010: southern Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore and Riau, Indonesia

period.label: Mid- to late October 2010

refs.quote: The air quality in Singapore also dipped to moderate levels on several days from 16th to 24th October reaching a peak 24hr PSI reading of 96 on 22nd October.
According to Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE), decline in air quality levels was first recorded around noon on Saturday, 16 October.

A short period of haze episode was experienced in southern part of Peninsular Malaysia, particularly in Muar, Johor from 19 to 23 October 2010 where the air quality reached unhealthy to hazardous level due to transboundary haze pollution.

period.note: Start and end follow NEA's statement that Singapore's air quality was moderate on several days from 16 to 24 October 2010; a 2013 peer-reviewed study of this event (Atmospheric Research), citing DOE, dates the first decline in Malaysian air quality to around noon on 16 October, although its abstract reports that high fine-particle (PM2.5) levels were measured at Singapore and Malaysia on 15 October, the day fire activity escalated, and treats this as the initial onset of the episode. DOE's chronology dates the episode in southern Peninsular Malaysia to 19–23 October, and a 2018 study (Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres) dates extreme haze in its visibility record to about 18–22 October (see Where sources disagree).

summary.text: Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) described a transboundary haze episode in October 2010, in which prevailing southwest to westerly winds brought smoke haze from fires in Sumatra to southern Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore for several days.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Transboundary Haze in October 2010
refs.pinpoint: p.5, section heading under 'Significant Weather Events in 2010'

refs.quote: The prevailing southwest to westerly surface winds brought smoke haze from the fires in Sumatra to southern Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore for several days.

summary.note: Source: NEA, Annual Weather Review 2010. Where the smoke came from is NEA's assessment (the review cites the prevailing winds and shows satellite images of smoke plumes over Riau) and is attributed as such.

summary.text: Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE) records a short haze episode in southern Peninsular Malaysia, particularly in Muar, Johor, from 19 to 23 October 2010, in which air quality reached unhealthy to hazardous levels, and attributes it to transboundary haze pollution.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: A short period of haze episode was experienced in southern part of Peninsular Malaysia, particularly in Muar, Johor from 19 to 23 October 2010 where the air quality reached unhealthy to hazardous level due to transboundary haze pollution.

During this brief haze episode, the air quality recorded on several days over southern Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore deteriorated into the moderate to unhealthy range, with certain places like Muar in Johore reporting air ... quality within the hazardous range.
refs.pinpoint: pp.2–3; the ellipsis marks the page break

summary.note: The air-quality levels are DOE's record; the attribution to transboundary pollution is DOE's assessment. NEA's review separately describes Muar as reporting air quality in the hazardous range. Malaysia's API did not include PM2.5 in 2010.

summary.text: A 2018 peer-reviewed study (Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres), analysing daily visibility records for June–October in 2005–2015, counts October 2010 among the four most significant haze events in Singapore in that record and among three severe haze events in the Malay Peninsula that cannot be explained by El Niño and positive Indian Ocean Dipole conditions; at Melaka (Malacca in the study) the October 2010 event was somewhat less extreme than in Singapore.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Figure 2. Time series of extreme anomalies in daily visibility reduction recorded in Singapore (Changi Airport) and Malacca during June–October 2005–2015.
Here we focus our analysis on the June–October time frame because conditions are relatively dry then
refs.pinpoint: PDF p.5 (journal p.6286), Section 3.1; the sentence just before the ranking

refs.quote: The four most significant haze events in Singapore over the past decade occurred in October 2006, October 2010, June 2013, and September–October 2015. The Malacca time series reveals the same four peaks, with the October 2010 and June 2013 events somewhat less extreme than those in Singapore and with an additional event in August 2005.

We show that June 2013 was not an exceptional event; inspection of visibility data during 2005–2015 reveals two other severe haze events in the Malay Peninsula (August 2005 and October 2010) occurring under similar conditions.
We therefore focus our analysis on the three extreme haze events that cannot be explained by the El Niño-pIOD paradigm: August 2005, October 2010, and June 2013.

summary.note: 'Most significant' and 'severe' refer to reductions in daily visibility at Changi Airport (Singapore) and Melaka, which the authors use as a proxy for particulate haze; this is not a PSI or API ranking. The ranking covers only June–October of each year, the months the study analyses because, it says, conditions are relatively dry then. 'pIOD' in the quote is the authors' abbreviation for a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.

regionalContext.text: NEA described the weather behind the episode: La Niña brought generally wet conditions to Sumatra, but dry periods in mid-October coincided with a persistent Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) dry phase that suppressed rainfall, and the hotspot count in Sumatra reached a maximum of 358 on the 18th of October.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: The La Niña also brought generally wet weather conditions to Sumatra during the Southwest Monsoon, despite this being the traditional dry season. However, the wet weather conditions were interspersed with dry periods, particularly in the middle of October. These dry periods coincided with a persistent MJO dry phase which inhibited convection and suppressed rainfall in October.

The hotspot count in Sumatra reached a maximum of 358 on the 18th of October. The prevailing southwest to westerly surface winds brought smoke haze from the fires in Sumatra to southern Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore for several days.
In 2010 a prolonged Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) dry phase caused a dry October, creating ideal conditions for biomass burning in the region and related haze in Singapore.
From annual weather reports by MSS
refs.pinpoint: Section 1, Introduction (source of the account above)

regionalContext.note: A 2019 modelling study (Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics) gives the same account of an MJO dry phase in October 2010, citing annual weather reports by the Meteorological Service Singapore, so it is not independent of NEA. The hotspot count is NEA's satellite-based count for Sumatra; counts from other satellite products and agencies differ (see Where sources disagree). A hotspot shows where a fire was detected, not who started it or who holds the land.

regionalContext.text: A 2018 peer-reviewed study (Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres) found that anomalously strong westerly winds over Riau, coinciding with the Madden–Julian Oscillation entering phase 4, carried smoke to the Malay Peninsula: satellite aerosol data show plumes moving almost directly eastward from Riau, back trajectories from Singapore indicate transport from Riau, and severe haze began in Singapore on 20 October, three days after enhanced fire activity in Riau on 15–17 October.
