selection.note: A: NEA ('Transboundary Haze in October 2010'; in NEA's assessment, smoke haze from fires in Sumatra), DOE ('due to transboundary haze pollution') and peer-reviewed studies (Atmospheric Research 2013; Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres 2018; Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 2019). B1: API above 100 in Muar on two days (162 on 19 October; 432 and 311 on 20 October) and at two locations on 20 October (Muar and Melaka City, 111), reported by Malaysiakini, which attributes the 432 reading to DOE's API, and by The Star, and consistent with DOE's own record of unhealthy to hazardous air quality from 19 to 23 October. B2: closure of all 170 schools in Muar District on 21 October 2010 (DOE) and directives to avoid or cancel outdoor school activities. B3: the 2018 Journal of Geophysical Research study ('severe'; among the four most significant haze events in Singapore's June–October visibility record for 2005–2015) and MEWR's 2014 public consultation paper, which lists 2010 among the years in which the haze was 'particularly severe'. According to NEA, Singapore's 24-hour PSI stayed moderate (peak 96), so B1 and B2 rest on Malaysian evidence.

attribution.note: Indonesian officials gave differing public accounts of where the smoke came from, as reported by The Jakarta Post: Indonesia's Forestry Ministry first rejected claims by Singapore and Malaysia that it came from Indonesia, and the next day the government said fires in Riau province were behind the haze. Singapore's National Environment Agency and the peer-reviewed studies quoted in this entry describe smoke from fires in Sumatra (the studies, mainly in Riau); Malaysia's Department of Environment, in its chronology of haze episodes, attributes the Malaysian episode to transboundary haze pollution without naming a source area. The positions are recorded as reported, under Response between governments; this record does not decide between them.

confidence.rationale: AI-assigned rating awaiting human review; it describes the evidence, not the severity of the episode. Medium under the pre-registered definitions. The core account (a short smoke-haze episode in mid- to late October 2010 that affected southern Peninsular Malaysia, where DOE names Muar in Johor as the worst-hit area, and Singapore) is supported by primary government sources in both countries (NEA's Annual Weather Review 2010; DOE's chronology; Singapore MFA statements of 21 and 22 October 2010) and corroborated independently by peer-reviewed studies (Atmospheric Research 2013, with its own PM2.5, Sun-photometer and lidar measurements in Singapore; Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres 2018, from visibility records), by a 2019 modelling study (Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics) whose authors include the Meteorological Service Singapore, and by contemporaneous news (Malaysiakini; Bernama via the Borneo Post; The Star; Reuters; Antara; The Jakarta Post; Batam Pos via JPNN.com). Key figures are quoted from primary sources: NEA's 24-hour PSI peak of 96 and 3-hour peak of 108, and DOE's API of 432 and its 170 school closures. It is not rated high because Singapore's peak readings (24-hour PSI 96; 3-hour PSI 108) rest on NEA's later annual review alone, DOE's 432 is undated, Malaysia's dated readings rest on news reports, and minor conflicts remain (see Where sources disagree): the number of schools in Muar (170 or 204), Muar's peak (432, or 431 in an analysis of DOE's hourly data), a Singapore PSI reading of 106 or 108, the episode's dates by measure, and MEWR's 'particularly severe' against NEA's moderate 24-hour PSI. None of these conflicts concerns whether the episode happened, roughly when, or that it affected both countries. Other gaps recorded under Evidence not found: no official health advisories or healthcare-use records for the episode were found or opened, and impacts in Indonesia rest on news reports. It would rise to high only if further records, such as NEA's daily PSI records for 16–24 October 2010, DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2010 or hourly API records, and an Education Ministry record of the Muar school closures, corroborated the peak readings and resolved these conflicts.

contradictions.text: Singapore's severity in 2010: NEA's Annual Weather Review 2010 gives a peak 24-hour PSI of 96 (moderate band) on 22 October and says the 3-hour PSI only briefly reached 108, in the unhealthy range; MOH's FAQ (last updated in November 2016) says the health advisory in the daily haze situation update is based on the 24-hour PSI forecast, a statement about practice at that time, not necessarily in 2010. MEWR (2014) lists 2010 among the years when the haze in Singapore was 'particularly severe', without giving a reading or its basis. Not resolved; this record follows NEA's review, the agency's own account of the episode, in describing Singapore's 24-hour PSI as moderate. SingStat's annual table (data source: NEA) gives 2% of days in 2010 as 'Unhealthy', but its footnote describes the PSI used as including PM2.5, which Singapore's PSI did not include in 2010, and the table does not say how the 2010 share was derived; whether it conflicts with NEA's 2010 readings cannot be assessed from the sources opened, so the two are not compared (see Unresolved questions).

The reading above 100 on 21 October 2010: Eco-Business (a 2013 Channel NewsAsia report) says the PSI 'hit 106' on 21 October 2010 without stating the averaging period, in a passage that follows the report's 3-hour PSI readings for June 2013, and Singapore's MFA said on 22 October that the PSI 'went over 100 yesterday'. NEA's review says the 3-hour PSI 'briefly peaked at 108' without giving a date, and that the 24-hour PSI peaked at 96 on 22 October. If 106 was meant as the day's 3-hour peak it differs from NEA's 108; it may instead be one of the hourly 3-hour PSI readings rather than the peak (AI agent's suggestion). Not resolved.

Number of schools in Muar: DOE says all 170 schools in Muar District were closed on 21 October 2010. Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister was quoted on 20 October 2010 as saying 'We have 204 schools there', and Bernama reported on 22 October 2010 that 80,282 primary and secondary students from 204 schools in Muar would return to school. Reuters reported that 'hundreds of schools' in Johor had been forced to close. No source explains the difference between 170 and 204. Not resolved.

Muar's peak reading: DOE's chronology gives 432 (no date or time). Malaysiakini reported on 20 October 2010 that Muar's reading on DOE's API had worsened to 432 'by late morning' that day, and Bernama and The Star also give 432, in wording that dates it to 20 October 2010. A 2018 analysis of DOE's hourly API data for the Sekolah Menengah Teknik Muar monitoring station (Polish Journal of Environmental Studies) reports the highest hazardous-band value as 431 at 10:00 on 20 October 2010. No source explains the one-unit difference (a different hour, station or data version are possibilities; AI agent's suggestion). Not resolved.

Episode dates differ by source and measure: NEA gives moderate air quality in Singapore on several days from 16 to 24 October; the 2013 Atmospheric Research study gives 16–24 October for degraded air quality, with fire activity escalating on 15 October and, in its abstract, high fine-particle (PM2.5) levels measured at Singapore and Malaysia on the same date as the initial onset of the episode, and, citing DOE, a first decline in Malaysian air quality around noon on 16 October; DOE's chronology gives 19–23 October for southern Peninsular Malaysia; the 2018 Journal of Geophysical Research study gives 18–22 October as the time of extreme haze in its visibility record, 17–23 October for the haze event in a figure caption (satellite aerosol averages) and elevated haze in the Malay Peninsula during 20–23 October in a later section, with severe haze in Singapore beginning on 20 October. These differences may reflect different measures and places (AI agent's reading); none of the sources questions that the episode happened. Not resolved; this record uses 16–24 October, following NEA.

Hotspot counts differ widely by satellite product, agency and area: NEA reports a maximum of 358 hotspots in Sumatra on 18 October; the 2013 Atmospheric Research study reports more than 500 satellite hotspots in Riau alone on 15 and 17 October; The Jakarta Post reports that Indonesia's Environment Ministry recorded 61 hotspots in Bengkalis on 20 October and that its Forestry Ministry recorded 37 in Riau province on 19 October. The counts are not comparable and are reported as published.

evidenceGaps: NEA's daily haze updates and PSI tables for October 2010 were not found: the legacy app2.nea.gov.sg pages are offline, NEA's historical-readings page covers only the past 365 days, and searches of NEA and the National Archives of Singapore found no 2010 release. Singapore's readings in this record rest on NEA's Annual Weather Review 2010 and news reports; an NEA press release of 19 October 2010, cited by the 2013 Atmospheric Research study, was not found.

No Singapore government health advisory (NEA or MOH) from October 2010 was opened. The Straits Times of 21–22 October 2010 on NewspaperSG could not be read: the National Library's site returned no text to automated download.

DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2010 (cited as reference 20 by the 2018 Polish Journal of Environmental Studies analysis for haze in Johor from fires in Riau) and DOE's daily API records and press statements for October 2010 were not found online, so Malaysian daily readings rest on news reports and DOE's later chronology. No Ministry of Health Malaysia advice or healthcare-use records for the episode were found.

No official record of an emergency declaration in Malaysia during this episode was found; DOE's chronology records none for 2010. No source opened describes the activation of the central disaster relief and management committee, reported by Malaysiakini on 20 October 2010 (see Malaysia: Government response), as an emergency declaration.

Contemporaneous reports that could not be opened: AsiaOne, 'Schools in Muar close as haze worsens' (21 October 2010) and 'Singapore urges Indonesia to act on haze' (22 October 2010), whose October 2010 archive copies could not be read (the Internet Archive returned HTTP 429, too many requests, to automated download); a Reuters news report of 21 October 2010 on the haze in Malaysia and Singapore, for which no archive copy was found (its headline, which compares the haze with earlier years, could not be verified and is not used); and a report on IOL (iol.co.za returned HTTP 403).

The ASEAN media release of the 6th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (Bandar Seri Begawan, 13 October 2010), held days before the episode, could not be opened (asean.org returned HTTP 307 to automated download); no ASEAN statement issued during the episode was found.

No Indonesian official records for the episode (environment, forestry, disaster-management or meteorological agencies) and no health records for Riau or the Riau Islands in October 2010 were found; impacts in Indonesia rest on news reports (Antara on Dumai; Batam Pos on Batam) and on Singapore MFA's account of the Indonesian Foreign Minister's remarks.

No search was made for legal or enforcement records arising from the October 2010 fires (investigations, enforcement actions or court decisions); that none is listed under What changed reflects this gap, not evidence that there were none.
unresolvedQuestions: SingStat table M890861 gives 2% of days in 2010 as 'Unhealthy', measured, according to its footnote, by a PSI that includes PM2.5, which Singapore's PSI did not include in 2010. Was the 2010 share recalculated on that later basis, or derived in another way, and from which NEA data?
When exactly did Singapore's 3-hour PSI peak at 108, and was the 106 reported for 21 October 2010 a 3-hour value?
How many schools in Muar District were closed, and on which days (170 according to DOE; 204 cited by the Deputy Prime Minister and Bernama)?
At what hour and station was Muar's 432 reading recorded, and why does an analysis of DOE's hourly data give 431?
Did NEA or MOH issue health advisories for the public or for schools in Singapore during 16–24 October 2010?
Was cloud seeding carried out in Malaysia during the episode, and was any assistance offered by Singapore or Malaysia accepted by Indonesia?
What health effects were recorded in Riau and the Riau Islands during the episode, for example in provincial or city health office records of acute respiratory infections for October 2010?

NEA's Annual Weather Review 2010 says that wetter conditions returned to Sumatra and the region 'on the 23th of October' (p.3) and, in its section on the haze, 'on 24th October' (p.5). Which date is right?

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study of the 2013 Sumatran fires, published in Scientific Reports, found that a three-million-hectare area of Riau Province in central Sumatra was the source of 71% of Sumatra's fire radiative power in June 2013 and accounted for 72% of the island's burned area detected by the same satellites that month.

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports reports that the fires, which followed a two-month dry spell in a wetter-than-average year, were short-lived (one week) and burned an estimated 163,336 hectares in a localised area of central Sumatra, including 137,044 hectares (84%) on peat.
regionalContext.label: analysis

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports describes the June 2013 episode as a trans-boundary haze event that occurred although neither ENSO (El Niño) nor Indian Ocean Dipole conditions were present in 2013; in Riau, the twelve months to June 2013 were wetter than average but May and June 2013 had rainfall deficits.

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres found that the June 2013 haze occurred in the absence of an El Niño, during negative Indian Ocean Dipole conditions, with smoke carried eastward to the Malay Peninsula from fires in Riau province, central Sumatra.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: the June 2013 haze occurred in the absence of an El Niño, during negative Indian Ocean Dipole conditions, with smoke carried eastward to the Peninsula from fires in the Riau province of central Sumatra

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres identified anomalously strong westerly winds over Riau, concurrent with late phases of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and negative Indian Ocean Dipole phases, as common to three severe non-El Niño haze events on the Malay Peninsula: August 2005, October 2010 and June 2013.

regionalContext.text: A peer-reviewed source-attribution study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics classes June 2013 as an atypical (off-season) haze event for Singapore, attributes it to a typhoon coinciding with intense burning in Riau, and estimates from modelling that about 98% of the PM10 emissions reaching two Singapore monitoring stations in June came from Riau.

regionalContext.note: Jakarta Post report of 25 June 2013 ('Monday' is 24 June 2013); BBC report of 21 June 2013. The Jakarta Post page gives 'The Jakarta Post' as author; its opening paragraphs match an AP report, but this paragraph does not appear in the copy of that AP report checked during review, so it is attributed to The Jakarta Post (see the source note).

diplomaticResponse.text: According to Singapore's environment minister, NEA contacted Indonesia's Ministry of Environment on 14 June 2013 to request urgent measures, and on 18 June 2013 the minister telephoned his Indonesian counterpart to ask Indonesia to put out the fires and to offer assistance; Singapore's foreign and environment ministers had conveyed the seriousness of the situation to their Indonesian counterparts and urged immediate action.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: The PSI readings had moved from Good to Moderate by 1.00 pm on 14 June 2013. That same day, NEA issued a public haze advisory. NEA also updated its website. NEA contacted the Head of the Forest Fires Division of the Indonesian Ministry of Environment to seek an urgent update of the ground situation and to request that urgent measures be taken to mitigate the haze.

On 18 June 2013, the next day, ... That same day, I telephoned my counterpart, the Indonesian Environment Minister ... to express my grave concern. I requested Indonesia to take action to put out the fires and offered our assistance.

The Minister for Foreign Affairs and Minister for the Environment and Water Resources had earlier conveyed the seriousness of the situation to their Indonesian counterparts and urged immediate action.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's own account (release of 19 June 2013 and the minister's reply to Parliament of 8 July 2013). Personal names in the source are omitted by ellipsis.

diplomaticResponse.text: According to Singapore's environment minister, the Indonesian Foreign Ministry, in response to Singapore's calls, convened an emergency meeting with Singapore in Jakarta on 20 June 2013, attended by a Singapore delegation led by NEA's chief executive; Indonesian officials said they were taking action at the provincial level against the fires.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: In response to our calls, the Indonesian Foreign Ministry called for an emergency meeting with Singapore on 20 June 2013 in Jakarta.
our delegation led by the CEO of NEA and comprising staff from MEWR, NEA and MFA, attended the meeting.
The Indonesian officials conveyed that they were taking action at the provincial level in tackling the on-going fires.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account (MEWR reply to Parliament, 8 July 2013); no Indonesian account of the meeting was opened.

diplomaticResponse.text: Singapore's Prime Minister sent the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources to Jakarta on 21 June 2013 as his special envoy to deliver a letter on the haze to Indonesia's President; Indonesia's environment minister received the letter on the President's behalf.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: travelled to Jakarta on 21 June 2013 as ... Special Envoy, to personally deliver ... letter to Indonesian President ... on the haze problem.
The Environment Minister of Indonesia received the letter on the ... behalf.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's accounts (MFA press statement on the Prime Minister's Office website; MEWR). Personal names omitted by ellipsis.

diplomaticResponse.text: Singapore offered help to put out the fires in Sumatra, including an aircraft for cloud seeding, satellite pictures and hotspot coordinates, and encouraged Indonesia to ratify the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution; according to Singapore, Indonesia's environment minister agreed to bring forward the Sub-Regional Ministerial Steering Committee meeting and promised to consider the offer.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: offered Singapore’s help to put out the fires in Sumatra, including an aircraft for cloud seeding, and satellite pictures and hotspot coordinates
He also encouraged Indonesia to ratify the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
agreed to convene the Sub-Regional Ministerial Steering Committee on Transboundary Haze earlier than the original date in August 2013
promised to consider Singapore’s offer of assistance
As with previous years, we offered a haze assistance package that included aircraft for cloud seeding, satellite imagery and hotspot coordinates.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account of the meeting of 21 June 2013. The minister told Parliament that a similar assistance package had been offered in previous years.

diplomaticResponse.text: AP reported that, in the week before the President's apology, Indonesia's Coordinating Minister for People's Welfare criticised Singaporean officials' public comments about the haze, saying they should have been conveyed through diplomatic channels rather than publicly.
diplomaticResponse.label: allegation

refs.quote: Last week, Indonesian Coordinating Minister for People's Welfare ... slammed critical comments by Singaporean officials about the haze, saying they should have been conveyed through diplomatic channels instead of publicly.

diplomaticResponse.note: A position in a dispute between governments, attributed. For context, Singapore's own account (MEWR, 8 July 2013; claims above) records contacts with Indonesian counterparts through calls, letters, a meeting and a special envoy between 14 and 21 June 2013. No Singapore government reply to this remark was found among the sources opened or in two further web searches made during review (15 October 2026). The minister's name is omitted by ellipsis; AP also quoted a further remark by him that is not reproduced here.

diplomaticResponse.text: Indonesia's President apologised to the people of Singapore and Malaysia for the haze at a press conference in Jakarta on 24 June 2013. AP reported him as saying that there should be a thorough investigation and that, in his analysis, 'there are both natural and human factors', and that the wind direction had caused the smoke to concentrate in Singapore and Malaysia; according to Singapore's Prime Minister's Office, he said the Indonesian police would investigate the man-made causes of the fires and take legal action against those responsible.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: comments at a press conference in Jakarta on 24 June 2013, apologising to the people of Singapore and Malaysia for the haze.
"For what is happening, as the president, I apologize to our brothers in Singapore and Malaysia,"

"There should be a thorough investigation. In my analysis, there are both natural and human factors," he said, adding that the wind direction has caused the smoke to concentrate in Singapore and Malaysia.
stated that the Indonesian Police would investigate the man-made causes of the fires and take the necessary legal action against those responsible.

diplomaticResponse.note: AP's report (carried by The Jakarta Post; the apology and the remarks quoted here also appear in AP's original as carried by Yahoo News, checked during review) gives the President's own words; the Prime Minister's Office gives Singapore's account. An announced investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing, and neither statement identifies any party. No official Indonesian transcript was opened.

diplomaticResponse.text: Singapore's Prime Minister said Singapore accepted the apology 'wholeheartedly', welcomed the President's promise to spare no efforts to tackle 'this serious problem which has caused suffering to the people of Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia', and reiterated Singapore's offer of assistance in putting out the fires.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: We accept his apology wholeheartedly.
promise to spare no efforts to tackle this serious problem which has caused suffering to the people of Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia
I would also like to reiterate Singapore’s offer of assistance to Indonesia in putting out the fires.

diplomaticResponse.note: Statement by Singapore's Prime Minister's Office, issued the day after the press conference. The quoted description of the problem, including its effect on people in Indonesia, is the Prime Minister's.

diplomaticResponse.text: Malaysia's environment minister said Malaysia would send water-bombers to Sumatra to help put out peat fires once Indonesia agreed.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: Malaysia will send water-bombers to Sumatra to help put out peat fires once Indonesia agrees to it

diplomaticResponse.note: The Star, 25 June 2013; its headline says the minister was travelling to Indonesia to discuss the issue with his counterpart. The rest of the report is behind a paywall, and no Malaysian government statement was opened.

diplomaticResponse.text: According to Singapore's environment minister, Indonesia's President replied formally to Singapore's Prime Minister on 3 July 2013, acknowledging the seriousness of the situation, reiterating his apologies, and stating that the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution was in the final stages of resubmission to Indonesia's House of Representatives for ratification.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: replied formally to ... on 3 July 2013. He acknowledged the seriousness of the situation this year

The President also stated that the government of Indonesia has been in the final stages of resubmitting the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution to Indonesia’s House of Representatives (DPR) for ratification by the House.
The President also very graciously reiterated his apologies and reassured us that they would spare no effort to address this problem.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account of the letter; the letter itself was not opened. Personal names omitted by ellipsis.

diplomaticResponse.text: Senior officials of Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore held a first trilateral meeting on transboundary haze in Jakarta on 26 July 2013, following an agreement by the three foreign ministers at the ASEAN Ministerial Meeting in Brunei on 29 June; according to Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Singapore and Malaysia commended Indonesia for its commitment to expedite ratification of the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
diplomaticResponse.label: fact

refs.quote: trilateral meeting on transboundary haze between the senior officials of Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore in Jakarta on 26 July 2013
the meeting was a follow-up to the agreement by the Foreign Ministers of Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore at the sidelines of the ... ASEAN Ministerial Meeting in Brunei on 29 June
Both countries commended Indonesia for its commitment to expedite the process of ratification of the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

diplomaticResponse.note: Singapore's account (MFA spokesman, 27 July 2013); no Indonesian or Malaysian account was opened.

aftermath.text: Weeks after the June episode, haze returned to parts of Malaysia: AFP reported on 22 July 2013 that three areas, two in Malacca and one in Selangor, had recorded 'unhealthy' Air Pollutant Index readings above 100 that day, according to DOE.
aftermath.label: observation

refs.quote: Haze blanketed parts of Malaysia on Monday, weeks after the region suffered its worst pollution from forest fires in Indonesia in more than a decade.

Three areas -- two in southern Malacca state and a third in Selangor near the capital Kuala Lumpur -- recorded "unhealthy" air quality with readings above 100, according to the Department of Environment.
In Malaysia, Air Pollutant Index readings of 100-200 are branded "unhealthy".
Published July 22, 2013

aftermath.note: AFP report published on 22 July 2013 (a Monday). API readings; averaging period and reading times not stated.

selection.note: A is met: NEA said the smoke haze came from fires in Sumatra and was carried by prevailing winds, DOE describes the episode as due to transboundary pollution, and MEWR, NASA Earth Observatory and three peer-reviewed studies concur. B1, B2 and B3 are met: Singapore's air quality was Unhealthy on 5 days and Very Unhealthy on 3 days (MEWR), with NEA's 24-hour PSI above 100 on 19 and 21 June, DOE reports unhealthy and hazardous levels across most of Peninsular Malaysia, and two Malacca stations exceeded API 300 on 23 June (news citing DOE) (B1); a haze emergency was declared in Muar and Ledang, schools closed in several Malaysian states, and Singapore's Ministry of Social and Family Development required childcare centres and kindergartens to cancel all outdoor activities, while Singapore's standard band-linked health advisories (MOH's of 19 June and NEA's of 21 June) are not counted, being treated as routine, as in the 2016 entry (B2); MEWR lists 2013 among particularly severe haze years, DOE's chronology calls it a severe haze episode, a 2014 peer-reviewed study calls its 24-hour PSI peak an all-time record and a 2018 peer-reviewed study describes it as a severe haze event (B3).

attribution.note: Singapore's National Environment Agency and NASA describe smoke from fires in Sumatra. Singapore's environment minister told Parliament that Riau was the source of most of the haze, and the peer-reviewed studies quoted in this entry locate the fires, or the smoke's source, in Riau, central Sumatra. Malaysia's Department of Environment, in its chronology, attributes the episode to transboundary pollution without naming a source area. No public dispute about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. An Indonesian minister criticised how Singapore's officials raised the haze in public; that is recorded under Response between governments as an allegation.

confidence.rationale: AI-assigned rating awaiting human review; it describes the evidence, not the severity of the episode. Medium under the pre-registered definitions. The core account (as NEA, MEWR, NASA Earth Observatory and three peer-reviewed studies describe it, smoke haze from fires in Sumatra affected Singapore from 13 June 2013, and, as DOE describes it, haze due to transboundary pollution affected most parts of Peninsular Malaysia from 15 June, with readings peaking between about 19 and 23 June) rests on primary government sources in both countries (NEA, MEWR and MOH in Singapore; DOE in Malaysia), a scientific agency (NASA Earth Observatory) and peer-reviewed studies (Scientific Reports, 2014; Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 2018; Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 2019), and is corroborated by independent reporting (AP, AFP, BBC, Bernama, The Star, Malaysiakini, The Jakarta Post). Singapore's readings and day counts are quoted from NEA and MEWR, the API above 500 in Muar and the emergency of 23–24 June from DOE's chronology, and Singapore's attendance records from MOH. Conditions in the medium definition hold: minor conflicts about peak readings remain (the date of Singapore's 24-hour PSI of 246, 20 or 22 June 2013, and whether it exceeded 236 on three consecutive days; Muar's API on the morning of 23 June, 746 or 750, where DOE's chronology gives only 'more than 500'; the time of the 3-hour PSI of 401 on 21 June); Malaysia's hourly and station readings, the Malaysian school closures and the reopening of schools rest on news reports citing DOE and the Education Ministry; and no Malaysian healthcare-use record was found. Impacts in Riau also rest on news reports. NEA's validated 2013 24-hour PSI record, DOE's hourly API record for 23 June 2013, an Education Ministry record of school closures and official Indonesian records of impacts in Riau would address these gaps.

contradictions.text: Date of Singapore's 24-hour PSI peak of 246: MEWR's February 2014 consultation paper gives 20 June 2013; a 2014 peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports, using NEA's 24-hour PSI as read at 4 pm, and a December 2013 commentary in the Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore give 22 June 2013. NEA's own contemporaneous material opened here shows no 24-hour PSI of 246 (on its PSI page 246 appears only as a 24-hour PM2.5 concentration in µg/m³, South region 20 June, East region 21 June): its PSI page archived on the afternoon of 20 June 2013 shows a 24-hour PSI of 152–173 for one of that day's three readings (which one cannot be identified); its 4 pm update of 21 June gave 173–225 and expected the day's readings in the upper part of the 200–300 range; and its page archived early on 22 June shows 3-hour PSI values of 177–190 between midnight and 6 am and a 24-hour table for 21 June of 170–198 (reading time not identifiable). NEA's readings for the evening of 20 June and for 22 June were not found. Unresolved: 246 is published with both dates disclosed.

Possible inconsistency between the 2014 Scientific Reports study and NEA's real-time readings: the study reports 'three consecutive days > 236' in the 4 pm 24-hour PSI series it obtained from NEA, with the peak of 246 on 22 June 2013. Singapore's readings had fallen by 23 June (The Jakarta Post reported readings between 'moderate' and 'unhealthy' that Sunday), so the three days would have to include 21 June (AI agent's reasoning); but NEA's own 4 pm update of 21 June 2013 gave a 24-hour PSI of 173–225. A possible explanation is that the study used NEA's validated archive, which may differ from the real-time values (hypothesis, unverified).
Time of the 3-hour PSI of 401 on 21 June 2013: NEA's 4 pm update says 1 pm; the BBC says 12:00 (04:00 GMT) and does not give the averaging period. NEA's primary record is preferred here.

Singapore's previous record: NASA and the BBC give 226 in 1997 without stating the averaging period; MEWR gives the previous 24-hour PSI records as 138 (1997) and 128 (2006), and the 2014 Scientific Reports study gives 138 on 19 September 1997. The 226 may be a 3-hour value (unverified); the figures are probably different measures and should not be compared.

Muar API on the morning of 23 June 2013: 746 at 7 am according to The Star (citing DOE's website) and a Bernama report carried by Malaysiakini (citing DOE); Malaysiakini's own report gives 746 'this morning' and The Jakarta Post '746 early Sunday'; 750 according to AFP quoting Malaysia's environment minister (Malay Mail); 'exceeded 750 at 7am' in a 2026 retrospective by The Star; DOE's chronology says only 'more than 500'. A 2023 article in EnvironmentAsia, citing an earlier study, gives '746 µg/m3' but compares it with 'the lower end of the hazardous level', an API band, so the unit appears to be wrong (AI agent's analysis): the value is treated here as an API reading and the µg/m3 unit is not adopted.

Date of the Muar and Ledang emergency declaration: DOE's chronology and same-day reports (Bernama, carried by Malaysiakini) give 23 June 2013; a 2019 Bernama report carried by Free Malaysia Today, giving NADMA's list of past haze emergencies, gives 'June 3, 2013'. The primary DOE record and the same-day reports agree on 23 June, so the 3 June date appears to be an error in the list or in its reporting (AI agent's judgement).

Malaysian economic losses for 2013: SUHAKAM (2024), citing a 2018 review article, gives RM1.49 billion in total household losses (cost of illness, foregone income opportunities and willingness to pay); a 2019 Malay Mail report of a university research paper gives RM1.57 billion in healthcare costs and lost income opportunities. The scopes may differ; neither the review nor the university paper was opened.

evidenceGaps: NEA's 24-hour PSI readings for the evening of 20 June and for 22 June 2013 were not found: the Internet Archive holds copies of NEA's PSI page from the afternoon of 20 June and early 22 June 2013 only, and the archived 'Historical PSI Readings' page shows only the current day. NEA's validated 2013 PSI record was not opened, so the date of the 246 peak cannot be settled.

No DOE record of hourly or daily API values for June 2013 was opened; the Muar readings (746 at 7 am, 690 at 11 am on 23 June) and the Malacca station readings come from news reports citing DOE's website, and DOE's chronology gives only 'more than 500'.
No Malaysian healthcare-utilisation record for June 2013 (Ministry of Health Malaysia or the Johor State Health Department) was found; searches returned 2019 data instead.

Malaysia–Indonesia government exchanges during the episode are thinly documented here: only a news report of Malaysia's offer of water-bombers was opened; no statement from Malaysia's Foreign Ministry, Prime Minister's Office or environment ministry was found.

Official Indonesian records of impacts and responses in Riau (provincial health office, education offices, BNPB) were not opened; those claims rest on reports by the BBC and The Jakarta Post. A web search during review returned Indonesian-language news reports (Kontan, JPNN) described in the results as covering statements by the head of BNPB on respiratory illness in haze-affected areas; they were not opened, checked or used.
No national total of Malaysian school closures from the Ministry of Education was found.

Studies cited second-hand by the opened sources were not opened: a 2015 study cited by the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres study for particulate levels in Singapore and Malaysia, a 2016 study cited by the EnvironmentAsia article for the Muar reading, and the 2018 review article that SUHAKAM cites (footnote 41) for its cost estimate.
Legal and enforcement follow-up in Indonesia to the 2013 fires was not researched here.
unresolvedQuestions: On which date and at which reading time did Singapore's 24-hour PSI reach 246: 20 June 2013 (MEWR) or 22 June 2013 (the Scientific Reports study; the Annals commentary)? NEA's validated records should settle this.
Does the Scientific Reports study's 'three consecutive days > 236' reflect NEA's validated data, which may differ from the real-time 4 pm values published on 21 June 2013 (173–225)?
What index and averaging period lie behind the reading of 400 in Riau reported by the BBC on 21 June 2013?
Was the 1997 value of 226 cited by NASA and the BBC a 3-hour PSI reading?

How do the tropical-cyclone explanation (Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 2019) and the MJO and westerly-wind explanation (Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 2018) of the smoke transport relate to each other?
What averaging period applied to the Muar API values reported on 23 June 2013 (746 at 7 am, 690 at 11 am)?

events.title: June–October 2014: Peninsular Malaysia, Sarawak and Singapore

period.label: June–October 2014

refs.quote: During Southwest Monsoon, the country had experienced transboundary haze pollution from June to October.

From 22 June to 24 July 2014, west coast of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality status where the highest Air Pollutant Index (API) recorded was 260 (very unhealthy), in Seri Manjung, Perak on 22 July 2014.

From 17 September to 12 October 2014, west coast and northern parts of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality status with the highest API recorded was 129, in Nilai,Negeri Sembilan on 10 October 2014.

Singapore experienced a total of six haze episodes in September and October. Three episodes occurred on 14-15, 17-19 and 21-22 September 2014 while another three episodes on 6-7, 8 and 11-12 October 2014.
The haze was due to forest and peatland fires in several States namely in Selangor, Perak, Pahang, Johor, Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu.
refs.pinpoint: Entry 9 (2014), PDF p.3 (February–March 2014 haze, outside this entry)

period.note: Month precision follows DOE's statement that Malaysia experienced transboundary haze 'from June to October' 2014. Within that span DOE dates unhealthy air quality in Malaysia from 22 June to 12 October 2014 (in three periods), and NEA dates Singapore's six haze episodes from 14 September to 12 October 2014. A short further episode in Singapore on 2–3 November 2014 is reported under 'Aftermath' rather than inside the period: NEA describes it in a separate section of its review as an uncommon late inter-monsoon event brought by winds from a Bay of Bengal depression, and DOE's period ends in October (AI agent's judgement). The February–March 2014 haze, which DOE attributes to fires within several Malaysian states and which NEA links, for Singapore's March haze, to fires in southern Johor, is not part of this entry; it is handled in the list of considered periods.

summary.text: Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE) records that the country experienced transboundary haze pollution from June to October 2014, during the Southwest Monsoon.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: During Southwest Monsoon, the country had experienced transboundary haze pollution from June to October.

From 22 June to 24 July 2014, west coast of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality status where the highest Air Pollutant Index (API) recorded was 260 (very unhealthy), in Seri Manjung, Perak on 22 July 2014.

summary.note: DOE's retrospective chronology (undated in its text; PDF metadata give a creation date of 21 September 2015). The description of origin is the agency's assessment. Contemporaneous reports attribute Sibu's reading of 270 on 28 July 2014 to a local bushfire, and ASMC, as reported by Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister on 29 July 2014, placed burning on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sarawak as well as in Riau and West Kalimantan; see 'Where sources disagree'.

summary.text: Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) reports that drier conditions in September and October 2014 led to an escalation of hotspot activity in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and that widespread smoke haze was occasionally observed emanating from hotspot clusters and was carried by the prevailing low-level winds to affect parts of Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Drier weather conditions prevailed in for the southern ASEAN region in September and October 2014 as the monsoon rain belt was located further north, away from the equator.
During this period, the drier conditions led to an escalation of hotspot activities in Sumatra and Kalimantan.
Widespread smoke haze was occasionally observed emanating from hotpot clusters and the smoke haze was carried by the prevailing low level winds to affect parts of Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore.

summary.note: NEA's Annual Weather Review 2014, section 2.4 ('Haze in September and October 2014'); undated in its text, PDF created in December 2015. Where the smoke came from is NEA's assessment. 'hotpot' is the source's spelling. A hotspot is a satellite detection of heat, not evidence of who started a fire.

summary.text: NEA records six haze episodes in Singapore in September and October 2014: on 14–15, 17–19 and 21–22 September and on 6–7, 8 and 11–12 October.
summary.label: observation

refs.quote: Singapore experienced a total of six haze episodes in September and October. Three episodes occurred on 14-15, 17-19 and 21-22 September 2014 while another three episodes on 6-7, 8 and 11-12 October 2014.

summary.text: NEA's State of the Environment report lists 2014 among the years in which Singapore's air quality was affected by transboundary haze from the region (2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019).
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Air quality was affected by transboundary haze from the region in 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019.
refs.pinpoint: PDF p.5, notes to Figure 2 ('Air Quality in terms of PSI')

refs.quote: On several days between 7 and 15 March 2014, air quality over several parts of Singapore deteriorated in the afternoon and early evening as the prevailing north-easterly winds transported smoke haze from the fires in southern Johor to Singapore.

summary.note: The statement covers the whole of 2014. NEA's Annual Weather Review 2014 (second ref) also reports smoke haze from fires in southern Johor affecting parts of Singapore in March 2014, outside this entry, so the statement cannot be tied to the June–October episode alone and is not tagged as evidence for criterion A.

impact.text: The Star reported on 30 July 2014 that many areas in Malaysia had recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings over Hari Raya and that visibility in Petaling Jaya had dropped to less than one kilometre.
impact.label: observation

refs.quote: Hari Raya turned out to be a hazy one nationwide with many areas recording unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings.
Visibility in Petaling Jaya dropped to less than one kilometre due to the thick smog while in Subang, it dropped to less than five kilometres.

impact.note: Republished by Eco-Business with credit to The Star. The report does not say who measured the visibility or on which day. The report also calls Hari Raya 'a hazy one nationwide'; that is the newspaper's characterisation and is not part of this statement. The minister's statement of 29 July 2014 (see 'Malaysia: Air quality') listed nine areas with unhealthy API readings at 7 am and, according to the same report, 20 areas with average and 23 with good air quality.

airQuality.text: DOE reports that from 22 June to 24 July 2014 the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality, with the highest API reading of the period, 260 ('very unhealthy'), recorded at Seri Manjung, Perak, on 22 July 2014.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: From 22 June to 24 July 2014, west coast of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality status where the highest Air Pollutant Index (API) recorded was 260 (very unhealthy), in Seri Manjung, Perak on 22 July 2014.

airQuality.note: API; hour and averaging period not stated in the chronology. 'Highest' is DOE's word, in its chronology, which is undated in its text (PDF created in September 2015). Malaysia's API and Singapore's PSI are different indices and are not comparable.

airQuality.text: DOE reports that from 25 July to 17 September 2014 several areas in Sarawak experienced unhealthy air quality, with the highest API reading of the period, 270 ('very unhealthy'), recorded in Sibu on 28 July 2014.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: From 25 July to 17 September 2014, several areas in the state of Sarawak experienced unhealthy air quality status with the highest API recorded were 270 (very unhealthy), in Sibu, Sarawak on 28 July 2014.

airQuality.note: API; hour and averaging period not stated in the chronology. 'Highest' is DOE's word, in its chronology, which is undated in its text (PDF created in September 2015). Contemporaneous reports attribute this reading to a local fire at Bukit Lima Forest Park in Sibu; see the New Straits Times claim of 31 July 2014 below and 'Where sources disagree'. For that reason this statement is not counted towards criterion B1 (see 'Why it is included').

airQuality.text: DOE reports that from 17 September to 12 October 2014 the west coast and northern parts of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality, with the highest API reading of the period, 129, recorded in Nilai, Negeri Sembilan, on 10 October 2014.

refs.quote: From 17 September to 12 October 2014, west coast and northern parts of Peninsular Malaysia experienced unhealthy air quality status with the highest API recorded was 129, in Nilai,Negeri Sembilan on 10 October 2014.

airQuality.note: API; hour and averaging period not stated in the chronology. 'Highest' is DOE's word, in its chronology, which is undated in its text (PDF created in September 2015). No contemporaneous Malaysian report of this phase was found; it overlaps Singapore's September–October episodes.

airQuality.text: The New Straits Times reported on 22 July 2014 that Taiping, Ipoh, Seri Manjung and Tanjung Malim in Perak recorded unhealthy API readings, between 101 and 195 at 6am, and that Seri Manjung's reading rose to 208 at 8am and, according to DOE's website, to 215 at 9am; a Bernama report carried by the New Straits Times the next day gave the API in Manjung as 260 ('very unhealthy') at 6 pm.

Seri Manjung recorded the worst API when its readings spike up to 208 at 8am.
A check on the Department of Environment website found the API readings in Seri Manjung also increased to 215 at 9am.
As at 6 pm, the API in Manjung was at the 'very unhealthy' level of 260.

airQuality.text: Bernama reported that Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister said nine areas recorded unhealthy air quality on the API at 7 am on 29 July 2014: Port Klang (135), Petaling Jaya (102), Banting (137), Batu Muda, Kuala Lumpur (123), Cheras (121), Putrajaya (124), Sibu (191), Samarahan (126) and Sri Aman, Sarawak (114).

said 20 areas recorded average air quality and 23 at good level

refs.quote: said Natural Resources and Environment Minister
Tuesday, 29 Jul 2014

The same report says 20 areas recorded average air quality and 23 good (time not stated). airQuality.text: The New Straits Times reported on 31 July 2014 that on the first day of Hari Raya Aidilfitri (a Monday) a bushfire at Sibu's Bukit Lima Forest Park had caused the API in Sibu to rise to 270 by noon, the highest in the country, with visibility reduced to 300 m, and that Sarawak's State Local Government and Community Development Minister said the fire had been the main contributor to the haze since the Saturday.

selection.note: A is met: DOE describes transboundary haze in Malaysia from June to October 2014; NEA attributes the September–October 2014 haze in Singapore and parts of Peninsular Malaysia to smoke from hotspots in Sumatra and Kalimantan; and a peer-reviewed source-attribution study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics models Singapore's September–October 2014 biomass-burning PM10 as coming mainly from Central Kalimantan, South Sumatra and West Kalimantan. B1 is met: NEA reports 24-hour PSI in the Unhealthy range on 15, 18 and 19 September 2014 and a 24-hour peak of 125 on 7 October (its hourly data show all five regions above 100 at that hour); DOE reports unhealthy air quality on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia from 22 June to 24 July 2014 (highest API 260, at Seri Manjung on 22 July) and on the west coast and in northern parts of Peninsular Malaysia from 17 September to 12 October 2014 (highest 129, at Nilai on 10 October); and Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister reported unhealthy API readings at nine places at 7 am on 29 July 2014. Readings from Sibu (DOE's Sarawak peak of 270 on 28 July; 191 on 29 July) are not relied on for B1, because contemporaneous reports and a Sarawak state minister attributed the haze in Sibu to a local bushfire. No source opened says where the smoke behind the Seri Manjung peak came from. B2 is met for Malaysia: the afternoon sessions of 15 schools in Manjung, Perak, were ordered closed on 22 July 2014, closures that Bernama's report attributes to the haze, although no source says whether the smoke there that day was local or transboundary; the Penang state health committee chairman's advice to reduce exposure, reported on 23 July 2014, is recorded under 'Health evidence' but not tagged. B3 is not claimed: the same study classes the August–October 2014 event as 'significant' (a term it defines), says the two most recent August–October episodes 'with highest concentrations' were in 2014 and 2015, and lists it among 'the seasons with the most significant haze events' in Singapore in 2010–2015; whether that amounts to 'among the worst' is left for human review.

attribution.note: Singapore's National Environment Agency and a peer-reviewed modelling study quoted in this entry describe smoke from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan reaching Singapore in September–October 2014 (NEA says it also affected parts of Peninsular Malaysia). Malaysia's Department of Environment describes the June–October haze in Malaysia as transboundary without naming where the smoke came from; ASMC, as reported by Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister, reported smoke haze from burning areas in Riau and West Kalimantan and on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sarawak. No public dispute between governments about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. A Sarawak state minister attributed Sibu's highest reading of the period to a local bushfire (see Where sources disagree).

confidence.rationale: Medium under the pre-registered definitions. Evidence for the core account: DOE's chronology (government) records transboundary haze pollution in Malaysia from June to October 2014 and unhealthy air quality in three periods between 22 June and 12 October; NEA's Annual Weather Review 2014 (government) records six haze episodes in Singapore in September–October 2014, 24-hour PSI in the Unhealthy range on 15, 18 and 19 September and a 24-hour peak of 125 on 7 October, and attributes the haze to smoke from hotspots in Sumatra and Kalimantan; NEA's hourly dataset shows all five regions above 100 at 9:00 on 7 October; NEA's State of the Environment report lists 2014 among the years affected by transboundary haze; and a peer-reviewed study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics models Singapore's September–October 2014 biomass-burning PM10 as coming mainly from Central Kalimantan, South Sumatra and West Kalimantan. Independent reports corroborate Malaysia's late-July readings and school closures (New Straits Times, Bernama, The Star; DOE's peaks of 260 at Seri Manjung on 22 July and 270 at Sibu on 28 July match news reports of readings on those days) and haze in Singapore in mid-September (Al Jazeera, The Jakarta Post). Key figures are quoted from DOE and NEA. MEDIUM conditions recorded in this entry hold: Malaysia's period boundaries and its September–October phase rest on DOE's retrospective chronology alone, and the unhealthy readings in Peninsular Malaysia reported for 29 July fall outside the chronology's Peninsular dates; where the smoke behind Malaysia's July peaks came from is incompletely documented and partly disputed (contemporaneous reports and a Sarawak state minister attributed Sibu's 270 to a local bushfire; ASMC, as reported by Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister, reported burning on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sarawak as well as in Riau and West Kalimantan; no source opened says where the smoke behind the Seri Manjung peak came from); and minor conflicts remain (Singapore's reading at 7 am on 15 September; whether all 102 Manjung schools or the afternoon sessions of 15 were closed on 22 July; 127 or 128 for the 2 November 3-hour peak). AI-assigned rating awaiting human review.

contradictions.text: Singapore, 15 September 2014: a wire report carried by Al Jazeera said NEA reported the PSI 'reached a high of 111 at 7:00 am' that day, without stating the averaging period. NEA's hourly regional 24-hour PSI data give a highest regional value of 104 (west) at 07:00 that day (record '15/9/2014 7:00': north 76, south 81, east 82, west 104, central 76); in the AI agent's reading of that day's rows, the day's highest regional 24-hour value was 107 (west) at 11:00. The Jakarta Post (17 September 2014) reported that NEA's website showed the three-hour PSI 'broke above 100' and stayed above that level into the daylight hours, which suggests the 111 was a 3-hour reading, but no NEA 3-hour PSI record for 2014 was found to confirm it. Not resolved; NEA's own data and review are used for 24-hour values.

Origin of Malaysia's peak readings: DOE presents the June–October 2014 haze in Malaysia as transboundary and gives Sibu's API of 270 on 28 July 2014 as Sarawak's highest reading of the period. The New Straits Times (31 July 2014) attributed Sibu's 270 to a bushfire at Bukit Lima Forest Park in Sibu and quoted a Sarawak state minister as saying the fire had been the main contributor to the haze since the Saturday; The Star (30 July 2014) also said Sibu's poor air quality was due to a forest fire in Bukit Lima Forest Park. Bernama (29 July 2014) reported the Malaysian environment minister citing an ASMC report of smoke haze from burning areas on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sarawak as well as in Riau and West Kalimantan, and NOAA images showing 11 hotspots in Malaysia. No source opened says where the smoke behind the Seri Manjung peak of 260 on 22 July 2014 came from. The relative contribution of local and transboundary smoke to Malaysia's peak readings is not resolved.

Manjung school closures, 22 July 2014: a New Straits Times report published at 2 pm that day stated, without attribution, that all 102 schools in the district had been ordered closed after the API recorded a very unhealthy level; it cited an unnamed source for the detail that morning-session pupils were allowed home at 11am and all afternoon sessions were cancelled, and reported a school's senior assistant as confirming that the state education department had instructed all schools in the state to close. Bernama's report published the next day quoted Perak's state education director as saying six primary and nine secondary schools in the district, with an enrolment of 5,945, were ordered to close their afternoon sessions. The entry uses the education director's account as reported by Bernama; the difference is not resolved.

Singapore, 2 November 2014: NEA's Annual Weather Review 2014 gives the 3-hour PSI peak as 128 at 9 pm, while a Bloomberg report carried by Malay Mail on 3 November 2014, citing NEA, says the 3-hour PSI peaked 'at 127 at 9pm yesterday'. The difference is small and unexplained (possibly a provisional value later revised); NEA's review is used.

evidenceGaps: No contemporaneous NEA, MEWR or MOH press release, haze advisory or PSI update for September–November 2014 was opened. When the Internet Archive's index was queried for haze.gov.sg pages of September–November 2014 (15 October 2026), it returned 'Temporarily Offline', so archived copies could not be checked. Singapore's 2014 episodes are known from NEA's Annual Weather Review 2014, NEA's hourly dataset, NEA's State of the Environment report and news reports.

No NEA 3-hour PSI dataset for 2014 was found, so the reported '111 at 7 am' on 15 September and the 3-hour peaks of 156 (6 October) and 128 or 127 (2 November) could not be checked against data. A republication of a Yahoo News report of 11 October 2014, which a search-engine summary suggested may give a different figure for the 6 October 3-hour peak, returned HTTP 403 to two automated download attempts; its figure is unverified and is not used.

DOE's hourly API records for June–October 2014 were not opened; DOE's chronology gives period peaks without the hour or averaging period. Malaysia's September–October 2014 phase (highest API 129 at Nilai on 10 October) rests on DOE's chronology alone: no Malaysian news report of that phase was found.

No school closures, emergency declarations or haze-specific outdoor-activity advisories were found for Singapore in 2014, and none for Sarawak in July–September 2014. Newspaper archives were searched only through a general web search, so this is not evidence that none occurred.

No official healthcare-utilisation records for this episode were found (Malaysian or Singapore Ministry of Health; polyclinic attendances; hospital admissions). The Star (30 July 2014) reported a percentage increase in patients at the clinics and hospitals it had checked, without naming the clinics, the comparison period or a reporting agency; it is not an official record, it does not show that any visit was caused by haze, and it is not used.

ASMC's own 2014 haze reports were not found online (its online alert archive starts in January 2015); ASMC's July 2014 assessment is known only through a Bernama report of a Malaysian minister's statement.

Indonesian primary sources (BNPB situation reports, provincial emergency declarations, ISPU readings) for June–October 2014 were not opened; impacts in Indonesia rest on The Jakarta Post and Mongabay. No NASA Earth Observatory article on the September–October 2014 fires was found; a NASA/Goddard image caption for July 2014 (posted on EurekAlert) repeats a news report's text and is not used.

NEA's Annual Weather Review 2014 contains evident year errors (in the September–October section the Figure 17 caption and the sentence referring to it say '6 October 2015'; p.1 refers to a dry spell 'since 13 January 2015'). Dates were taken from the main text.

NEA's hourly regional data show 24-hour PSI above 100 on 19 October 2014 (highest 102, in the south from 17:00 and the west from 18:00) and 20 October 2014 (highest 106, west, at 10:00), dates that are not among the six episodes NEA lists; no source explaining these readings was found (AI agent's reading of the dataset; not used as claims).

A 30 July 2014 Astro Awani report on the cause of the haze in Sibu, found by a web search on 15 October 2026, could not be opened: its address returned HTTP 404, the copy listed in the search results was on a host that did not resolve, and the Internet Archive had no copy. It is not used.

No public disagreement between governments about where the June–October 2014 smoke came from was found in the sources opened or in two web searches run on 15 October 2026. The searches were not exhaustive, so this is not evidence that none occurred.
unresolvedQuestions: Was the '111 at 7:00 am' reported for 15 September 2014 a 3-hour PSI, and what were NEA's 3-hour PSI values during the September 2014 episodes?
What raised Singapore's regional 24-hour PSI above 100 on 19–20 October 2014, after the last of the six episodes NEA lists?

How much did fires inside Malaysia (the Bukit Lima Forest Park fire in Sibu; the burning on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sarawak that ASMC reported, according to Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister) contribute to DOE's July 2014 peaks of 260 at Seri Manjung and 270 at Sibu, compared with smoke from Sumatra and Kalimantan?
How many schools in Manjung district closed on 22 July 2014 (afternoon sessions of 15 schools, or all 102), and did any other Malaysian schools close because of haze between June and October 2014?

Which Indonesian provinces or regencies declared haze emergencies between June and October 2014 (The Jakarta Post reported on 15 October 2014 that Riau's acting governor had not declared a health-related state of emergency), and what ISPU readings did Indonesian agencies report beyond the single Jambi City reading recorded here?

DOE's chronology dates unhealthy air quality on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia from 22 June to 24 July 2014 and next from 17 September, but Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environment Minister reported unhealthy API readings at six places in Peninsular Malaysia (Port Klang, Petaling Jaya, Banting, Batu Muda, Cheras and Putrajaya) at 7 am on 29 July 2014. Did unhealthy air quality in Peninsular Malaysia continue after 24 July, and how were the chronology's periods defined?
