selection.note: Criterion A is met: MSS, a Singapore government haze update, DOE, Malaysia's science minister and ASMC attribute the haze in Singapore or Malaysia to smoke from fires in Sumatra and/or Kalimantan (MSS and the minister call it transboundary), as do peer-reviewed studies (PNAS 2016; ACP 2019). B1 is met by MSS's 10 episodes of Unhealthy 24-hour PSI (peak 322) and SingStat's share of Unhealthy days, and by DOE's 34 areas with unhealthy air on 15 September 2015 and news reports of DOE readings above 100 on other days. B2 is met by school closures in both countries (DOE; MSS; news reports of the Education Ministry's orders); Malaysian official advice to reduce outdoor activities is also tagged; Singapore's standard advisory for a forecast Unhealthy PSI is not (treated as routine, as in the 2016 entry). B3 is met by MSS's annual climate assessment ('the worst in recent history') and by peer-reviewed publications that describe 2015, citing earlier work, as the worst haze in recent history in Singapore or the worst after 1997. The PNAS (2016) comparison with 2006 concerns Indonesia's fire season and is not counted for B3.

attribution.note: Meteorological Service Singapore, Malaysia's Department of Environment, ASMC and the peer-reviewed studies quoted in this entry describe smoke from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan. No public dispute about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. The disputed exchanges recorded under Response between governments (whether Indonesia had accepted Singapore's offer of help, and the Vice-President's remarks and the replies to them) are labelled allegations; documented offers and deployments are labelled facts.

confidence.rationale: AI-assigned rating awaiting human review. Medium under the pre-registered definitions. The core account — smoke haze, which MSS, DOE, MOSTI, ASMC and peer-reviewed studies attribute to fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, affected Singapore from late August to the end of October 2015 and Malaysia from August into October, with Unhealthy to Hazardous 24-hour PSI in Singapore, unhealthy to very unhealthy API readings reported by DOE in Malaysia, and school closures in both countries — is supported by government sources (MSS's Annual Climate Assessment 2015; NEA's hourly 24-hour PSI data on data.gov.sg; Singapore government releases of 10 and 25 September 2015; MOH Singapore; DOE Malaysia's chronology; MOSTI statements of 12 September and 3 October 2015), an intergovernmental source (ASMC's alert record) and peer-reviewed studies (PNAS 2016; ACP 2019), which corroborate one another. Singapore's key figures are quoted from primary sources: the 24-hour PSI peak of 322 (MSS, matched in NEA's data) and MSS's 10 Unhealthy episodes. For Malaysia, DOE's chronology gives 34 areas with unhealthy air quality on 15 September and school closures on 15 and 18 September, but it was created on 21 September 2015 (AI agent's reading of the PDF metadata), so its 'highest' reading (211) covers the season only to about that date. Malaysia's peak readings and the period are therefore incomplete or rest on news reports only, which the medium definition names: no DOE record of the season's maximum was found, the October readings (including the hazardous 308 at Shah Alam) and the October school-closure counts rest on news reports citing DOE and the Education Ministry, and no official source opened dates the end of the episode in Malaysia. Minor conflicts also remain, recorded under Where sources disagree: the date of Singapore's school closure in the Environment Minister's statement, Malaysia's peak reading, and the averaging period of some PSI values reported in the press. Indonesian impacts rest on NASA, the World Bank and news reports because official Indonesian sites could not be opened. Records that would strengthen the rating: DOE's 2015 hourly API records or annual report (season maximum and end date), Malaysia's Education Ministry statements on the closures, Singapore's Ministry of Education release on the closure, and Indonesian official records (BNPB, Ministry of Health, provincial emergency decrees).

contradictions.text: Singapore readings on 24–25 September 2015: MSS and NEA's hourly data give the 24-hour PSI peak as 322 at 8am on 25 September (NEA: 309 south at 4am, 318 at 6am). A Reuters photo caption on The Star's page gives 317 at 8pm on 24 September as a three-hour PSI; The Jakarta Post gives 341 on the Friday morning (25 September) as a three-hour PSI; NASA SVS gives 313, 317 and 341 without an averaging period; The Star's report says a reading 'hit 309 at 4am ... before climbing to 334 at 6am' in the sentence after one giving the 24-hour PSI, without naming the index. NEA's highest 24-hour regional value at 8pm on 24 September was 263, and no 24-hour value of 334 appears in NEA's records for 22 May–31 December 2015. Primary evidence settles the 24-hour peak (322); 317 and 341 are three-hour values according to the Reuters caption and The Jakarta Post; The Star does not name the index or averaging period of 334, and whether it is a three-hour value is unverified because NEA's 2015 three-hour data were not found.

Singapore school closure date: the Environment Minister's statement dated 25 September 2015 says 'we had to close Primary and Secondary schools yesterday', which would imply 24 September. MSS says the ministries decided on 24 September to close schools on 25 September, The Star reports the closure for Friday 25 September as announced on Thursday night, and The Jakarta Post (29 September) says schools shut 'last Friday'. The closure date used is 25 September (MSS); the minister's 'yesterday' may refer to the decision. No Ministry of Education release was opened.

Malaysian peak reading: DOE's chronology gives the 'highest API reading' as 211 at Banting on 14 September 2015, but the PDF was created on 21 September 2015; Malay Mail, citing DOE, reported 308 (hazardous) at Shah Alam on 4 October 2015. The figures cover different periods; 211 should be read as the highest as of about 21 September 2015, not as the season's maximum (AI agent's reading of the PDF metadata). No DOE record of the season's maximum was found.

Headline modelled 2015 mortality estimates in the studies opened range from 11,880 to 100,300 (106,000 in one sensitivity calculation): 11,880 (6,153–17,270) from short-term exposure in September–October 2015 (Scientific Reports 2016); about 75,600 per year in the same study's hypothetical long-term-exposure scenario; 44,040 from long-term exposure with the GEMM function (Environmental Research Letters 2020; its table gives 44,041, 95% uncertainty interval 34,672–53,948); 56,000 with the GEMM function (Nature Communications 2021); and 100,300 (Environmental Research Letters 2016). The 2020 study attributes the difference between its estimate and the 75,600 and 100,300 figures to different methods of estimating health impacts, and estimates 106,000 when it applies the 2016 Environmental Research Letters study's function; the 2021 study attributes its figure being lower than previous estimates to a less sensitive relative risk function. All are modelled estimates, not counts; this record does not choose between them.

Modelled and officially recorded deaths: the 2016 Environmental Research Letters study estimates 6,500 (1,700–11,300) excess deaths in Malaysia, 2,200 (600–3,800) in Singapore and 91,600 (24,000–159,200) in Indonesia, while Malay Mail reported in September 2016 that Malaysia's deputy health director-general said Malaysia had no deaths in 2015 directly related to the haze, that Indonesia's Health Ministry said the figures far exceeded the country's own recorded death toll, and that The Straits Times reported experts in Singapore felt the figure did not reflect what actually happened, although it quoted a respiratory physician calling the estimate possible. Statistical excess-mortality estimates and deaths recorded as directly caused by haze measure different things.

Singapore's Haze Subsidy Scheme uptake in 2015: MOH's release of 16 November 2015 gives around 50,000 haze-related attendances, while MOH's later FAQ says around 77,000 Singaporeans benefited in 2015, more people than the attendances first reported. The November figure was a preliminary estimate, as clinics had up to a month after the scheme ended to submit claims, and the two figures count different things (attendances and people); MOH does not reconcile them in the documents opened.

Singapore's offer of assistance: on 11 September 2015 Singapore's Defence Minister said Indonesia had accepted the offer (The Straits Times); on 29 September The Jakarta Post reported that Indonesia's Environment and Forestry Minister had previously turned it down and that the Cabinet Secretary said Indonesia was continuing without outside help, while the Vice-President said Indonesia was open to help. Singapore's Ministry of Defence states that it deployed on 10 October 2015 following Indonesia's acceptance, and AFP reported on 11 October that the Indonesian government had for weeks insisted it did not need international help before agreeing to accept offers from several countries. The accounts differ by speaker and date; this record does not resolve what was agreed in September.

Cost of the 2015 fires: the World Bank estimates at least US$16.1 billion for Indonesia only (1 June–31 October 2015, excluding regional and global losses), while the Nature Communications (2021) study estimates total losses of US$28 billion, including modelled health costs in Malaysia and Singapore and an imputed value of CO2 emissions. The difference reflects scope and method, not necessarily an error.

Cloud-seeding threshold in Malaysia: the science minister's statement of 12 September 2015 says MetMalaysia and the air force were ready to seed clouds if the API stayed above 101 (the unhealthy level) for 72 continuous hours; the New Straits Times reported on 17 September 2015 that the same minister said cloud seeding would be conducted when the API persisted above 150 for 72 hours. This record does not resolve which threshold applied.

Characterisation of severity in Singapore: MSS's annual climate assessment (March 2016) calls the three-month 2015 event the worst in recent history, while Gulf Times, in an article of 25 September 2015 apparently from AFP, called the situation then 'the worst such episode since mid-2013'. The statements were made at different times about different things (the whole season versus the situation at one date), and Singapore's PSI changed in April 2014, so readings from 2013 and 2015 are not directly comparable. This record does not choose between them.

Last major event before 2015: MSS's annual climate assessment (March 2016) says the last major haze event to affect the region was in 1997/1998, while the PNAS (2016) study, writing about fire activity and smoke pollution over Sumatra and Kalimantan, says the last major event occurred in 2006 over southern Sumatra and south-central Kalimantan. The two statements may differ in scope (haze affecting the region; fires and smoke over parts of Indonesia); this record does not choose between them.

evidenceGaps: No DOE (Malaysia) record of the 2015 season's maximum API was found: the DOE chronology predates October 2015, and DOE's historical hourly API data for 2015 were not found online. October readings rest on news reports citing DOE.

No primary statement from Malaysia's Education Ministry or Ministry of Health from 2015 was opened; school-closure counts and health advice rest on Malay Mail, Borneo Post, The Malaysian Insider and the New Straits Times. No official Malaysian counts of haze-related clinic visits or admissions for 2015 were found.

Singapore's Ministry of Education release on the 25 September 2015 closure was not opened (an earlier search during this research found that moe.gov.sg returned an empty page); the closure is sourced to MSS, MEWR and news reports.
NEA's historical three-hour PSI data for 2015 were not found on data.gov.sg, so the press values 317, 334 and 341 could not be checked against NEA data.

Official Indonesian sources could not be opened: sehatnegeriku.kemkes.go.id (host not found; Internet Archive copy blocked with HTTP 429), berkas.dpr.go.id (HTTP 403) and setkab.go.id (empty page). Indonesian provincial emergencies, school closures (including the national figure of about 25,000 schools), evacuation measures, ISPU readings and case counts therefore rest on NASA, the World Bank, BBC, Antara and The Jakarta Post; no ISPU values were found.

The 2016 Environmental Research Letters study was read only from an Internet Archive copy of the publisher's PDF (publisher site blocked automated access); a 2018 study of Malaysian station data for 2015 (Environmental Research Letters) could not be opened (HTTP 403 in an earlier search during this research).

Economic estimates for Malaysia (RM1.07 billion) and Singapore (US$500 million; S$1.83 billion) cited in SUHAKAM's 2024 haze report were not used because the underlying studies and their scope could not be identified from the report.

No Thai, Philippine, Vietnamese or Bruneian official measurements for 2015 were opened. The spread of haze to (southern parts of) the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam rests on MSS, and to Thailand also on the PNAS (2016) study; no source opened says the haze reached Brunei.
unresolvedQuestions: What was the highest API reading in Malaysia during the 2015 season according to DOE's own records, and at which station and hour?
Was the 334 reported for 6am on 25 September 2015 a three-hour PSI value, and what were NEA's three-hour PSI values on 24–25 September 2015?
Did the Environment Minister's 'yesterday' (statement of 25 September 2015) refer to the closure decision on 24 September rather than to the closure itself?
How many school days and schools were affected by haze closures in Malaysia over the whole 2015 season, according to the Education Ministry?
Which modelled mortality estimate, if any, should be presented for Malaysia and Singapore, given that estimates differ mainly by exposure-response function?
What exactly did Indonesia accept from Singapore in September 2015, and when, given the differing official accounts before the deployment of 10 October 2015?

What did DOE mean by 34 areas recording unhealthy air quality 'for the first time in Malaysia's history since 1997' on 15 September 2015, given that its chronology also records unhealthy and hazardous air quality in 2013 and 2014?
Which level of Indonesian government declared the state of emergency in Riau in September 2015, and on what date?

events.title: 26–30 August 2016: Singapore, central Peninsular Malaysia and Riau, Indonesia

period.label: 26–30 August 2016

refs.quote: In 2016, the only significant transboundary haze episode that affected Singapore occurred from 26 to 28 August.
The haze situation in Riau, central Sumatra deteriorated rapidly between 25 and 26 August 2016 and persisted until 29 August 2016 under dry weather and strong winds conditions.
As of 9am, Nilai's API reading stood at 118, followed by Banting (101), Shah Alam (105) and Putrajaya (102).
refs.pinpoint: Article published 30 August 2016 (10:16 +08:00, page metadata), para 3 of the AMP copy

refs.quote: Transboundary haze periods refer to: 26–30 August 2016, 14 September to 5 October 2019 and 7–19 October 2023.

period.note: Dates differ by place and source. MSS dates Singapore's significant episode 26–28 August 2016; NEA's hourly data show the north region's 24-hour PSI above 100 again until 14:00 on 29 August (see 'Singapore: Air quality'); ASMC dates the haze in Riau from 25–26 to 29 August. News reports of 30 August give unhealthy API readings in Peninsular Malaysia for 29 and 30 August (one report citing DOE information), so the end date of 30 August rests on those reports; no official source opened links those readings to the smoke from Riau. A 2025 study also used 26–30 August as its 2016 haze period. No single official start and end date covering both countries was found.

summary.text: Meteorological Service Singapore (MSS) states in its Annual Climate Assessment for 2016 that the only significant transboundary haze episode affecting Singapore that year occurred from 26 to 28 August, and that a sudden intensification of fire hotspot activity over Riau province in central Sumatra on the night of 25 August led to smoke haze being carried towards Singapore by strong westerly winds the following day.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: In 2016, the only significant transboundary haze episode that affected Singapore occurred from 26 to 28 August. A sudden intensification of fire hotspot activities over Riau province in central Sumatra on the night of 25 August 2016 led to smoke haze being transported by strong westerly winds towards Singapore the following day.

summary.note: The agency's retrospective assessment (Annual Climate Assessment 2016, PDF created July 2017); 'only significant' is MSS's characterisation, and its account of where the smoke came from is MSS's assessment. It says where fire hotspots were detected, not who started any fire.

summary.text: In its review of regional weather and smoke haze for August 2016, the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) reported that the haze situation in Riau deteriorated rapidly between 25 and 26 August 2016 and persisted until 29 August, and that moderate to dense smoke haze from the fires in Riau was blown by south-westerly to westerly winds over the Strait of Malacca to central Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore, where air quality deteriorated to Unhealthy levels.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: The haze situation in Riau, central Sumatra deteriorated rapidly between 25 and 26 August 2016 and persisted until 29 August 2016 under dry weather and strong winds conditions. Moderate to dense smoke haze from the fires in Riau were blown by the southwesterly to westerly winds over the Strait of Malacca to central Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore, where the air quality deteriorated to Unhealthy levels.
refs.pinpoint: Section 2 ('Review of Land/Forest Fires and Smoke Haze Situation'), para 2.3

refs.quote: The haze situation improved by 29 August 2016 with the return of shower activities over central Sumatra for the next few days.

summary.note: ASMC's monthly review for August 2016 (published 14 September 2016); its account of where the smoke came from is ASMC's assessment. The review gives no readings, dates or stations for Malaysia or Singapore and does not say which index its 'Unhealthy' refers to (AI note: probably each country's own index, Malaysia's API and Singapore's PSI). ASMC adds that the haze situation improved by 29 August with the return of showers over central Sumatra.

summary.text: MSS reports that Singapore's 24-hour PSI entered the Unhealthy range in the late afternoon of 26 August 2016 and reached a high of 143 at 8am on 27 August, before gradually returning to normal levels in the late afternoon of 28 August; NEA's hourly regional records show 143 in the north and west at 7:00 and in the north at 8:00 on 27 August.
summary.label: observation

refs.quote: The 24-hr Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) entered the Unhealthy range in the late afternoon of 26 August 2016 and reached a high of 143 at 8am on 27 August 2016, before gradually returning to normal levels in the late afternoon on 28 August 2016.

summary.note: 24-hour PSI (Singapore's index, which has included PM2.5 since April 2014); above 100 is the Unhealthy band. NEA's records are regional values (north, south, east, west, central); timestamps as published on data.gov.sg.

airQuality.text: The New Straits Times reported on 30 August 2016, citing information released by Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE), that four areas recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings at 9am — Nilai 118, Shah Alam 105, Putrajaya 102 and Banting 101 — and that by 11am two remained in the unhealthy band: Nilai (112) and Shah Alam (103); the first report says API readings are based on 24-hour averaging.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: The haze situation in the country continues to deteriorate, with four areas recording unhealthy air pollutant index (API) readings this morning.
As of 9am, Nilai's API reading stood at 118, followed by Banting (101), Shah Alam (105) and Putrajaya (102).
The Department of Environment website recorded an Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of between 102 and 105 from 6am to 9am for Shah Alam.

The haze situation in Malaysia today is showing a slight improvement, with two areas recording unhealthy Air Pollution Index (API) readings, according to information released by the Department of Environment (DOE).
As of 11am, Nilai continues to record the unhealthiest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading at 112, followed closely by Shah Alam (103).
Two hours earlier, Nilai's API reading was at 118, followed by Banting (101), Shah Alam (105) and Putrajaya (102).
API readings are determined based on an international acceptable protocol which calculates the 24 hour averaging times.

airQuality.note: Malaysia's API, which in 2016 did not yet include PM2.5; both reports class 101 to 200 as 'unhealthy'. The 9am readings appear in both reports; the second (12:53pm) attributes the readings to information released by DOE, while the first mentions DOE's website only in a photo caption giving Shah Alam's readings (102 to 105 from 6am to 9am). The second report's first paragraph writes 'Air Pollution Index'. Neither report says where the haze came from, and no official source opened links these readings specifically to smoke from Riau (ASMC's review says, without dates or stations, that smoke from Riau reached central Peninsular Malaysia, where air quality deteriorated to Unhealthy levels). DOE's own hourly records for these stations were not opened.

airQuality.text: Malay Mail reported that Tanjung Malim in Perak had recorded an API of 119 at 5pm on 29 August 2016, and that Nilai in Negeri Sembilan recorded 104 at 2pm on 30 August, in the unhealthy category.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 30 ― ... The Perak township of Tanjung Malim has shown a slight improvement in its API reading at 86 at 2pm today, compared to a reading of 119 at 5pm yesterday.
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 30 ― ... the town of Nilai in Negri Sembilan which recorded 104 at 2pm on Air Pollutant Index (API), sending it into the “unhealthy” category.
According to Malaysia’s Department of Environment, an API reading of over 100 is unhealthy, 201 and above is very unhealthy, and a reading of more than 300 is hazardous.

airQuality.note: 'Yesterday' in a report datelined 30 August 2016. The report does not name the source of the readings; it cites DOE for the band thresholds. Averaging period not stated in the report. The report describes the haze over Kuala Lumpur and Selangor as blown in from forest fires in Indonesia (the reporter's own description, not attributed to an official) and cites a forecast by Indonesia's BMKG, issued over the preceding weekend, that smoke from fires in Riau would spread over Malaysia and Singapore; it does not attribute any particular reading to a source of smoke.

airQuality.text: AFP reported on 26 August 2016 that smog had been visible in Kuala Lumpur over a few days in the previous week without reaching unhealthy levels, and that, according to local media, an area in Perak had briefly been in the unhealthy range for a few hours that week.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: SINGAPORE, Aug 26 — ... Smog was also visible in Kuala Lumpur, the capital of neighbouring Malaysia, over a few days last week but did not breach unhealthy levels. An area in the Malaysian state of Perak had briefly tipped over to the unhealthy range for a few hours last week, according to local media.

airQuality.note: Refers to the week before the Singapore episode, outside this entry's period. AFP cites unnamed local media for the Perak reading and gives no index, averaging period or place name for it, and it does not say where the smog over Kuala Lumpur came from. No DOE record for that week was opened.

airQuality.text: The National Environment Agency (NEA) reported that, as at 6pm on 26 August 2016, Singapore's 24-hour PSI was 82–112, in the Moderate to Unhealthy range, and the 1-hour PM2.5 concentration was 69–85 µg/m³ (Band II, Elevated); NEA's hourly regional record for 18:00 gives north 104 and west 112, with the other three regions between 82 and 95.
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: Singapore, 26 August 2016 – It has been hazy in Singapore today with the air quality in the Moderate to Unhealthy range. ... As at 6pm today, the 24-hr PSI was 82-112, in the Moderate to Unhealthy range, and the 1-hr PM2.5 was 69-85 µg/m3, in Band II (Elevated).

airQuality.note: 24-hour PSI; above 100 is Unhealthy. NEA's published range spans its five regional values: the 18:00 record (north 104, south 95, east 82, west 112, central 91) matches 82–112, with two regions above 100. 1-hr PM2.5 bands were introduced by NEA 'this haze season' (para 6 of the release). NEA's assessment of where the smoke came from is recorded separately (next claim).

airQuality.text: NEA said on 26 August 2016 that the smoke haze over Singapore that day had been blown in from central Sumatra by the prevailing westerly winds.
airQuality.label: analysis

refs.quote: Singapore, 26 August 2016 – It has been hazy in Singapore today with the air quality in the Moderate to Unhealthy range. The smoke haze was blown in from central Sumatra by the prevailing westerly winds.

airQuality.note: The agency's assessment of where the smoke came from, in its evening haze update. It names the region where fire hotspots were detected, not who started any fire.

airQuality.text: NEA reported that, as at 6pm on 27 August 2016, Singapore's 24-hour PSI was 70–126, in the Moderate to Unhealthy range, and the 1-hour PM2.5 concentration was 21–46 µg/m³ (Band I, Normal).
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: Singapore, 27 August 2016 – The haze situation in Singapore has continued to improve today, as less dense haze from central Sumatra was being blown in by the prevailing winds. As at 6pm today, the 24-hr PSI was 70-126, in the Moderate to Unhealthy range, and the 1-hr PM2.5 was 21-46 µg/m3, in Band I (Normal).

airQuality.note: 24-hour PSI range across NEA's regional values (as for 26 August); with 26 August, a second calendar day on which NEA reported values above 100. NEA also said that the haze situation had continued to improve that day, as less dense haze from central Sumatra was being blown in by the prevailing winds (the agency's assessment).

airQuality.text: An analysis by the AI agent of NEA's hourly regional 24-hour PSI records for late August and early September 2016 finds that regional values above 100 occurred only between 16:00 on 26 August (west, 105) and 14:00 on 29 August; that the north region stayed above 100 until 8:00 on 28 August (101) and was above 100 again from 1:00 to 14:00 on 29 August, reaching 109; and that the east region's highest value in those records was 91.
airQuality.label: analysis

refs.pinpoint: Record for 27/8/2016 2:00 (_id 21098); east 91 is the east region's maximum in the episode
Record for 29/8/2016 4:00 (_id 21148); 109 is the north region's maximum on 29 August

refs.quote: Singapore, 29 August 2016 – There was an improvement in the haze conditions this morning as the prevailing winds gradually strengthened to blow from the south.

airQuality.note: Computed by the AI agent from all records on this datastore page for 20 August–10 September 2016: 55 hourly records had at least one region above 100, all between 16:00 on 26 August and 14:00 on 29 August (calendar days 26–29 August); hours above 100 by region: north 54, west 26, south 13, central 13, east 0; at most four regions were above 100 in the same hour (from 23:00 on 26 August to 10:00 on 27 August) and no hour had all five. The page's earlier records, from 12 July 2016, show no value above 100. MSS dates Singapore's episode 26–28 August 2016, while this analysis shows the north region above 100 until 14:00 on 29 August; the entry's period (26–30 August) also reflects Malaysian news reports and the 2025 study's haze period. The difference is recorded, not resolved (see 'Where sources disagree').

airQuality.text: Reports citing NEA gave Singapore's three-hour PSI on 26 August 2016 as 165 at 0400 GMT (AFP, which added that the 24-hour reading was then in the higher band of the Moderate range) and as 215 at 2pm (BBC; Bloomberg), easing to 127 at 6pm (Bloomberg).
airQuality.label: observation

refs.quote: SINGAPORE, Aug 26 — ... Singapore’s National Environment Agency said the three-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) was at 165 as of 0400 GMT today. The reading for the 24-hour period, however, was on the higher band of the moderate range.
refs.pinpoint: Dateline and para 5 (first published 26 August 2016, 1:29 PM MYT)

refs.quote: Anything over 100 is considered unhealthy. Though the 24-hour average so far on Friday was only slightly over that, the three-hour reading at 14:00 local time was 215

SINGAPORE, Aug 27 ― Singapore’s air quality stood at unhealthy levels as haze ... intensified yesterday ... The three-hourly air pollution index peaked at 215 as of 2pm before easing to 127 at 6pm, according to the National Environment Agency.

airQuality.note: Three-hour PSI values (averaging period three hours), not the 24-hour PSI, which peaked at 143 (MSS) and on which NEA's health advisories were based. The Bloomberg report is datelined 27 August and dates the intensification of the haze to 'yesterday' (26 August); the BBC gives 215 at 14:00 on Friday 26 August and links the figure to NEA's PSI readings page. The BBC also says that the 24-hour average 'so far on Friday' was only slightly over 100 but gives no time for that remark; in NEA's hourly records no regional 24-hour value exceeded 100 before 16:00 on 26 August (west, 105), so the remark should not be read as the 24-hour value at 2pm. Bloomberg's description of readings above 200 as 'very unhealthy' is not adopted here. 0400 GMT is noon in Singapore. NEA's own record of these three-hour values was not found. Singapore phased out the three-hour PSI at the end of 2016 (see the milestones under 'How haze is measured').

responses.text: NEA began daily haze advisories on 26 August 2016; in its update that evening, with the 24-hour PSI forecast to be in the Unhealthy range, it advised healthy persons to reduce prolonged or strenuous outdoor physical exertion, the elderly, pregnant women and children to minimise it and those with chronic lung or heart disease to avoid it; its updates of 27, 28 and 29 August said everyone could continue with normal activities.
responses.label: fact

refs.quote: Haze Situation Update (26 August 2016, 11AM) ... NEA to commence daily haze advisory from today

Given the air quality forecast for the next 24 hours, healthy persons should reduce prolonged or strenuous outdoor physical exertion. The elderly, pregnant women and children should minimise prolonged or strenuous outdoor physical exertion, while those with chronic lung or heart disease should avoid prolonged or strenuous outdoor physical exertion.

Singapore, 27 August 2016 ... Overall, the PSI for the next 24 hours is forecast to be in the Moderate range. ... Given the air quality forecast for the next 24 hours, everyone can continue with normal activities.
Singapore, 28 August 2016 ... Given the air quality forecast for the next 24 hours, everyone can continue with normal activities.
Singapore, 29 August 2016 ... Given the air quality forecast for the next 24 hours, everyone can continue with normal activities.
The 24-hour PSI is accompanied with a health advisory that provides advice to the public on the general effects associated with atmospheric pollution
refs.pinpoint: p.5, 'Pollutant Standards Index (PSI)' and Figure 1 ('Health advisory for the general public')

responses.note: Government health advice (the advice was issued). It is NEA's standard health advisory for a forecast 24-hour PSI in the Unhealthy range (the same advice appears in the health advisory table that NEA says accompanies the 24-hour PSI; State of the Environment Report 2021, Figure 1), and NEA's next update returned to 'normal activities'. It is not tagged for criterion B2: 'official advice to reduce outdoor activity beyond routine forecasts' is read as excluding NEA's standard advisory for a forecast PSI band (an AI reading, pending human review). No school closures, emergency declarations or other extraordinary measures in Singapore were found for this episode.

health.text: A retrospective time-series study published in BMJ Open in December 2025, using records from one Singapore public healthcare cluster that the authors describe as covering 20% of the nation's adult asthma population (about 20% of Singapore's adult population, according to the paper's Methods), reported a mean of 2.60 (SD 1.95) asthma-related emergency department visits per day during its defined 2016 haze period of 26–30 August, against 1.78 (SD 1.45) in non-haze periods; in the study's comparison this 2016 difference was not statistically significant, and only the 2019 haze period differed significantly from non-haze periods.
health.label: analysis

refs.quote: A public healthcare cluster that covers 20% of the nation’s adult asthma population.
This healthcare cluster covers about 20% of Singapore’s adult population.

refs.pinpoint: Table 4, row 'ED visits' (haze, non-haze, p value, 2016, 2019, 2023, Welch ANOVA p value, significant post-hoc differences)

refs.quote: Transboundary haze periods refer to: 26–30 August 2016, 14 September to 5 October 2019 and 7–19 October 2023.
We observed more asthma ED visits during the haze periods of 2016 and 2019 compared with non-haze periods, but not for the 2023 haze.

PSI–ED association peaked on the same day of exposure but was no longer significant after adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Pollution-linked festivals, transboundary haze and the Northeast monsoon were associated with increased asthma ED visits

health.note: Population-level research (analysis): averages of recorded visits, not a count of visits caused by haze. In Table 4 the haze vs non-haze difference in ED visits had p=0.125 and the Welch ANOVA p=0.097, with '2019>non-haze' the only significant post-hoc difference, although the authors' discussion says more visits were observed in the 2016 and 2019 haze periods and their conclusions say transboundary haze was associated with increased asthma ED visits. Across the whole study (2016–2024) the PSI–ED association was not significant after adjustment. The abstract says the cluster covers 20% of the nation's adult asthma population; the Methods say about 20% of Singapore's adult population. Authors' limitations include data from one healthcare cluster and no indoor air-quality measurements (possible exposure misclassification).

regionalContext.text: MSS assessed in its Annual Climate Assessment for 2016 that, compared with 2015, when prolonged dry weather due to a strong El Niño contributed to what it called the worst smoke haze event in the region, the relatively wet Southwest Monsoon of 2016 helped to mitigate the occurrences of transboundary haze in the region.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: Compared to 2015 when prolonged dry weather (due to a strong El Nino) contributed to the worst smoke haze event in the region, the relatively wet Southwest Monsoon in 2016 helped to mitigate the occurrences of transboundary haze in the region.

regionalContext.note: The characterisation of 2015 as the worst event is MSS's, in its Annual Climate Assessment 2016 (PDF created July 2017).

regionalContext.text: ASMC reported that in August 2016 most of the near-equatorial part of the southern ASEAN region received near-normal rainfall, except central Sumatra and West Kalimantan, where rainfall was below normal, and that in the second half of the month central Sumatra had dry weather with isolated hotspot activity while showers fell over most of Sumatra.

In the southern ASEAN region, near-normal rainfall was received in most parts of the near-equatorial region, except in central Sumatra and West Kalimantan where below-normal rainfall prevailed.

In the second half of August, an increase in shower activities over Kalimantan helped to ease the fire situation there. Showers fell over most parts of Sumatra, except in central Sumatra, where dry weather conditions with isolated hotspot activities were observed.

regionalContext.text: Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said that forest and land fires had worsened in Riau and that smoke from 67 hotspots in the province had reached Singapore, according to The Jakarta Post; Bloomberg quoted a BNPB spokesman as saying the haze from fires in Riau was being carried by wind toward Singapore.

Based on data from the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), 67 hot spots in the form of forest and land fires were detected in Riau on Friday morning.

The Jakarta Post calls the agency the 'Disaster Mitigation Agency' and Bloomberg the 'National Disaster Mitigation Authority'. 'Friday' is 26 August 2016. Hotspot counts differ by source (see 'Where sources disagree'). The Chief Executive Officer of the National Environment Agency (NEA) wrote to his Indonesian counterpart today to register Singapore’s concerns over additional episodes of deterioration in air quality in Singapore should the fires continue. NEA urged Indonesia to continue taking the necessary actions to prevent and mitigate the fires during this dry season, and asked for an update on the situation in Sumatra and Kalimantan.

refs.pinpoint: Paragraph beginning 'On Friday, the NEA registered'

aftermath.text: NEA's inaugural State of the Environment Report (2021) lists 2016 among the years in which Singapore's air quality was affected by transboundary haze from the region: 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019.
aftermath.label: analysis

refs.quote: Air quality was affected by transboundary haze from the region in 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019.
refs.pinpoint: p.5, note to Figure 2 ('Air Quality in terms of PSI')

aftermath.note: An official retrospective; it does not describe the 2016 episode further.

selection.note: Criterion A is met: MSS's Annual Climate Assessment 2016, ASMC's August 2016 review and NEA's update of 26 August 2016 describe smoke haze blown to Singapore from Riau or central Sumatra (and, per ASMC, to central Peninsular Malaysia), and NEA's 2021 State of the Environment Report lists 2016 as a transboundary-haze year. B1 is met by NEA's and MSS's reports of Singapore's 24-hour PSI in the Unhealthy range on 26 and 27 August (peak 143; up to four of five regions above 100 in NEA's data), supported by New Straits Times reports of API above 100 at four Malaysian stations on the morning of 30 August (the later report citing information released by DOE). B2 is not evidenced: the only official advice found in Malaysia or Singapore was NEA's standard health advisory for a forecast Unhealthy 24-hour PSI, treated as routine (an AI reading of 'beyond routine forecasts', pending human review; if that advisory counted, 2016 would also meet B2). B3 is not evidenced (MSS calls it 2016's only 'significant' episode).

attribution.note: Meteorological Service Singapore and ASMC describe smoke haze from fires in Riau, central Sumatra, carried by westerly winds towards Singapore (MSS) and over the Strait of Malacca to central Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore (ASMC); Singapore's National Environment Agency said the haze over Singapore on 26 August had been blown in from central Sumatra. Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) was reported by The Jakarta Post as saying that smoke from hotspots in Riau had reached Singapore, and quoted by Bloomberg as saying the haze was being carried by wind toward Singapore. No public dispute about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened.

confidence.rationale: Medium (AI-assigned, awaiting human review). The core account rests on government and intergovernmental sources: MSS's Annual Climate Assessment 2016 gives the dates of Singapore's episode (26–28 August) and the peak 24-hour PSI of 143 at 8am on 27 August; NEA's haze updates report the 24-hour PSI in the Unhealthy range on 26 and 27 August, and NEA's hourly regional records on data.gov.sg show the same peak; and ASMC's review for August 2016 describes smoke haze from Riau reaching central Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore. Independent corroboration comes from BNPB statements reported by The Jakarta Post and Bloomberg, from AFP, BBC and Bloomberg reports relaying NEA's figures, and from a 2025 BMJ Open study that uses 26–30 August 2016 as a haze period. The rating is medium because important elements rest on news reports only or are incomplete, and a minor conflict remains: the Malaysian readings rest on New Straits Times reports (the later one citing information released by DOE) and Malay Mail, no DOE record was opened, the start and end of unhealthy conditions in Malaysia are unknown, and no official source links specific Malaysian readings to the smoke from Riau; the end date of 30 August rests on those reports and the study's definition, while MSS dates Singapore's episode 26–28 August and NEA's hourly records show one region above 100 until 29 August (unresolved); and the readings and impacts reported in Riau rest on The Jakarta Post only. Health evidence is limited to one study, and no records of healthcare use in Singapore were found. DOE's hourly API records or a Malaysian government statement for late August 2016, an official account of the episode's end date, and BNPB or BMKG releases for the Riau readings would fill these gaps. Confidence describes the evidence, not severity.

contradictions.text: End of the Singapore episode: MSS dates the episode 26–28 August 2016 and says the 24-hour PSI returned to normal levels in the late afternoon of 28 August, but NEA's hourly regional records show the north region above 100 again from 1:00 to 14:00 on 29 August (maximum 109; AI agent's analysis); ASMC says the Riau haze persisted until 29 August (and, in its next paragraph, that the haze situation improved by 29 August); the BMJ Open study used 26–30 August. The difference may reflect island-wide description versus a single region's values; not resolved here.

Hotspot counts on 26 August 2016 differ by source: NEA reported 11 hotspots in Sumatra that day, while The Jakarta Post reported 67 hotspots detected in Riau alone on Friday morning (BMKG data; BNPB's statement also refers to 67 hotspots in the province), falling to 47 by Friday evening according to the head of Riau's regional disaster management agency (BPBD); Bloomberg reported that BNPB recorded 67 hotspots without saying where or when. The sources do not explain the difference; satellites, detection methods and times may differ (AI note). Not resolved.

Riau ISPU on Monday 29 August 2016: The Jakarta Post of 29 August gives 361 at Duri Camp (Mandau district), citing the Riau task force; its report of 30 August gives 364 'as of Monday morning', citing the Riau forest fire emergency unit, without naming the station. Different stations or hours may explain the difference; not resolved.

evidenceGaps: No primary record from Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE) for this episode was opened: DOE's hourly API archive for August 2016, DOE press statements and the Environmental Quality Report 2016 were not found or not readable. Malaysian readings rest on the New Straits Times (citing DOE information) and Malay Mail. DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2023 (Figure 1.5, p.18 of the PDF on storage.data.gov.my) gives annual counts of unhealthy-API days in 2016 at Banting (27), Shah Alam (29) and Cheras (33), but these are whole-year, all-cause counts (the report's text for 2023 names traffic ozone and local open burning among causes) and cannot be assigned to this episode.
Malaysian API readings for 26–28 August and after 30 August 2016 were not found, so the start and end of unhealthy conditions in Malaysia are unknown.
No Malaysian government response (health advice, school measures, DOE statement on the origin of the haze) for late August 2016 was found.
NEA's own record of the three-hour PSI values reported for 26 August 2016 (165, 215, 127) was not found; they rest on AFP, BBC and Bloomberg reports.

Indonesian primary sources (BNPB and BMKG releases, Riau task-force data) were not opened; Indonesian statements, readings and impacts rest on The Jakarta Post and Bloomberg. A Tempo report of 29 August 2016 on Riau hotspots returned HTTP 403 and has no archive copy.
No Singapore records of healthcare use (for example MOH polyclinic attendances) for 26–30 August 2016 were found; the only health evidence for Singapore is the 2025 BMJ Open study.

No Indonesian reply to NEA's letter of 26 August 2016 was found, including in two further web searches on 15 October 2026, which also found no official dispute over where the smoke came from during this episode.

Indonesian government measures during the episode are not recorded as claims. The Jakarta Post (27 August 2016) reports the government as saying it had declared states of emergency in six provinces, and describes BNPB's firefighting and cloud-seeding deployments; AFP (26 August 2016) instead says that three provinces on Sumatra and three in Indonesian Borneo had officially declared they were on alert. BNPB's own releases were not opened, so the status, dates and authority of these declarations were not checked.

Planned searches for statements by DOE and the Ministry of Health Malaysia, for BNPB releases and for NEA's original statement on the three-hour PSI could not be run during this research because the web-search budget ran out.
unresolvedQuestions: Did DOE's hourly records show unhealthy API readings in Malaysia on 26–28 August 2016, and how many stations exceeded 100 during the episode?

Were the unhealthy API readings in Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Putrajaya and Perak on 29–30 August 2016 due mainly to smoke from Riau, or partly to local sources? ASMC's review says smoke from Riau reached central Peninsular Malaysia, and Malay Mail's report of 30 August describes the haze as blown in from fires in Indonesia, but neither attributes specific readings.
Was the north region's renewed exceedance in Singapore on 29 August 2016 a fresh smoke intrusion or a lingering effect of the 27–28 August haze?
Why do hotspot counts for 26 August 2016 differ so much between NEA (11 in Sumatra) and BMKG/BNPB (67 in Riau)?

ASMC's alert table shows Alert Level 1 for the southern ASEAN region from 30 June 2016 (start of the dry season) and an upgrade to Level 2 for Kalimantan only on 16 August 2016, with no alert change for Sumatra during the Riau episode; did any regional alert or ASMC daily update address the Riau haze specifically?

events.title: Mid-August 2018: parts of Peninsular Malaysia, Sarawak and West Kalimantan, Indonesia

period.label: Mid-August 2018

refs.quote: Penang shrouded in haze, as seen in Butterworth on August 15, 2018.
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 15 — Several states in the country recorded moderate Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as of 2pm, today.
According to the readings, the air quality in several areas started to climb from green or moderate (where the API is between 51-100) to yellow, or unhealthy (101-200), from Wednesday (Aug 15).
At least five areas in Sarawak recorded moderate Air Pollution Index (API) readings this morning.
This follows the presence of haze in Kuching, Serian, Sibu, Mukah and Bintulu.
On 16 August 2018, visible smoke haze from fire hotspots in Riau, central Sumatra spread across the Strait of Malacca, and brought hazy conditions to parts of Peninsular Malaysia.
Although the haze eased for much of the country today, Miri, Sarawak found itself shrouded in smoke.
The fire has also worsened the haze, recording an Air Pollutant Index (API) level at 113 on Sunday (Aug 19) morning. A reading of 0-50 is considered good, 51-100 moderate and 101-200 unhealthy.
In the last week of August 2018, increased shower activities over Kalimantan helped to subdue the hotspot activities there and brought some relief to the haze situation in Kalimantan and Sarawak.
In mid-August 2018, Malaysia experienced slight haze episode due to local and transboudary haze. However, the haze episode lasted for a short period of time only.

period.note: Start: given as August 2018, because no official source gives a start date: DOE describes a haze episode in 'mid-August 2018', and ASMC reports smoke haze from Riau bringing hazy conditions to parts of Peninsular Malaysia on 16 August. The earliest reports of haze in Malaysia found for this episode are from 15 August 2018 (Bernama: moderate API readings in several states as of 2pm, and a photograph of haze in Penang; the New Straits Times, 9:19am: moderate readings that morning in at least five areas of Sarawak, following the presence of haze in five towns); they do not say when the haze began. The Star reported on 16 August that readings in several areas had started to climb from moderate towards the unhealthy band from Wednesday 15 August; its wording does not make clear whether any reading was already unhealthy on 15 August (see 'Where sources disagree'). Unhealthy or very unhealthy readings were reported for named locations from 16 to 18 August (stations in Perlis, Kedah and Penang, and Klang, Johan Setia, Banting, Mukah and Miri), and The Star reported an unhealthy reading of 113 on the morning of 19 August in a report datelined Miri, without naming the station. End: given only as August 2018: ASMC reports some relief for Kalimantan and Sarawak in the last week of August, and DOE describes the episode as short. ASMC's Alert Level 2 for the southern ASEAN region (13 August–2 September 2018; see 'Regional context') is a regional alert, not the period of haze in Malaysia. Unhealthy and very unhealthy API readings were reported in parts of Malaysia on 16–19 August 2018.

summary.text: The ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) reported that on 16 August 2018 visible smoke haze from fire hotspots in Riau, central Sumatra (Indonesia), spread across the Strait of Malacca and brought hazy conditions to parts of Peninsular Malaysia, and that the return of showers over the following days helped to improve the haze situation in Riau; it described a satellite image of 21 August as showing showers that helped to alleviate the haze in Sumatra and Peninsular Malaysia.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: On 16 August 2018, visible smoke haze from fire hotspots in Riau, central Sumatra spread across the Strait of Malacca, and brought hazy conditions to parts of Peninsular Malaysia.
The return of shower activities over the following days helped to improve the haze situation in Riau Province.
Figure 3: Himawari-8 satellite image on 21 Aug 2018 shows the return of shower activities that helped to alleviate the haze situation in Sumatra and Peninsular Malaysia.

summary.note: ASMC's account of where the smoke came from is its assessment from satellite imagery (Himawari-8) and is attributed as such. ASMC does not name the parts of Peninsular Malaysia that were affected. A hotspot's location says nothing about who started a fire or who holds the land.

summary.text: ASMC reported that in the second half of August 2018 smoke haze from persistent hotspots in West Kalimantan (Indonesia) reduced visibility in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, to 2 km and was blown by the prevailing winds to affect parts of western Sarawak (Malaysia), and that increased showers in the last week of August brought some relief to the haze situation in Kalimantan and Sarawak.
summary.label: analysis

refs.quote: Smoke haze from the persistent hotspots in West Kalimantan reduced visibility in Pontianak, West Kalimantan to 2 km, and was blown by the prevailing winds to affect parts of western Sarawak.
In the last week of August 2018, increased shower activities over Kalimantan helped to subdue the hotspot activities there and brought some relief to the haze situation in Kalimantan and Sarawak.

summary.text: Malaysia's Department of Environment (DOE) states in its Environmental Quality Report 2018 that in mid-August 2018 Malaysia experienced a 'slight haze episode' due to local and transboundary haze from neighbouring countries, that there were a few incidents of local bush fires that caused deterioration in local air quality as well as transboundary haze caused by land and forest fires in neighbouring countries, and that the episode lasted only a short time because of humid weather in the region.

However, the haze episode lasted for a short period of time due to the humid weather condition in the region.

impact.text: Fires inside Malaysia were also reported during the episode: Bernama reported on 17 August 2018 that the director of the Selangor Fire and Rescue Department said fires in a peat soil area at Johan Setia, Klang, were under control, with eight hectares still burning compared with 16 hectares the day before, and The Malaysian Insight listed areas that it said were affected by the smoke at Johan Setia; The Star reported on 19 August that the Sarawak Fire and Rescue Department in Miri had intensified aerial water-bombing of a forest fire in Kuala Baram district, and that an API reading of 113 was recorded that morning, without naming the station.

impact.note: No official finding on how these fires started was found, and this record identifies no one. Some news reports describe open burning at Johan Setia in general terms; those descriptions are not used here to say how these fires started or who started them. The Star also wrote that the Kuala Baram fire 'has also worsened the haze'; that link is the newspaper's own statement, not an official assessment, and no source opened measures the fire's contribution. The Star does not name the monitoring station for the 113 reading (averaging period not stated). Only the first two paragraphs of The Star's report are open access. Bernama report as republished by Malaysiakini.

confidence.rationale: Medium (AI-assigned, awaiting human review; confidence describes the evidence, not the severity of the episode). The core account, a short haze episode in mid-August 2018 that brought unhealthy and some very unhealthy API readings to parts of Peninsular Malaysia and Sarawak while no regional 24-hour PSI in Singapore exceeded 100, rests on two independent official sources: DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2018 (government), which attributes the episode to local and transboundary haze and records very unhealthy readings at ILP Miri (229) and Klang (227); and ASMC's review of the second half of August 2018 and its alerts (intergovernmental), which describe smoke haze from hotspots in Riau and West Kalimantan reaching parts of Peninsular Malaysia and western Sarawak. Independent reporting corroborates it (New Straits Times, The Star, Bernama, The Malaysian Insight; The Straits Times' report of 17 August is credited to The Star/Asia News Network and is not counted separately). Singapore's figures come from the AI agent's scan of NEA's hourly 24-hour PSI dataset. The rating is medium because important elements rest on news reports only or are incomplete, and minor conflicts remain: every dated API reading (16–19 August) comes from news reports citing DOE's website or APIMS, as no DOE hourly record or daily statement was found; DOE's own readings for ILP Miri and Klang have no dates or hours; no official source gives the start or end date of the episode in Malaysia; and conflicts about the highest reading on 16 August, whether any reading was unhealthy on 15 August and when PM2.5 entered the API remain unresolved (see 'Where sources disagree'). Interpretation is also limited: the API began to include PM2.5 on 16 August 2018, the first day for which unhealthy readings at named stations were found; DOE's highest readings were in areas where local fires were also reported; Malaysian officials gave differing accounts of how much local fires contributed; and no source quantifies local and transboundary contributions. DOE's hourly or daily API records, or a dated DOE statement, for 14–19 August 2018 would fill these gaps.

contradictions.text: Peak API reading on 16 August 2018: the New Straits Times (16 August, citing DOE's website) gave Kangar's 160 at 11am as the day's highest reading and Alor Setar's 145 (spelt 'Alor Star') as the highest at 6pm, while The Star (citing APIMS) gave Alor Setar's 157 as the worst so far as at noon; The Straits Times' report of 17 August, credited to The Star/Asia News Network, repeats Alor Setar's 157 as the highest API reading in Peninsular Malaysia, without an hour, and is the same reporting, not a third account. The figures may refer to different hours; no DOE hourly record was found to settle which was highest, so neither is preferred.

Where the haze in Malaysia came from, as described by Malaysian officials: the environment minister was reported on 16 August 2018 (New Straits Times) as saying that the haze affecting the country was due to open burning in Sumatra and Kalimantan and that the Johan Setia peat fire was also contributing to haze in nearby areas; the Defence Minister was reported on 17 August (Bernama) as saying that the hazy conditions in the country were not caused by forest fires 'here' but had been blown from Sumatra; and DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2018 attributes the episode to both local and transboundary haze. Both ministers named Sumatra. Whether the Defence Minister's statement conflicts with the other two depends on what 'here' means (Malaysia, or the Johan Setia area, where the same Bernama report describes 'forest fires in the peat soil area'), which Bernama does not say. No public exchange between these officials was found, and no source opened quantifies local and transboundary contributions; this record does not resolve the difference.

Date PM2.5 entered Malaysia's API: a DOE presentation on API calculation (PDF created April 2020) labels the 24-hour PM2.5 sub-index 'Started on 2017' (p.8), while DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2018 says PM2.5 was included in the API calculation from 16 August 2018, and the environment minister was reported on 16 August 2018 as saying that the API on the APIMS website was now based on PM2.5. AI agent's note: DOSM's monthly dataset has PM2.5 averages for every month of 2018, so PM2.5 was being measured before 16 August 2018, and has no PM2.5 value for any month of 2017 (DOSM notes that some 2017 values are null because data were unavailable); the presentation does not say what 'Started on 2017' refers to. Here, the dated statements are followed for the change to the published API.

When readings first reached the unhealthy band: The Star (16 August 2018, citing APIMS readings) reported that the air quality in several areas 'started to climb' from moderate to unhealthy 'from Wednesday (Aug 15)', whereas Bernama (Malay Mail, 15 August) reported moderate API readings in several states as of 2pm on 15 August and mentioned no unhealthy reading, and the New Straits Times (16 August) wrote that the haze 'began creeping across the country today', with unhealthy readings as of 6pm on 16 August. The Star's wording does not make clear whether any reading was unhealthy on 15 August, and no DOE hourly record was found to settle it. AI agent's note: this matters because PM2.5 was added to the API on 16 August 2018; the difference is not resolved here.

evidenceGaps: No DOE or environment ministry press statement from August 2018 was opened. The ministry's press-clipping files for 16 and 17 August 2018 (now on the website of the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation), found by search, redirect to that ministry's home page and have no Internet Archive copy.

DOE's hourly APIMS records for 15–19 August 2018 were not found online, so the dated readings rest on news reports citing DOE's website or APIMS; DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2018 gives 229 (ILP Miri) and 227 (Klang) without dates or hours, and its counts of unhealthy days in Sarawak (Mukah 5, Sibu 2, Kuching 2, Bintulu 1) are annual and undated.

No Ministry of Health Malaysia advisory, healthcare-use data or Ministry of Education measure linked to this episode was found; searches returned only items from other years. The only advice found was the environment minister's call to monitor API readings. Singapore health advisories were not searched for separately, since NEA's data show no 24-hour PSI above 100 in 2018.

Singapore: NEA's own press releases or haze updates for August 2018 were not found; Singapore's position rests on NEA's dataset (AI agent's scan), Reuters' 2019 report of NEA data (which does not hold for every reading; see 'Singapore: Air quality'), and an NEA spokesman quoted in a Straits Times report credited to The Star/Asia News Network.

No diplomatic exchange between Malaysia and Indonesia about this episode, and no Indonesian response to the Malaysian ministers' statements, was found. Further searches during this research, in English and Indonesian, for an Indonesian government response to reports of haze reaching Malaysia in August 2018 returned only items about other years (2019, 2023 and later). A Straits Times report credited to The Star/Asia News Network quoted the environment minister as saying 'I am trying to pay them a visit' when asked about meeting the Indonesian authorities; no record of such a visit was found.

The Malaysian Insight (17 August 2018) wrote that Johan Setia's readings on 16 August were 'more than 300' (the hazardous band); it gives no time or source, and no DOE source opened confirms it, so the figure is not used.

No peer-reviewed study or official retrospective other than DOE's annual report and ASMC's fortnightly review was found that discusses this episode, and no source ranks it. A DOAJ article record returned by a literature search could not be opened (HTTP 403).

Indonesia: official air-quality (ISPU) readings for Pontianak and Riau, BNPB and Environment and Forestry Ministry releases for August 2018, and whether haze affected Palembang during the Asian Games were not established from official or reputable independent sources.

The National Haze Action Plan (November 2018 update), which also dates the public display of a PM2.5-based API to 16 August 2018, was found only as a copy in a university repository whose cover is marked 'Salinan Terhad / Restricted Copy'; it is not cited here, and an official public copy was not found.
unresolvedQuestions: Did any station record an unhealthy API reading on 15 August 2018, before the switch to a PM2.5-based API (The Star reported readings climbing towards the unhealthy band from 15 August; Bernama reported moderate readings, and no unhealthy one, as of 2pm that day)? How much of the change from 'moderate' readings on 15 August to 'unhealthy' readings on 16 August 2018 reflects the index change rather than a change in air quality? DOE's hourly API values and PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations for 14–18 August 2018 would answer this.

On which dates and hours were DOE's 'very unhealthy' readings at ILP Miri (229) and Klang (227) recorded? Was ILP Miri's 229 recorded at the same station as the 228 that the New Straits Times reported for Miri at 3pm on 18 August, at a different hour? Were these readings driven mainly by nearby fires (Kuala Baram; Johan Setia) or by transboundary smoke?
What does the 'Started on 2017' label for PM2.5 in DOE's API calculation presentation refer to, as distinct from the public display of a PM2.5-based API from 16 August 2018?
Which Sarawak stations did smoke from West Kalimantan reach in the second half of August 2018, and did any of them record unhealthy readings then?
Was Johan Setia a fixed DOE station or a temporary monitoring point in August 2018, and what did it record on 16 August?

What did Malaysia's Defence Minister mean by 'forest fires here' on 17 August 2018: fires anywhere in Malaysia, or the Johan Setia fires he had just visited? A recording or full transcript of his remarks would show whether his statement differs from DOE's later assessment of local and transboundary haze.

health.text: A peer-reviewed retrospective study of asthma emergency department (ED) visits at one Singapore public healthcare cluster, which the authors say covers 20% of the nation's adult asthma population, reported more asthma ED visits during the 2016 and 2019 haze periods than in non-haze periods, although the study's table lists only the 2019 difference as significant; mean daily visits were 2.36 during the 2019 haze period (14 September–5 October 2019), against a non-haze average of 1.78.
health.label: analysis

refs.quote: A public healthcare cluster that covers 20% of the nation’s adult asthma population.
This healthcare cluster covers about 20% of Singapore’s adult population.
We observed more asthma ED visits during the haze periods of 2016 and 2019 compared with non-haze periods, but not for the 2023 haze.
Mean daily visits declined across successive haze events, from 2.60 (in 2016) to 2.36 (in 2019), and further to 1.46 (in 2023), dropping below the non-haze average of 1.78
refs.pinpoint: Results, 'Transboundary haze, festival periods and monsoons'
Table 4, row 'ED visits' (columns: haze, non-haze, p value, 2016 haze, 2019 haze, 2023 haze, Welch-ANOVA p value, significant post-hoc differences)

refs.quote: 2617 adult patients accounting for 5337 asthma ED visits between 2016 and 2024.
Transboundary haze periods refer to: 26–30 August 2016, 14 September to 5 October 2019 and 7–19 October 2023.

health.note: Population-level analysis of 2,617 adult patients with 5,337 asthma ED visits (2016–2024) in one public healthcare cluster; it describes associations, not the cause of any individual visit. The abstract says the cluster covers 20% of the nation's adult asthma population; the Methods say about 20% of Singapore's adult population. Limitations stated by the authors include incomplete weather-station coverage. In Table 4, mean daily visits (± standard deviation) were 2.36 ± 1.05 in the 2019 haze period and 1.78 ± 1.45 on non-haze days; the pooled haze versus non-haze comparison gave p = 0.125 and the Welch ANOVA across the three haze periods and non-haze days gave p = 0.097, with '2019>non-haze' the only significant post-hoc difference listed. The authors' statement that visits were higher in 2016 and 2019 should be read with these statistics.

In a separate statement ... said “The data clearly shows that the haze is from Indonesia,” and added that she had discussed the matter with the Malaysian prime minister, who agreed to write to Indonesia’s president about the transboundary haze.

The estimate was based on its assessment in eight affected provinces from June to October 2019, though analysts at the multinational bank said fires had continued to rage until November.

selection.note: Criterion A is met: ASMC and Meteorological Service Singapore describe smoke haze from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan affecting Malaysia and/or Singapore, NEA and MSS attribute haze in Singapore on 21–23 September 2019 to fires in Kalimantan, and CAMS and a peer-reviewed study of Kota Kinabalu describe the haze as coming from fires in Indonesia; statements labelled allegations (including those of Malaysia's Department of Environment on 20 September and NEA on 12 and 14 September) are not counted. B1 is met in both countries (Singapore's 24-hour PSI in the Unhealthy range on several days between 14 and 24 September 2019, per MSS, NEA's haze updates and its hourly data; unhealthy or worse API readings at many Malaysian stations per DOE and APIMS as reported by Bernama on 17 and 18 September, and per the Ministry of Health Malaysia for 15–22 September), and B2 is met in Malaysia (school closures that Sarawak's education department, the Education Ministry and Selangor's disaster committee tied to the haze or to API readings, and advice to reduce outdoor activity from NADMA and the Selangor Health Department; NEA's standard band-linked advisory is not tagged (treated as routine, as in 2016), pending a human ruling on 'beyond routine forecasts'); B3 was not evidenced for Malaysia or Singapore.

attribution.note: Ministers publicly disagreed about where the smoke came from. Indonesia's environment and forestry minister said that not all of it came from Indonesia, and disputed that haze from Riau was reaching Singapore; Malaysia's environment minister cited ASMC hotspot data to say it came from Indonesia; Singapore's National Environment Agency attributed Singapore's haze to smoke from Sumatra; and Malaysia's Department of Environment said that fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan were causing transboundary haze. These positions are labelled allegations, under Response between governments and, for the Department of Environment, under What happened; this record does not decide between them. ASMC and Meteorological Service Singapore assessed that smoke haze from Sumatra and Kalimantan affected Malaysia and Singapore.

confidence.rationale: AI-assigned, awaiting human review. Medium under the pre-registered definitions. The core account, that smoke haze affected Malaysia and Singapore from August to early October 2019, with the highest readings reported here between about 14 and 24 September, is supported by intergovernmental and government sources (ASMC's alerts and fortnightly reviews; Meteorological Service Singapore's 2019 annual climate assessment; NEA's haze updates, its January 2020 release and its hourly regional PSI data; the Ministry of Health Malaysia's statement of 23 September 2019; Malaysia's monthly open data), by a scientific agency (CAMS; NASA Earth Observatory describes smoke over Borneo and Sumatra without naming Malaysia or Singapore) and by peer-reviewed studies (AIMS Environmental Science, 2023; BMJ Open, 2025), and is corroborated by independent news reports (Bernama, Malaysiakini, The Malaysian Insight, The Straits Times via ANN, The Guardian). Singapore's key figures are quoted from MSS and NEA. Where the smoke came from is attributed: ASMC and MSS assessed that it came from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and CAMS and the 2023 study from fires in Indonesia; statements about its origin by Indonesia's environment and forestry minister, Malaysia's environment minister, Malaysia's Department of Environment (20 September) and NEA (12 and 14 September) are labelled allegations, because the point was publicly disputed at the time, and are not resolved. The rating is medium because important Malaysian elements rest on news reports only: every numeric API reading (including Sri Aman's 402–420 and the station values of 17 and 18 September) was read in Bernama or Malaysiakini reports citing DOE, APIMS or Sarawak's disaster management secretariat, and all Malaysian school-closure and flight-cancellation figures come from news reports, most of them relaying ministry, state or NADMA statements. The closure counts also differ between sources, a minor conflict that remains unresolved (see Where sources disagree). The only primary Malaysian air-quality records opened are the Ministry of Health's status counts for two epidemiological weeks and one evening, and monthly PM2.5 averages. The other recorded disagreements (the date on which Singapore's PSI first exceeded 100 in all five regions, which NEA's hourly data settle; Indonesia's burned area; El Niño's role) do not concern the core account.

contradictions.text: When Singapore's 24-hour PSI first exceeded 100 in all five regions: Bernama (via The Malaysian Insight, 22 September 2019) said the readings 'first entered the unhealthy range (101-200) across the republic on September 18'. NEA's hourly regional data show all five regions above 100 at 1am on 15 September 2019 (north 105, south 115, east 105, west 117, central 101), matching The Straits Times report relayed by ANN; MSS gives 14 September as the first Unhealthy day (west 103 at 4pm in NEA's data). The primary NEA data settle this in favour of 15 September: all five regions were above 100 again on 18 September, but not for the first time.

Counts of Malaysian school closures on 18 September 2019 differ: NADMA (via Bernama, published by Malay Mail) said 553 schools nationwide were closed that day, involving 312,337 students, while The Malaysian Insight reported 1,484 schools closed nationwide that day, affecting more than a million students, with the closures ordered on the basis of API readings at 1pm. These may reflect statements issued at different times of day (AI agent's assessment); not resolved.

Indonesia's 2019 burned area: a peer-reviewed study (Earth System Science Data, 2021) reports the Ministry of Environment and Forestry's official estimate as 1.64 Mha (manual visual interpretation of Landsat imagery), the MODIS MCD64A1 product as 2.03 Mha, and its own Sentinel-2-based estimate as more than 3.11 Mha. Mongabay (2024) gives 1.65 million ha for 2019; Reuters (via Al Jazeera, 11 December 2019) cites 'official figures' of more than 942,000 ha burned 'this year'. AI agent's assessment: 1.64 versus 1.65 is probably rounding, the 942,000 ha figure predates the final official estimate, and the 3.11 Mha figure uses a different satellite method. These are Indonesia-wide measures of fire extent, not of haze impact in Malaysia or Singapore.

Role of El Niño in 2019: Mongabay (2024) describes 2019 as an El Niño year ('that year's El Niño brought a prolonged dry season') and quotes an official of Indonesia's environment ministry comparing 2023's El Niño with 2019's; Reuters (via Al Jazeera, 11 December 2019) reported that officials said the spike in burning was due to El Niño weather patterns lengthening the dry season. Meteorological Service Singapore's 2019 assessment says 'Overall, 2019 was a neutral year for the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO)' and attributes the dry conditions to a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole; a peer-reviewed study (Communications Earth & Environment, 2024) says a relatively weak El Niño occurred but ceased by August 2019. Not resolved here. AI agent's note: the meteorological agency and the peer-reviewed study both describe any El Niño as weak or over before the September 2019 peak.

evidenceGaps: Department of Environment Malaysia: no DOE primary record of 2019 API readings was opened (APIMS historical data and the 2019 Environmental Quality Report were not obtained during this research); all hourly Malaysian API values here come from news reports citing DOE, APIMS or Sarawak's disaster management secretariat.

Ministry of Health Malaysia: the 19 September 2019 Director-General's statement could not be read (moh.gov.my HTTP 403; archive copy HTTP 429); only the 23 September 2019 statement was read, from an Internet Archive copy.
Ministry of Education Singapore: the 15 September 2019 press release returned an empty HTTP 202 page and its archive copy returned HTTP 429; MOE's measures are cited from The Straits Times via ANN.

No haze emergency declaration in Malaysia in 2019 was found, and no official list of daily school closures by the Education Ministry was opened; counts come from news reports of ministry, state and NADMA statements.

Indonesian official sources could not be opened: KLHK's SiPongi burned-area site (host did not resolve), the Indonesian parliament's research brief on the 2019 fires (HTTP 403) and Tempo English (HTTP 403). Indonesian impacts rest on Antara reports published by Republika, Mongabay Indonesia and The Guardian; no Kalimantan provincial emergency declaration was found.

No Singapore healthcare-use records for 2019 (for example polyclinic attendances for haze-related conditions) were found; the only Singapore health evidence is a peer-reviewed study of one public healthcare cluster.
NEA's hourly data show regional 24-hour PSI values of 101–105 on 13–14 November 2019; no source opened explains these readings, so they are not treated as part of this episode.
The World Bank's December 2019 report with the US$5.2 billion estimate was not opened; the figure is cited from Al Jazeera and a peer-reviewed study.

Diplomatic exchanges: the text of Malaysia's diplomatic note (sent, per The Guardian, on the Friday before 12 September 2019), any letter from Indonesia's minister to her Malaysian counterpart, and the Malaysian prime minister's letter to Indonesia's president were not found; the exchanges rest on news reports (The Guardian, Mongabay, The Straits Times via ANN), and no Indonesian government statement on the note was opened.
unresolvedQuestions: What were the Department of Environment's official hourly API maxima in 2019, and how many station-hours were above 200 and above 300 (from the APIMS archive)?
How much of Sri Aman's hazardous API readings on 17–20 September 2019 came from the local fires near the monitor that DOE and NADMA described, and how much from transboundary haze?
What were the Education Ministry's official daily totals of school closures in Malaysia between 10 and 20 September 2019?
What caused the regional 24-hour PSI values above 100 in Singapore on 13–14 November 2019, and are they connected with this episode?
Did any provincial government in Kalimantan declare an emergency over smoke in 2019, and on what dates?

Mongabay (12 September 2019) reported that Indonesia's environment ministry had sealed off concession areas where fires had occurred and that some companies had been charged in connection with the fires. What proceedings followed, and with what outcomes? These steps were not researched for this entry, and a seal, charge or investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing.
