selection.note: Criterion A is met: Meteorological Service Singapore's 2023 climate assessment, ASMC (transboundary smoke haze from West Kalimantan into western Sarawak in July and September 2023) and a peer-reviewed study (GRL 2024) describe the haze as transboundary; DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2023 does too, but as a position Indonesia's environment ministry disputed it is labelled an allegation and not counted. B1 is met in both countries (DOE: two consecutive unhealthy days at Cheras and Nilai, and 11 locations with unhealthy readings on 2 October 2023 as reported by news citing DOE; NEA: 24-hour PSI above 100 in the east and central regions on 7–8 October 2023), and B2 by Malaysia's Ministry of Health advice to reduce outdoor physical activities, the environment minister's communication with the education and health ministries to temporarily stop outdoor activities, and Singapore's measures for preschools and advice to workplaces; NEA's standard band-linked health advisory (treated as routine, as in 2016) and the National Haze Action Plan's standing thresholds (as in 2025) are not counted, no school closure was found, and DOE's hedged, whole-year description of 2023's haze as 'relatively severe' is not counted for B3.

attribution.note: Governments publicly disagreed about where the smoke came from. Indonesia's environment ministry denied that haze from fires in Indonesia was reaching Malaysia, and later said it had detected no transboundary haze episodes in 2023; Malaysia said fires in Indonesia were causing the pollution. ASMC, Meteorological Service Singapore (for Singapore) and a peer-reviewed study quoted in this entry describe the haze as transboundary; Malaysia's Department of Environment does so in its 2023 report, a position Indonesia's ministry disputed. Each government's position is recorded and labelled an allegation; this record does not decide between them.

confidence.rationale: Medium (AI-assigned, awaiting human review; confidence describes the evidence, not the severity of the episode). Singapore: NEA's release of 7 October 2023 and its hourly 24-hour PSI data, Meteorological Service Singapore's 2023 annual climate assessment and the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment's written parliamentary reply of 7 November 2023 together record Unhealthy 24-hour PSI on 7–8 October 2023, with a peak of 123 in the east; ASMC's October 2023 review, a peer-reviewed study in Geophysical Research Letters (2024; abstract only) and a peer-reviewed study in BMJ Open (2025), which defines a 7–19 October haze period, corroborate haze in Singapore in October, and AFP reported the readings the same day. Malaysia: DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2023 gives the period (1 September–20 October), the areas affected, the peak API of 174 at Batu Pahat and the two-day unhealthy spells at Cheras and Nilai; ASMC reports lighter smoke haze over parts of Peninsular Malaysia in early October and transboundary smoke haze drifting into western Sarawak on some days in September. The rating is medium because important Malaysian elements rest on a single source or on news reports only, or are incomplete: the peak reading rests on DOE's report alone and has no date, hour or averaging period; every dated Malaysian reading (2 October 2023) rests on news reports citing DOE (Malay Mail; Reuters), as DOE's own statement was not found; and the same report says air quality in Sarawak and several other regions was 'good' to 'moderate' at all times in 2023 while listing unhealthy days at stations there, an inconsistency that remains unresolved. Indonesia's environment ministry disputed that haze from Indonesia reached Malaysia; this concerns the origin of the haze, which the entry attributes to each party, not whether haze affected Malaysia and Singapore, and it is recorded, not resolved.

contradictions.text: Whether smoke haze from fires in Indonesia reached Malaysia: Reuters reported on 3 October 2023 that Malaysia had said the previous week that fires in Indonesia were causing the pollution. Indonesia's environment ministry said on 2 October 2023, citing BMKG and ASMC imagery for 28–30 September 2023, that no transboundary haze was reaching Malaysia, and an Indonesian ministry official later said no transboundary haze episodes were detected in 2023 (Mongabay, January 2024). Malaysia's environment minister said on 3 October that data indicated burning outside the country, and DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2023 describes the haze episodes of 1 September–20 October 2023 as transboundary. ASMC's reviews describe transboundary smoke haze drifting from West Kalimantan into western Sarawak on some days in September 2023 (days not given) and lighter smoke haze affecting parts of Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore in early October 2023 (origin not stated in that passage). The statements partly refer to different dates and places. Not resolved here.

Two CAMS articles on Indonesia's 2023 fire season differ. On October, the article of 6 November 2023 says that for Indonesia as a whole 'in October FRP values were generally above average for the month', while the article of 12 December 2023 says that 'in October FRP values were slightly above average on some days, but average overall for the month'. On the preceding seasons, the first says Indonesia had had 'four years of comparatively quiet fire seasons' and the second 'three years'. Not resolved here.

evidenceGaps: Department of Environment Malaysia: the DOE statements of late September and 2 October 2023 were not found on DOE's website; the Malaysian daily API readings and Action Plan measures here come from Malay Mail, Bernama, Reuters and The Diplomat. APIMS historical hourly data for September–October 2023 were not obtained.

The date, hour and averaging basis of DOE's highest 2023 haze-period reading (API 174 at Batu Pahat) and the dates of the two-day unhealthy spells at Cheras and Nilai are not stated in the Environmental Quality Report 2023.

School closures: no report of a school closure in Malaysia or Singapore due to haze in 2023 was found. The Diplomat's headline ('Malaysia could shut schools') refers to the closure threshold of API 200; the highest API reading DOE reported for the 2023 haze period (174) was below it (AI observation). Singapore's agencies said on 7 October 2023 that schools remained open.

Cloud seeding: Malaysian officials set conditions for cloud seeding (API above 150 for more than 24 hours); no source opened says whether any cloud seeding was carried out in Malaysia in September–October 2023.

Healthcare-use records (for example Malaysia's Ministry of Health sentinel-clinic data, which the ministry said it would monitor, or Singapore's polyclinic attendances) for September–October 2023 were not found.

The Geophysical Research Letters paper (doi 10.1029/2023GL107667) returned HTTP 403 from the publisher; only its abstract (from the Crossref record) was read. The UNDRR 'Indonesia wildfires 2023 forensic analysis' returned HTTP 403 in an earlier search during this research.

Impacts in Indonesia: Tempo English reports on distance learning in Jambi and on acute respiratory infection (ISPA) cases in Banjarmasin were blocked (Cloudflare HTTP 403). Indonesian health records were read only as reported by Medcom.id (South Sumatra's provincial health office); no Indonesian health ministry or provincial dataset was opened. Indonesia's environment ministry statement of 2 October 2023 was read only as reported by Bernama/Antara and The Diplomat.

No economic cost estimate for the 2023 episode was found. The web-search budget for this research was exhausted, so further searches (Malaysian Education Ministry circulars, Hansard of 9 October 2023, ASEAN statements) could not be run.

Enforcement: two cited statements mention administrative enforcement connected with fires (Indonesia's environment ministry statement of 2 October 2023, as reported by Bernama/Antara, and Malaysia's ministry statement of 19 October 2023 on the Kota Tinggi fire). They were not compiled as legal developments, their outcomes were not researched, and no court finding connected with the 2023 fires was looked for. A warning, a sealing order or a planned enforcement action is not a finding of responsibility.
unresolvedQuestions: On which dates and hours did DOE record its 2023 haze-period peak (API 174 at Batu Pahat) and the two-day unhealthy spells at Cheras and Nilai?

How much of Malaysia's unhealthy air in September–October 2023 came from transboundary smoke rather than local fires, ozone and traffic, all of which DOE's annual report mentions? No source opened quantifies this. DOE said on 2 October 2023 that a regional meteorological agency had detected nearly 250 hotspots on Sumatra and in Indonesia's part of Kalimantan, with none in Malaysia (Reuters); Malaysia's environment minister said on 3 October 2023 that there had been no forest burning in Malaysia of late except in May, which he said caused localised haze (Bernama); and the ministry's statement of 19 October 2023 reported a 32-hectare peat fire in Kota Tinggi, Johor.

How do DOE's statements about Sarawak in its Environmental Quality Report 2023 fit together, and on which dates were Sarawak's unhealthy days recorded? The report lists Sarawak among the areas whose air quality deteriorated during what it describes as transboundary haze episodes from 1 September to 20 October 2023 (PDF p.16); attributes the unhealthy API days at five Sarawak stations to PM2.5 from forest and bush fires in the local area (PDF pp.22–23); and says that air quality in Sabah, the Federal Territory of Labuan and Sarawak was 'good' to 'moderate' at all times in 2023 (PDF p.22), wording it also uses for regions of Peninsular Malaysia where it lists unhealthy days (PDF pp.18–21). ASMC observed transboundary haze drifting from West Kalimantan into western Sarawak on 28 July 2023 and on some days in September 2023. (AI note: the transboundary listing and the local-fire attribution need not conflict if transboundary haze raised readings without reaching the unhealthy band, but no source opened says so.)

What did ASMC's imagery for 28–30 September 2023 show about smoke crossing into Malaysia, given that Indonesia's ministry cited ASMC for its denial while ASMC's reviews describe transboundary smoke haze drifting into western Sarawak on some days in September and lighter smoke haze affecting parts of Peninsular Malaysia in early October?
Was any cloud seeding carried out in Malaysia during the episode, and did any Malaysian school close because of haze in 2023?
What does the full GRL 2024 study conclude about the share of fire emissions in the October 2023 haze in Singapore and southern Peninsular Malaysia?
Was the South Sumatra figure of 31,816 ISPA cases for the third week of October 2023 a weekly count or a running total, and how did it compare with the same weeks of earlier years?

aftermath.note: An intergovernmental retrospective, read from an Internet Archive copy of the ASEAN Secretariat's media release. It describes moderate transboundary smoke haze observed to affect parts of the southern ASEAN region on a few days in July 2025; it does not name the countries affected and does not call the episode major or severe. Not tagged for criterion A because it does not describe haze in Malaysia or Singapore.

selection.note: Criterion A is met by official and intergovernmental sources: DOE's haze status statements of 19–25 July 2025 describe the haze in Peninsular Malaysia, and on 25 July at Kuching, as smoke haze moving into the country (19–20 July) or as transboundary haze (from 21 July), and ASMC's 19 July alert and July 2025 review describe transboundary smoke haze drifting from central Sumatra into Peninsular Malaysia and from western Kalimantan into Sarawak; AP's report of an Indonesian forecaster is supporting news evidence only, and the ASEAN ministers' release of 3 September 2025 does not name Malaysia. B1 is met: DOE reported API readings above 100 at five areas at 3pm on 20 July and at nine areas at 3pm on 21 July 2025 (it linked two of the nine to a landfill fire in Kuantan), and at further areas on 19, 24 and 25 July. B2 is not evidenced: DOE's statements restate the National Haze Action Plan's standing thresholds (stopping activities outside classrooms above an API of 100 and closing schools, kindergartens and nurseries above 200), and no source reports that these measures were taken during the episode; the DOE advice to limit outdoor activities reported by Bernama comes from an 'earlier statement' that Bernama does not date and that was not found among DOE's statements, so it cannot be dated; and no emergency declaration or school closure in Malaysia or Singapore was found (Riau's emergency response status was declared in Indonesia and does not count towards B2). B3 is not met: the ASEAN release describes moderate transboundary smoke haze on a few days in July 2025, and no peer-reviewed study or official retrospective calling the episode major or severe was found.

attribution.note: ASMC describes transboundary smoke haze drifting from central Sumatra into Peninsular Malaysia and from western Kalimantan into Sarawak; Malaysia's Department of Environment linked the decline in air quality to smoke haze moving into the country, which it described from 21 July as transboundary haze. No public dispute between governments about where the smoke came from was found in the sources opened. The Department of Environment also attributed some unhealthy readings to a local landfill fire, and one of its statements is inconsistent about the source of the smoke at Kuching (see Unresolved questions).

confidence.rationale: AI-assigned, awaiting human review; it describes the evidence, not the severity of the episode. The core account (smoke haze that DOE and ASMC described as transboundary affected parts of Peninsular Malaysia from 19 July 2025 and, according to DOE, Kuching on 25 July) rests on DOE's haze status statements of 19, 20, 21, 24 and 25 July 2025, which give its 3pm API readings and its attribution, and on ASMC's alert of 19 July and its July 2025 review, whose satellite observations of smoke drifting from central Sumatra into Peninsular Malaysia and from western Kalimantan into Sarawak corroborate DOE's account independently of DOE's readings. Key figures are quoted from DOE's statements; Bernama, the New Straits Times and Malay Mail relay DOE and are not independent of it. No material conflict about the core account was found. The rating is medium because conditions in the medium definition hold: the peak readings are incomplete (DOE's statements give 3pm snapshots only, and its hourly APIMS data were not opened); the period is incomplete (no source documents when the haze in Malaysia ended: DOE's last haze status statement found is dated 25 July, while ASMC observed transboundary plumes drifting into Sarawak on 29 July); the impacts reported in Riau rest on news reports only; and a minor conflict remains between DOE's and ASMC's descriptions of the wind direction (see 'Where sources disagree'). The source of the smoke at Kuching on 25 July is also unresolved, no impacts on people in Malaysia were documented, and Singapore's status rests on NEA's 2026 statement and the AI agent's computation from NEA data.

contradictions.text: Wind direction: DOE's 19, 20 and 21 July 2025 statements, relaying ASMC's regional haze maps, describe smoke haze or wind 'blowing towards the south-west' ('bertiup ke arah barat daya'), whereas ASMC's 19 July alert expected prevailing winds from the south-east or south-west and its July review shows smoke drifting north-eastwards from central Sumatra into Peninsular Malaysia. The AI agent suspects that DOE's wording renders 'south-westerly' (blowing from the south-west), but this is not verified.

Penalty for open burning cited by DOE during the episode: its 19 July 2025 statement says a person convicted of open burning under section 29A of the Environmental Quality Act 1974 may be fined not more than RM500,000 and that a maximum compound of RM2,000 may be imposed, while its 20 and 21 July 2025 statements (and later ones) give a fine of up to RM1,000,000 and a compound of up to 50% of the maximum fine. The text of the Environmental Quality (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1712) settles this in favour of the later statements: its new section 29A(5) sets a fine of not less than RM25,000 and not exceeding RM1,000,000, and its amended section 45(1) caps the compound for a compoundable offence at 50% of the maximum fine; Malaysia's environment ministry states that the amendments came into force on 7 July 2024. DOE's 19 July figures match sections 29A(2) and 45(1) of the Act as reprinted with amendments up to 1 January 2006. The amendment is also recorded as a Malaysia milestone (July 2024).

evidenceGaps: Ministry of Health Malaysia: no July 2025 haze advisory or press statement could be opened (moh.gov.my returned HTTP 403); the web-search budget for this research ran out after five searches, so no other route was tried.

APIMS (DOE's Air Pollutant Index Management System) hourly data for 19–31 July 2025 were not opened; DOE's statements give 3pm snapshots only, so peak hourly values and the total number of stations above 100 at any hour are unknown.

DOE's media page lists no haze status statement for 22–23 July or after 25 July 2025. Readings for 26–31 July were not established from official sources; a news report (Malay Mail, from The Borneo Post, 31 July 2025) relayed an unhealthy APIMS reading at Mukah, Sarawak, with no stated cause, so it is not attributed to this episode and is not cited.

No record was found of school closures, suspension of outdoor school activities, activation of disaster management committees by Malaysia's National Disaster Management Agency (NADMA) or cloud seeding in Malaysia during the episode; only the National Haze Action Plan's standing thresholds were found.

No record was found of a specific Malaysia–Indonesia or Singapore–Indonesia exchange about the July 2025 haze; the first searches stopped when the web-search budget for this research ran out, and three later web searches found no statement by Indonesia's government, dated to this episode, disputing DOE's or ASMC's description of the haze in Malaysia as transboundary.

Indonesia: the Ministry of Health page on medical aid for the Riau fire emergency was blocked (HTTP 403; its Internet Archive copy returned HTTP 429); no counts of health-care visits, school closures or flight disruptions in Riau were found, and no statement by Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) was opened. Three further web searches during this research (in Indonesian and English) for July 2025 records of acute respiratory infection cases, school closures and air-quality (ISPU) readings in Riau found none dated to the episode.
DOE's Environmental Quality Report 2025 requires login and was not read; no peer-reviewed study of the July 2025 episode was found (the web-search budget for this research ran out early).
NOAA's Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), now NOAA's official ENSO index, was not opened for 2025; Singapore's computed PSI maximum lacks 03:00–13:00 on 20 July 2025 and the 00:00 hour of each day.

Singapore: one web search during this research found no NEA or Meteorological Service Singapore haze update for July 2025, and their own archives were not opened, so whether Singapore had hazy conditions below the Unhealthy range during the episode is not documented here.
unresolvedQuestions: DOE's statement of 25 July 2025 attributes Kuching's unhealthy reading to transboundary haze and says that no major fire had occurred that could cause local haze, but it relays ASMC's regional haze map of that day as showing moderate smoke plumes from hotspots in Sarawak, and ASMC's July review shows smoke plumes from hotspots in Sarawak as well as transboundary plumes from western Kalimantan on 29 July 2025. How much did smoke from fires in Sarawak, as opposed to transboundary smoke from western Kalimantan, contribute to Kuching's unhealthy reading on 25 July 2025?
What were the peak hourly API values, and how many Malaysian stations exceeded an API of 100 at any hour, during 19–25 July 2025?
Did any Malaysian schools stop outdoor activities under the National Haze Action Plan threshold (API above 100) during the episode?
When did transboundary smoke stop affecting Malaysia: DOE's last haze status statement found is dated 25 July 2025, but ASMC observed transboundary plumes drifting into Sarawak on 29 July 2025?

regionalContext.text: ASMC's Alert Level 3 notice of 26 August 2026 said widespread moderate to dense smoke haze was emanating from clusters of hotspots in Kalimantan, with moderate to dense transboundary haze drifting northwards from the hotspot clusters in West Kalimantan, and that, with El Niño conditions predicted to strengthen, the hotspot and smoke haze situation could escalate further.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: 26 Aug 2026 Level 3 Activation of Alert Level 3 for the Southern ASEAN Region

Based on satellite surveillance, widespread moderate to dense smoke haze was observed to emanate from clusters of hotspots detected in Kalimantan, with moderate to dense transboundary haze observed to drift northwards from the hotspot clusters in West Kalimantan.

Coupled with El Niño conditions that are predicted to strengthen over the coming months, the hotspot and smoke haze situation could escalate further, thereby increasing the risk of severe transboundary haze occurrence in the southern ASEAN region.

regionalContext.note: Hotspots are satellite detections of possible fires; they do not establish land ownership, who started a fire or legal responsibility.

regionalContext.text: ASMC also observed moderate to dense smoke plumes emanating from hotspots in the western parts of Peninsular Malaysia during August 2026, as well as from other parts of Kalimantan, central and southern Sumatra and eastern Java.
regionalContext.label: analysis

refs.quote: Moderate to dense smoke plumes were also observed to emanate from hotspots detected in other parts of Kalimantan, the central and southern parts of Sumatra, the western parts of Peninsular Malaysia and the eastern parts of Java (Figures 6, 7, 8 and 9).

regionalContext.note: ASMC's description of satellite imagery, so labelled analysis. ASMC observed smoke from hotspots in Malaysia as well as in Indonesia; the review does not quantify how much each source contributed to haze in Malaysia or Singapore.

regionalContext.text: ASMC assessed strong El Niño conditions in August 2026, with the relative Niño3.4 index at 1.7°C for August, and reported signs of a positive Indian Ocean Dipole developing, although positive IOD conditions had yet to become established.

diplomaticResponse.text: BNPB said on 23 August 2026 that Indonesia understood concerns over possible transboundary haze and was deploying 'very substantial resources' to control the fires; it urged neighbouring countries such as Malaysia and Singapore 'to avoid blaming one another' over the impact of smoke from fires in Kalimantan, saying countries should work together rather than make 'unfounded claims about the source of the smoke', and that smoke movement should also be assessed using meteorological data, satellite imagery and field monitoring.
diplomaticResponse.label: allegation

refs.quote: Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) on Sunday urged neighbouring countries such as Malaysia and Singapore to avoid blaming one another over the impact of smoke from forest and land fires in Kalimantan.
said Indonesia understood concerns over possible transboundary haze and stressed that Indonesia had deployed significant resources to control the fires
“What we need to convey is that Indonesia is currently making optimal efforts and deploying very substantial resources to control forest and land fires,”
Forest and land fires do not recognise administrative or national borders, he said, adding that countries should work together rather than make unfounded claims about the source of the smoke.
Smoke movement should also be assessed using meteorological data, including wind direction and speed, atmospheric conditions, satellite imagery, and field monitoring, he said.

diplomaticResponse.note: Antara article dated 23 August 2026 (a Sunday). Labelled allegation: BNPB's position on blame, on claims about the source of the smoke and on the response to the fires. BNPB did not say which claims or statements it meant; no earlier statement by the Malaysian or Singaporean government faulting Indonesia, and no protest note, was found in the sources opened. On the source of the smoke, ASMC's satellite observations and the assessments of NEA and Malaysian agencies are recorded here as analysis, and BNPB itself was reported (The Jakarta Post) to have confirmed transboundary haze from West Kalimantan into Malaysian Borneo in early August. On Indonesia's efforts, see the Malaysian Foreign Minister's remarks reported on 13 October below.

legalDevelopments.text: Indonesia's Environment Ministry announced in early September 2026 that civil servant investigators were on the ground conducting field verification and sealing off sites affected by forest and land fires.
legalDevelopments.label: fact

refs.quote: Civil Servant Investigators (PPNS) are currently on the ground conducting field verifications and sealing off affected sites.

legalDevelopments.note: An investigative step announced during the episode: field verification and sealing of sites are not findings of liability or wrongdoing, and no party is named. Indonesian enforcement in 2026, with numbers, is recorded among Indonesia's milestones, not duplicated here.

selection.note: Criterion A is met: ASMC (its August 2026 review and its regional haze situation current at the research date), NEA (advisories of 4 September and 14 October), Singapore's Ministry of Health and CAMS describe the haze in Malaysia or Singapore as transboundary or as smoke from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan; news reports of statements by Malaysia's DOE and Meteorological Department and by BNPB and Indonesia's Foreign Ministry say the same; they are tagged too, but criterion A does not depend on them. B1 is met by NEA's 24-hr PSI above 100 on several days from 4 September (all five regions on 15 September; the west above 200 from 9pm on 14 October; 28 calendar days with at least one region above 100 in the AI agent's scan of NEA's provisional real-time data) and by APIMS readings above 100 at many Malaysian stations, as reported in the news. B2 is met by the Serian haze emergency (4–7 September), school closures in Sarawak and Peninsular Malaysia, NADMA's advice of 14 October to reduce outdoor activity, and the reminder to Singapore's community care providers to replace outdoor activities with indoor ones; NEA's standard health advisory for the forecast 24-hour PSI band is treated as routine and not counted, as in 2016. B3 is not met: the episode was still under way at the research date (15 October 2026), and no peer-reviewed study or official retrospective was found.

attribution.note: Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said on 23 August 2026 that countries should work together rather than make 'unfounded claims about the source of the smoke', without saying which claims it meant (recorded as an allegation, under Response between governments). ASMC, Singapore's National Environment Agency and Malaysia's Meteorological Department describe smoke from fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra crossing into neighbouring countries; BNPB was reported by The Jakarta Post to have confirmed transboundary haze from West Kalimantan into Malaysian Borneo; and Indonesia's President is reported as saying that the fires were in Indonesia and their impact was felt by its neighbours. This record does not decide between these positions. Malaysia's Meteorological Department also described local haze in some areas.

confidence.rationale: AI-assigned, awaiting human review; medium under the pre-registered definitions. Evidence: the core account (haze that ASMC, NEA and Singapore's Ministry of Health describe as transboundary, affecting Sarawak from August 2026 and Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore mainly from September, and continuing at the research date) rests on intergovernmental and government sources (ASMC's alerts, August review and regional haze situation; NEA's advisories and real-time PSI data; Singapore's Ministry of Health; NADMA's statements) and a scientific agency (CAMS), corroborated by independent news reports (Bernama, RTM, The Star, Malay Mail, FMT, The Edge, Antara, AFP, AP, Al Jazeera); Singapore's key figures are quoted from NEA. It is medium because conditions in the MEDIUM definition hold. Important Malaysian elements rest on news reports only: the API readings (including Serian's 521), the station counts, the Serian emergency and the school closures were read in news reports of APIMS data and of statements by the Prime Minister's Office, DOE, Sarawak's disaster management committee and education authorities, not at source (see Evidence not found). Minor conflicts remain over how many schools closed in the Serian area on 12 August (108, 107 or six) and which places the closures of 9 October covered (see Where sources disagree). The record is incomplete: the episode was ongoing at the research date, so its end and final peaks are unknown, and Singapore's September–October readings rest on NEA's provisional real-time data. BNPB's call of 23 August to avoid 'unfounded claims about the source of the smoke', which did not say which claims it meant, is recorded as an allegation under Response between governments; Indonesia's Foreign Ministry was reported (Antara) as saying that smoke had reached Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore by 5 September.

contradictions.text: Sarawak school closures announced on 12 August 2026: The Edge, reporting the Sarawak State Disaster Management Committee's statement, gives 108 schools in the Serian area; The Star (13 August), reporting the same statement, gives 107, and RTM (17 August) reports that all 107 schools under the Serian district education office, closed since the previous Thursday (13 August), reopened that day; Eco-Business (19 August, a Mongabay report) says six schools in Sarawak, in a passage about Tebedu, switched to online classes. The scopes may differ (Tebedu versus the wider Serian area). The Sarawak government's own news page (UKAS) could not be opened. Not resolved.

Scope of Malaysian school closures on 9 October 2026: Malay Mail says all schools in Selangor, Melaka and Negeri Sembilan were closed; Al Jazeera says schools were ordered to close across Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya, Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang and Selangor, affecting roughly two million students. The difference may reflect whole-state versus district closures; no official consolidated list was found. Not resolved.

Status of Malaysia's offer of firefighting help: detikNews (18 September 2026) reports Indonesia's President welcoming the offer; CNN Indonesia (12 October) reports Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister saying Malaysia was still awaiting Indonesia's response; Antara (12 October) reports Indonesia's coordinating minister for political and security affairs saying the offer had not yet been discussed. This may reflect a welcome in principle without operational acceptance. Not resolved.

evidenceGaps: No NEA haze update dated 15 October 2026 existed when NEA's news feed (nea.gov.sg/rss/news_update) was read at about 04:00 SGT on 15 October; NEA's validated historical 24-hr PSI dataset on data.gov.sg ended at 31 August 2026, so September–October values rely on NEA advisories and its provisional real-time API.

Malaysia's DOE media-statements page (re-read 15 October 2026) lists no 2026 haze statements (latest July 2026), and the APIMS portal is JavaScript-only; Malaysian API readings, the emergency and school-closure figures were taken from news reports (Bernama, RTM, The Star, Malay Mail, FMT, The Edge) of APIMS data and of PMO, DOE, state-committee and education-department statements.

The Prime Minister's Office statements on the Serian emergency (4 and 7 September 2026) were not opened on pmo.gov.my; the Sarawak government's UKAS news page on the August closures failed (redirect loop) and has no archive copy; Reuters reports (HTTP 401) could not be read.

Ministry of Health Malaysia and Indonesia's Ministry of Health websites could not be read (moh.gov.my returned HTTP 403 earlier during this research; kemkes.go.id was blocked by Cloudflare, with no archive copy), so health-utilisation figures come from news reports of ministry statements (Bernama via Malay Mail and Malaysiakini; Katadata; Antara); the Indonesian cumulative counts have different or unstated start dates and areas.
No consolidated official count of Malaysian schools or pupils affected by the 9–14 October closures was found, and the school position on 15 October 2026 was not established.
ASMC had not yet published its review for September 2026; its daily situation panel is dynamic (the text cited was issued on 14 October 2026).

Indonesian provincial emergency statuses after 29 September (Central Kalimantan) and 20 September (West Kalimantan) were not checked; Indonesian school-closure totals come from AP citing government data, and a South China Morning Post report on remote learning (HTTP 403) could not be opened.

Impacts in Brunei and the Philippines are recorded here only for early September 2026; no peer-reviewed study, modelled health estimate or economic estimate for Malaysia or Singapore in 2026 was found.

No statement by the Malaysian or Singaporean government faulting Indonesia before BNPB's appeal of 23 August 2026, and no formal protest note, was found in the sources opened; the appeal does not say which statements it was responding to.

claims.text: The Act creates rebuttable presumptions: where an entity is proved or presumed to own or occupy land outside Singapore, and haze pollution in Singapore is proved or presumed to involve smoke from a fire on that land, the entity is presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have engaged in conduct, or in conduct condoning another's conduct, that caused or contributed to that haze pollution.

Read literally, A (Singapore) and B1 and B2 (Malaysia) are each met, and the period would qualify unless the rule excluding haze that sources describe as predominantly local in origin is read to cover it; that rule fits the haze in Malaysia but not the haze in Singapore. The two peer-reviewed studies refer to different source regions and are not in conflict: the source-attribution study (Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 2019) describes an atypical haze event in Singapore dominated by emissions from Peninsular Malaysia, while a study of the 2013 Sumatran fires (Scientific Reports, 2014) says February fires in Riau, such as those of early 2014, generally cause little transboundary haze. The AI agent did not treat that statement as describing the event as major or severe (B3), consistent with the June–October 2014 timeline entry; a human reviewer may judge otherwise.
